# Changelog

All notable changes to Talaria. Milestone labels refer to the historical plan, [`docs/history/PLAN-design-notes.md`](./docs/history/PLAN-design-notes.md).

## [Unreleased]

## 0.13.3 (2026-11-12)

- **New: a release is two merges. CI rolls the changelog, tags the promotion and writes the release notes.** When rc is verified and `changelog/` has entries, `promote.yml` opens the roll's pull request against rc (branch `release/roll`) at the version `scripts/release-version.mjs` works out:
  - the next patch by default;
  - more when an entry asks with a `<!-- bump: minor -->` line;
  - never below an RC already tagged past the newest stable;
  - or a `version` dispatch, which sticks until that roll merges.

  Once the roll merges and rc verifies again, it opens `promote: rc → main — vX.Y.Z`. That merge makes the new `tag-release.yml` tag main and dispatch `release.yml` at the tag, because a tag pushed with the workflow token starts no workflow. A re-run re-dispatches a tag that has no Release.

  Every promotion is a release now. `flow.yml`'s promotion gate fails while `changelog/` has entries, and `tag-release.yml` won't tag a main that carries any. An entry that lands after the roll extends the same section, and the roll refuses to open a second untagged section or to extend a tagged one.

  The GitHub Release body is no longer a stub. `scripts/release-notes.mjs` builds it from the section, plus a stable's RC sections:
  - the images, the newest Desktop release and the pull requests;
  - **Before you upgrade**: the migration count (from `MIGRATIONS` at the previous tag and this one) and each entry's new optional `Upgrade:` paragraph;
  - each entry's lead, then the full text.

  A dispatch at an older stable tag is refused rather than moving `latest` back. The roll and promotion pull requests need a `PROMOTION_TOKEN` (Contents and Pull requests write). Without one, the run prints the commands instead; the tag and the release need no token.

  Verified: `scripts/release-chain.test.mjs` (23 checks, in `bun run check`) covers:
  - the version arithmetic: RC floor, indented and malformed markers, overrides;
  - `--extend` and the roll's pending guard in a real git repo;
  - the notes' sections, RC folding, counts and body limit.

  Notes built for 0.13.2 from real history name #713, #716, #718, #719 and #720, with no migrations. The migration count reads 555 → 558 across v0.13.0 → v0.13.1, matching outcrop's 558 applied.

  Dry runs used the workflows' own step scripts against a scratch origin with `gh` stubbed:
  - promote: no token; a default minor roll; a 1.0.0 dispatch that survives the next run with no re-push; a late entry that extends 1.0.0 and holds the open promotion; the roll merged, giving a promotion titled v1.0.0 and the stale roll pull request closed;
  - the gate: entries present fails, a 404 passes, a 502 fails;
  - tag-release: a leftover entry is refused; a failed dispatch goes red, then is re-dispatched on the re-run; nothing happens once the Release exists;
  - `release.yml`'s resolve: dispatch at the newest tag, at an older one (refused), at an RC, and on a branch.

  Not run on GitHub itself until the next release.

- **The agent tools know the lanes: pr-watch, the judge and the cleanup sweep read `testing` beside `rc`, a `bun run gate:remote` run no longer passes for the pull request's own, and the judge's `must` fails the job again.**
  - `pr-watch` watches a pull request into `testing` the same way as one into `rc`. It names each lane: the `rc` → `main` and `promote/*` → `rc` promotions, the `backflow/*` → `testing` back-flow, and the `hotfix/`, `release/` and `sync/` heads into `rc`. Every lane but a feature is same-repository only. The conflict and red advice now follows the lane: a snapshot's conflict waits on the back-flow, and every other lane merges its own base. Red advice says CI is the compile; `bun run gate` is gone from it.
  - `pr-watch` ignores `CI offload` runs and any `ci/…` push run of the same sha. Before, an offload still in progress held a green pull request, and a cancelled one turned it red for good. When every failing check is also failing in the base branch's own push run, the verdict stays `red` and its first line says the red is inherited and not fixable from this branch.
  - `judge-pr` takes `--source`, the head branch (`GITHUB_HEAD_REF` in CI). It skips promotions, snapshots, back-flows and syncs, and the CHANGELOG.md checks on the `release/*` roll. The "`testing` is retired" must is gone. Two musts are new: `hotfix-adds-migration` (a hotfix into `rc` that adds a line inside `MIGRATIONS`) and `changelog-entry-rewritten` (a pull request into `testing` that edits or deletes an entry `origin/rc` already has). `gate:remote` and "CI: this PR's checks" count as verification.
  - `judge.yml` runs the judge under `set -euo pipefail`. Before, `| tee` masked exit 2, so a `must` never failed the job: promotion #722 reported 2 musts and passed. Both of those were false positives, and the lanes above skip them now. A fork's head is passed qualified, so it never matches a lane.
  - The cleanup sweep counts a worktree as possibly merged when it is 0 commits ahead of `origin/testing` as well as `origin/rc`. The pull request still decides.

  Verified: `bun run check` in the worktree, including `scripts/hooks/pr-watch.test.mjs` (70 checks), `scripts/judge-pr.test.mjs` (30) and `scripts/cleanup-sweep.test.mjs` (77).
  - The pr-watch tests cover every lane, an in-progress and a cancelled offload run, a pull request whose own head is named `ci/…` (its `pull_request` runs are kept), and end-to-end runs against a fake `gh`: an inherited red, a red that is partly the branch's own, a base whose jobs were only cancelled, and a base whose run cannot be read.
  - The judge tests run on a scratch repository: each lane skip, the roll, both new musts with their controls, and the claim forms.
  - The `MIGRATIONS` span finder matches the closing `]` in ten versions of `pg.ts` from across its history.
  - On real history: promotion #722's range, judged with `--source rc`, gives the lane line and no findings. Judged with any other source, it reproduces the two musts #722 reported (`targets-main`, `changelog-not-a-file`). Read-only against GitHub, `pr-watch --once` reads #723 as a green `feature` and #722 as `promotion:rc→main`.
  - actionlint 1.7.7 is clean on `judge.yml`. Its `pipefail` and `--source` are not yet run on GitHub; the first `judge (standards)` run of this pull request shows them.

- **CI is the compile: the rules and skills send compile and test to GitHub's runners, and keep only `bun run check` and cheap targeted runs on this machine.** Before, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, the skills and the PR template told every agent to run `bun run gate` before a push, and some docs still sent it to `verify`, `api:check` or a local gradle. Each of those compiles on the device, and the device is shared.
  - **The proof is CI.** Once a change is code-complete, the proof is its pull request's own checks; a draft is fine. `scripts/hooks/pr-watch.mjs` watches them in the harness's background mode. Before a pull request exists, `bun run gate:remote` runs, also in the background. Both are listed in AGENTS.md's commands table, the ship-a-change and dev-loop skills, and docs/AGENT-TOOLING.md ("Compiles run on CI").
  - **What runs locally.** `bun run check`, one `bunx vitest run <file>`, one `bun test <file>`, and `cargo fmt`. A heavy build runs only to reproduce one failure CI reported: `cargo test -p <crate> <test>`, or `bun run gate`. The workspace-cargo prohibition stands. `api:check`, `desktop:check` and `verify` are now marked CI's job, never local. That covers docs/RUST-MIGRATION.md, docs/MOBILE.md, docs/HARNESSES.md, docs/DESKTOP.md (`gate:remote --full` for macOS and Windows), docs/WORKTREES.md and docs/BRANCHES.md.
  - **Where run links go.** A changelog Verified line names the gate ("CI: this PR's checks", or `gate:remote`), never a run URL. A commit that only adds a link re-runs the whole battery. Run links go in the pull request body, and editing the body starts no compile. The PR template's checklist and Verified prompt say so.
  - The cleanup skill says what `gate:remote` leaves behind: nothing on green. A red ref stays until the daily prune or the sweep removes it, or `git push origin :refs/heads/ci/<name>` deletes it.

  Verified: `bun run check` in the worktree. Its `scoped-gate-anchors`, `pr-watch-anchors`, `cleanup-sweep-anchors` and `skills-index-drift` rules still hold, and every changed doc link resolves. `scripts/judge-pr.test.mjs` (30 checks) passes against the new PR template. AGENTS.md is 193 lines. `grep 'bun run verify\|api:check\|desktop:check'` over AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, the skills, HARNESSES, DESKTOP and BRANCHES finds only CI's-job, never-local or do-not-run contexts. CI: this PR's checks; `gate:remote` was used on this branch before the PR.

- **CI runs on a plain push to `ci/<branch>` — no pull request — and one planner decides what CI and `bun run gate` check.** A new workflow, `CI offload`, calls `ci.yml` for every push to `ci/**`, so an agent can have GitHub's runners compile and test a branch instead of its own machine. Its checks are named `offload / …`, so they can never satisfy or shadow a required check, and a daily job deletes `ci/**` refs whose tip is more than a day old.

  `scripts/surfaces.mjs` now holds the surface lists that lived twice, as bash in `ci.yml` and as a copy in `scripts/gate.mjs`. It also picks the run's mode and diff range:
  - **light**: a pull request into anything but rc or main, or a push to `ci/<branch>`. Linux jobs only; macOS, Windows, iOS and e2e are skipped.
  - **full**: a pull request into rc or main, a push to rc or main, a release, `ci/full/<branch>`, or the offload of a `hotfix/`, `release/`, `sync/`, `promote/` or `backflow/` branch.
  - **integration**: a push to `testing`, ready for when that branch returns.

  A pull request diffs its merge commit against the base tip it was built on, and the checkout now takes the event's own commit. Re-reading `refs/pull/N/merge` by name is how a changelog-only pull request once ran every job. A push to rc or main checks everything since that branch's last green run, so a cancelled or red run is covered by the next one. Pushes to long-lived branches queue instead of cancelling each other. Only those pushes write the Rust cache, which was over GitHub's 10 GB cap. A pull request is planned by its base's copy of the planner, so it cannot narrow its own CI. When the plan is missing a value, that surface runs.

  `bun run gate` diffs against the nearer of `origin/testing` and `origin/rc`. It exits 2 with `gate: base` or `gate: red — <command>` as its first stderr line. `bun run check` now finds every `scripts/*.test.mjs` itself. A new invariant, `ci-call-grants`, fails any workflow that calls `ci.yml` without granting `actions: read`. A caller like that dies at startup with no job run, as the September nightlies did.

  Verified: `scripts/surfaces.test.mjs` (66 checks, in `bun run check`) covers the glob semantics, every surface list, the gate's plan, base picking, the last-green lookup and every planning rule, against a fake git and a fake GitHub. The `ci-call-grants` check failed with both grants removed. `bun run gate --dry-run`, `node scripts/surfaces.mjs plan`, and actionlint on the three workflows. CI: this PR's checks and two offload probe runs.

- **Releases publish only promoted code, and the desktop updater key is reachable only from main.** `release.yml` refuses a stable `vX.Y.Z` whose commit is not on `main` and a `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` whose commit is not on `rc`, before CI starts. A tag cut on `testing` or a feature branch fails with `tag <t> points at <sha12>, which is not on <branch>`. The check fetches the two branches' commits and no files, so `resolve` still checks nothing out. The nightly and channel dispatches build the rc tip by name, as before.

  The updater signing key (`TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` and its password) and `OMAPAK_SUBMIT_TOKEN` move to a `desktop-release` environment that admits `main` only. `desktop-v*` tags are left out on purpose: anyone with write access can point a new tag at unreviewed code, and a dispatch at it would hold the key and could publish a signed update. `desktop-package.yml`'s linux, macOS and Windows builds name that environment only on `main`. Once the repository-level copies are gone, a dispatch from any other ref builds every installer unsigned. It waits on no environment, and it is how to exercise the workflow. `resolve` refuses a publish or a `release_tag` from such a ref before an hour of builds, and `attach` and `omapak` run on `main` only. `omapak-submit.yml` is now two jobs: `gate` decides, and only `submit` holds the environment. So a hand-published server `v*` release still skips quietly. Any other ref is refused with the dispatch from `main` to make, and that includes a `desktop-v*` release published by hand, whose run is at its tag.

  An edit to `desktop-package.yml` or `.github/actions/` reaching main no longer mints `desktop-vX.Y.0` and makes it Latest, and an edit to `mobile-package.yml` no longer mints `mobile-vX.Y.0`. Pull requests still build the mobile workflow's edits. Before this reaches main, an admin creates `desktop-release` with the one `main` branch policy and copies the secrets into it. If the environment does not exist, GitHub creates an unprotected one the first time a job names it. The repository-level copies go once a main build has signed through it. Until then, a job outside the environment still reads them.

  Verified: `scripts/release-provenance.test.mjs` (16 checks, in `bun run check`) runs the resolve step's own shell from `release.yml` against a local repository shaped like the real history. Stable tags on main and rc tags on rc publish, pushed or dispatched at the tag the way `tag-release.yml` hands a stable release off. Tags on a scratch branch, a stable tag on an rc-only commit, and an rc tag on main's promotion merge are refused. A malformed tag fails before any fetch, the schedule and channel dispatch skip the check, and an unreachable repository refuses. Pointing the check at the wrong branch failed two of the checks, and dropping the stable check failed seven, both dispatch checks among them. The same step, run against GitHub itself, passed `v0.13.2`, `v0.13.0` and `v0.1.0-rc.1` at their real commits and refused `v0.13.2` claimed at an unmerged branch tip. actionlint on the four workflows reports nothing beyond the six info-level shellcheck notes their base already had. `bun run check` passes.

- **`bun run gate:remote` compiles and tests a branch on GitHub before it has a pull request, and is red at the first failing job, with that job's log.** It pushes HEAD to `ci/<branch>` and watches the `CI offload` run, so an agent stops building on its own machine. `--full` pushes to `ci/full/<branch>` instead, and a `hotfix/`, `release/`, `sync/`, `promote/` or `backflow/` branch always goes there. Exit 0 prints one proof line naming the run, then deletes the ref. Exit 2 opens its verdict with a token line:
  - `dirty`: a tracked change is uncommitted. An untracked file only warns.
  - `base`: the branch is `main`, `rc` or `testing`.
  - `has-pr`: the branch already has an open pull request. That PR's checks are the proof, and `pr-watch` reads them.
  - `check` and `fmt`: before anything is pushed, it runs `bun run check`, then `cargo fmt --check` on the touched crates. That is rustfmt only, with no compile.
  - `no-run`: no `CI offload` run started for the commit.
  - `red`, `cancelled` and `timeout`: the run's verdict. `red` comes as soon as any job fails, with up to three log tails, while the other jobs still run.
  - `pending`: `--detach` was given.

  Only a run the ref did not already have counts. On a commit the ref already carries, the gate attaches to that commit's run instead of pushing again. `--watch <run-id>` resumes a run after a killed harness. `--rerun` re-runs a finished run's failed jobs and watches the new attempt, or with `--detach` starts it and exits `pending`. It refuses once the ref holds another commit, because a re-run would cancel that commit's run. A red ref is kept for both. The gate reads GitHub over REST with `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `gh auth token`, so a devbox needs no `gh`. The cleanup sweep now deletes a merged worktree's `ci/wt/<name>` and `ci/full/wt/<name>` when it stops the stack or removes the checkout. `.talaria-keep` is git-ignored, so a held worktree no longer reads as dirty.

  Verified: `bun run check`, including `scripts/hooks/remote-gate.test.mjs` (22 checks: the ref and mode, which run is the push's own, every verdict, the log trim, the poll schedule, the token order, and `dirty` and `base` driven in a scratch repository with no remote) and `scripts/cleanup-sweep.test.mjs` (79, with the offload refs of a merged stack and worktree deleted against stand-in git, a look-alike ref left alone, and an unreachable origin reported but not fatal). Live on this branch: a tracked edit gave `remote-gate: dirty` at once, with nothing pushed. A scratch commit with a failing cli test gave `remote-gate: red` 43 s after the start, `bun run check` included, while the api job and four others still ran. Its tail held the failing assertion with its source line, once passing-test lines were dropped. The scratch commit was then dropped. `--detach` printed the run and its resume command. `--watch <id> --timeout 0.5` attached to that run and ended `remote-gate: timeout`, naming the same command. `--watch` on another branch's superseded run read `cancelled`, named the newer run, and kept that ref. Before the review fixes, `bun run gate:remote` attached to that commit's run without pushing, waited out the api job, printed the proof line, exited 0 and deleted `ci/wt/remote-gate`. A second scratch commit broke the CI planner, pushed with `--no-check`. It gave `remote-gate: red` in 36 s, with the planner's error at the end of the log tail. `--rerun` then re-ran only that job, as attempt 2, which kept the invariants job's earlier pass and was red again. `--rerun --detach` first exited before GitHub showed the new attempt, so a `--watch` straight after read attempt 2's red back. Fixed, the same pair attached to attempt 4 and its new job. `--rerun --watch` on an older run of a ref that had moved on was refused, with no re-run started. The scratch ref was deleted and the commit dropped. Not yet exercised: a devbox. CI: this PR's checks.

- **New: every push to `testing` becomes an image the testing instance runs, and an agent can tell when its merge is live.** `testing-deploy.yml` builds the commit's dev-profile api package (`talaria-api:sha-<sha12>-dev`), then builds and smoke-tests the app image in a job that can only read packages. A separate job, which checks out nothing and runs no repository script, pushes `talaria:testing-<sha12>` and moves `:testing` to it while the commit is still testing's tip. Once the `TESTING_URL` variable is set, a last job waits for the instance to report the commit. On the VM, `docker/follow/talaria-follow.sh` (with its systemd timer) pins the checkout and the image to the revision `:testing` was built from, applies at most once every 10 minutes, and pauses while a hold file exists. `node scripts/hooks/testing-watch.mjs <pr|sha>` exits 0 once the instance runs a commit containing the merge, or 2 with `unmerged`, `red-deploy`, `down` or `timeout`. `promote-testing.yml` keeps the lane: a sticky `testing-red` issue, `sync: rc → testing` back-flow pull requests, a frozen `promote/testing-<sha12>` snapshot into rc on dispatch, a weekday readiness summary, and a daily full battery (macOS, Windows, iOS, e2e) on testing. It stays dormant until testing is brought up to rc. The api package now has one build cache per profile, so a dev nightly no longer evicts the release build's dependencies, and a dev build no longer overwrites a release `sha-<sha12>`. rc-deploy and testing-deploy queue instead of cancelling a run mid-build. A new invariant, `lane-write-jobs`, fails any job that a testing, `ci/**` or pull-request event can start, holds `packages: write` or `contents: write`, and runs a repository script or a local action. The VM's runbook is [docs/TESTING-INSTANCE.md](docs/TESTING-INSTANCE.md).

  Verified: `bun run check`. `scripts/hooks/testing-watch.test.mjs` (16 checks) covers each verdict and the argument, version and token rules. The CLI was run against a fake healthz: live on a later commit, `--json`, a timeout, and no token (exit 1). Against GitHub, open #723 gave `unmerged`. `lane-write-jobs` passes on the tree and caught each mutation: a repository script in `publish`, `build-smoke` raised to `packages: write`, `bun run` inside the called `api-package.yml`, `./scripts/` in ci-offload's prune, and `publish` renamed away. actionlint is clean on the four workflows, shellcheck on the follow script, and `systemd-analyze verify` on its units. Dry runs of the follow script against a scratch origin, with docker and bun shimmed, covered first apply, no change, the minimum gap, the hold, a revision not on testing, a missing label, local edits, a failed `deploy up` and its retry, a reset channel, a missing channel line and a missing `docker/.env` (refused: it holds the instance's generated secrets). A dry run of api-package's build step, with docker shimmed, checked dev, release and an unknown profile on main, rc and testing. Not run on GitHub until the cutover pushes testing.

- **The branch guards know `testing` again — as the integration lane — and a pull request can no longer reach rc on checks run against another base.** `scripts/flow-guard.mjs` stops refusing `testing`. A pull request into it passes, and a push to it must be a merge commit or a fast-forward to content rc or main already has. Deleting or rewriting it is refused, as for rc and main. `flow.yml` now checks pull requests into main, rc and testing. It refuses a title or body carrying `[skip ci]` and its variants, or a `skip-checks: true` trailer, because the merge commit carries both and the branch would move with no push checks run. It also refuses a pull request retargeted into rc or main until a push re-runs its checks, since CI does not re-run on a base change. Into main, the head must be this repository's `rc`, not a fork's branch with that name. The check is now named `pr target (flow)`, and the push check `branch push (flow)`. The promotion gate and `promote.yml` count only CI and rc-deploy runs made on rc as evidence; a pull request's run, a testing push or an offload of the same commit no longer counts. `promote.yml` wakes only for a push or dispatch run in this repository, and arms auto-merge when main's rulesets or its classic protection require the gate. Its roll and promotion bodies quote changelog leads and rc's commit subjects, so it now turns any bracketed skip marker in them into parentheses: its own pull requests never trip the new refusal, and their merges never skip rc's or main's push runs. `ci.yml` runs on pushes to `testing` in integration mode. A new invariant keeps the names `CI` and `rc-deploy` to their own workflow files, so no other workflow can stand in as the evidence.

  Verified: `scripts/flow-guard.test.mjs` (44 checks, in `bun run check`) runs every pull-request and push rule against a fake commit graph, the CLI's exit codes under bun and node, and a run from a symlinked path, which still blocks. Against the real history, `push refs/heads/testing 313a514d <rc tip>` exits 0, a delete exits 2, and a `[skip ci]` title into testing exits 2. Renaming `ci-offload.yml` to `CI` failed the new invariant. A promotion body quoting a commit subject with a skip marker is refused by the guard as written and passes once promote.yml's rewrite has run on it. actionlint on flow.yml, promote.yml and ci.yml found nothing new.

## 0.13.2 (2026-11-10)

- **New: every workbench harness stays current on its own. Oh My Pi and the harness's own bun now follow their upstream releases on every instance, the way the agent image follows Hermes stable.** #706 pinned Oh My Pi (`OMP_VERSION` 18.16.0) after its 28 Oct release raised its bun floor above the harness's bun and broke every `npx …@latest` job. That pin is now the bootstrap fallback, not a ceiling. A scheduled channel (`talaria-workbench-updates`, a step a minute) checks npm's version document for `@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent` and bun's GitHub releases every ~6 h. On every check it also re-reads the documents of what the instance runs, falls back to and pins. Each release soaks 24 h from the first check that saw it (`TALARIA_HARNESS_MIN_AGE_HOURS`), and its document is read again just before its smoke test. A release deprecated or withdrawn meanwhile is never run; a 404 counts as a withdrawal only the second time in a row. A release that jobs run and that upstream later deprecates is said to admins, and new jobs move off it. The candidate's `engines.bun` is checked against the harness's bun. When the candidate needs a newer bun, the bun moves first, and Oh My Pi follows. A candidate is installed beside what a workbench runs, by its own versioned paths only (a candidate bun under a mise data dir of its own, so a repo pinning `bun = "1.4"` never resolves an unverified bun mid-job), using #706's versioned dir, atomic symlink swap and `.retired` prune; the volume's shell `bun` is not touched until a provision promotes a verified pair. The candidate is then started, and the provisioning preflight runs through a job-shaped launcher (no model call). Only after that is it what new jobs run, with the pair before it kept as the fallback. A Pin made during the smoke test wins over the move it raced. The smoke test's install writes a `bun.lock`. That lockfile must name npm's `dist.integrity` for the tarball, and it is kept with the verified pair. Every later install of that pair, on any volume, a reinstall or a new department, is `--frozen-lockfile` from it. So no transitive dependency of a verified pair moves after its smoke test. A fresh instance smoke-tests the compiled pair first so its lockfile is kept too, and until then a provision installs it unfrozen. Every step that runs or downloads a release is bounded by `timeout`, with the install lock's fd closed for it. A release that hangs can never keep the volume's install lock. A step past its bound is a strike, retried 15 min later on another workbench when there is one, and held only on the second timeout in a row. A step killed with 137 (the OOM killer) is the host's. The whole run sits under an in-container bound, and a run the client gave up on is killed in the container. Only a release's own fault holds it: not there to install, a tarball that is not the documented one, a start that fails, two timeouts in a row, or a failed preflight. Admins are told when it is held, and jobs keep what they run. DNS, connection and TLS errors (bun's own `DNSResolveFailed`, `FailedToOpenSocket` and `ConnectionClosed` included), a full disk, a 5xx or 429 from npm or GitHub, docker and the install lock are the host's: retried with backoff, never held. Other running workbenches get the verified pair in the background, each with its own backoff. A volume that will not take the pair is recorded, and its provisions go straight to the previous pair, then the compiled one. A running job keeps the install it started on until it ends: a ready job is not re-provisioned onto a newer release, and the prune keeps any install a job's launcher names. It also never prunes the current or fallback install, and clears a stale `.retired` stamp from an install that is current again. Admins get **Manage → Workbench harnesses** and `GET/POST /api/workbench/harnesses`. They show the current, fallback, pinned, candidate and held versions per harness, and each workbench's pair, refusal or backoff. Check now reads every document at once under a 30 s bound. The actions are Check now, Update now, Pin (up or down; never a deprecated release), Unpin, Allow again and Reset. `TALARIA_HARNESS_NPM_REGISTRY` now reaches the workbench's `bun install` too. mise is not moved, because every repo toolchain's shims run through it; it is now the pinned release binary, checked against its SHA-256, instead of `curl https://mise.run | sh`, in the runtime, `prepare_env` and the workbench image, and a volume's older unpinned mise is replaced at its next provision. agent-browser rides the Hermes image's own lock. Also fixed in #706's runtime script: a version's first install no longer stamps itself retired; a release that will not start reports what it printed (omp's `Bun runtime must be >= …`); and the boot hook no longer pulls a provisioned volume's bun back to the compiled one. Not covered: bun's own binary is checked only as far as mise checks its GitHub download, and the per-volume bun download cache is trusted with a job's trust.

  Verified on this branch's stack (app :5304, api :5404) with a real Developer Agent container (Hermes v0.22.4) on a fresh volume. Every install ran inside it through the product's own runtime script, and fetched real packages from npm (through the stub's proxy) and bun from GitHub through mise. The version checks, and the install's registry, were a local stub on the docker bridge. It served the real npm and GitHub release documents, plus one doctored `engines.bun` and one fixture release whose start never returns, and proxied everything else to registry.npmjs.org. The soak was 0. The instance first smoke-tested the compiled pair (Oh My Pi 18.16.0 on bun 1.4.4) and kept its 41 kB `bun.lock` with npm's integrity. Pins then moved it down to Oh My Pi 18.13.2 on bun 1.3.14. A job slot laid out by the product's layout script and launcher held 18.13.2. Smoke tests never created or moved the volume's shell `bun`. With 18.16.0 advertised as needing only bun >=1.3.14, it installed and failed to start (`error: Bun runtime must be >= 1.4.4 (found v1.3.14)`). It was held, the admins got "Workbench harness update held: Oh My Pi 18.16.0", nothing was left installed, and the instance stayed on 18.13.2 on bun 1.3.14. The fixture release 18.99.0, whose start never returns, was stopped at its 60 s start bound ("did not finish starting within 60 s"), with the install lock free right after and no process of it left in the container. That rig run predates the two-strike rule, when one timeout held it and told the admins; now that first timeout is a strike and only a second one in a row holds, which the scripted-instance tests cover and the rig did not re-run. With the real documents and Allow again, the next step adopted bun 1.4.4 first ("Oh My Pi 18.16.0 needs bun >=1.4.4: bun 1.4.4 first"), and the step after adopted Oh My Pi 18.16.0. Each pair's lockfile was kept per pair, because bun 1.3.14 refuses bun 1.4.4's lockfile (`UnknownLockfileVersion`), which the rig surfaced. Throughout, the running job's launcher answered `omp/18.13.2` on bun 1.3.14 by path, while new jobs' launchers answered `omp/18.16.0` on bun 1.4.4. A stale, unheld install aged three days was pruned, and the current and fallback installs were kept. The panel rendered in headless Chromium with no page errors. Tests that fail without the change cover:
  - **the planner**: soak, Update now, held, deprecated, withdrawn, bun-first, a bun under the running floor, unreadable ranges, pins up and down, a deprecated pin, moving off a deprecated current, and smoke-testing the compiled pair once;
  - **the step on a scripted instance**: adopt, bun first, hold and notify once, host backoff, re-reading a candidate deprecated or withdrawn while it soaked, per-volume prewarm backoff, a refusing volume, a Pin made mid-smoke-test, and the lockfile and integrity kept with the pair;
  - **the classifier table**;
  - **npm range matching**;
  - **the real runtime script with stand-in buns**: a start and an install that hang are bounded, reported as a timeout (a strike, not a hold), and leave the lock free even with a child that escaped into its own session; a smoke test never moves the shell's `bun`; current and fallback installs are never pruned, and current loses a stale stamp; frozen installs are replaced on a lockfile mismatch and refused on an integrity mismatch; a running job keeps its release; a mirror reaches `bun install` with the trailing slash bun needs;
  - **provisioning's attempt order**: refused pair skipped, then fallback, then bootstrap;
  - **the boot hook's gate**.
  Round three, checked against real output: bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.4 in a throwaway Hermes v0.22.4 container, pointed at an unresolvable registry, a server that drops connections, a 500 and a 404. Their exact lines (`DNSResolveFailed`, `FailedToOpenSocket`, `ConnectionClosed` and `- 500`, each followed by `… failed to resolve`) seed the classifier's table and classify as the host's, while `- 404` and `No version matching` hold. In the same image's dash, the outer bound ended a 30 s script at 2 s (exit 124), and the backstop killed a marked run's whole process group. New tests cover: a repo pinning `bun = "1.4"` that keeps resolving the verified bun while a candidate is smoke-tested, with a stand-in mise resolving the newest installed match the way mise does; an unpinned mise replaced at a provision but not at a smoke test; a step killed with 137 counting as the host's; the kill script and the outer bound; a timeout held only the second time, on the other workbench; a single 404 healing; Check now answering within its bound against a slow upstream; and a two-tool move holding the bun when the bun failed. `bun run check` and `bun run gate` pass, with `-p` cargo only. Not verified: a real `start_job` on the new release (the job slot was laid out with the product's scripts, not by `start_job`), a provision promoting the shell `bun` live (it is tested with stand-ins), more than one workbench live, and the api reading registry.npmjs.org or api.github.com directly (the stub stood in; the installs did use them).

- **Fixed: loading /knowledge no longer crashes the whole view with `state_unsafe_mutation` when a tree shape is remembered in the tab.** With `talaria:knowledge-tree-state` present in sessionStorage, the tree store hydrated lazily on its first read, and on /knowledge that first read was KbDocRow's `$derived(kbTreeState.docExpanded(...))` or the sidebar's `{#if ... sectionExpanded(...)}` — reactive contexts where Svelte forbids writing state. The hydrate's `store.docs = saved.docs` write threw `state_unsafe_mutation: Updating state inside $derived(...) or a template expression is forbidden` and took the whole knowledgebase view down on arrival; with nothing stored, hydrate wrote nothing, so the crash only appeared for a tab that had opened or closed a branch earlier.
  - `kbTreeState.hydrate()` is now exposed on the store (idempotent, same latch as before) and Knowledge.svelte calls it once at the top of its instance script — a plain statement, before anything renders — so every later `$derived` and template read is a pure read. Nothing else changes: the lazy module-load latch stays, so tests can still install their sessionStorage before the first read.
  - Verified: the store suite (`ui/src/lib/knowledge-tree-state.test.ts`, now `// @vitest-environment runes`) passes 10 tests, including the new regression `THE $DERIVED CRASH`, which seeds the key, hydrates eagerly, and mounts a no-DOM harness of the row's reactive half (`$derived(kbTreeState.docExpanded(...))` evaluated inside `$effect.root`); without the eager hydrate that exact mount throws the live `state_unsafe_mutation`, with it the deriveds read back the restored `true`/`true`. `bunx svelte-check --tsconfig ./tsconfig.json`: 5752 files, 0 errors, 0 warnings.

- **Fixed: a design that a failed hire hands back into New agent no longer replaces what you are typing there, and describing or naming a new design no longer throws the returned one away.** A hire that fails before the agent exists hands its design back into New agent when New agent is empty. To the server, a New agent you have only typed into is empty: a description not yet sent, or a manual form with no name yet, is saved nowhere. So the returned design took the place of what you had typed on the modal's next read: the describe step jumped to the review step, or the form's fields were filled from the returned design. Now the modal keeps what you typed and says the design is back, with **Open it** and **Discard it**. If you carry on and describe the agent or name it, the returned design is set aside. It waits, as it already did behind any open design, and comes back when that one is hired or discarded. The server does this for a describe or a manual start over a returned design that nobody has edited or refined since (`set_aside` in `talaria-agent-design`). It is one Redis script, so the design is never in both places or in neither. A set-aside files no bell row: you set it aside from New agent, where its note already says why. Before, a manual start over it was refused as stale, and a describe replaced it. A refine of a returned design now ends its link to the failed hire, as a hand edit already did (#712). The hiring strip's **Retry** of that hire no longer spends the refined design on the old input. Two smaller fixes in the same flow:
  - **Discard design** with a returned design waiting no longer leaves an empty describe step while New agent holds the returned design. The next save used to write the typed form over it.
  - A **Create** clicked right after naming a manual form spends the design that the name's save created, whether that save was still waiting or already sent. It no longer leaves a copy of it in New agent.

  Verified: `bun run gate` passed. It ran `check`, svelte-check with 0 errors, 3163 ui tests, and fmt, clippy and the unit tests of `talaria-agent-design` and `talaria-routes-fleet`. `cargo test -p talaria-agent-design --lib -- --include-ignored`, run against this worktree's Postgres and Redis, passed 44 tests. Four are new:
  - two pure tests: a refine ends the link to the failed hire, and a returned design steps aside for a manual start and comes back unchanged;
  - `design_live_a_new_design_over_an_untouched_hand_back_sets_it_aside`, which covers a manual start and a describe over a returned design, that neither set-aside files a bell row, the return of that design when each is discarded, and the old rules once the design has been edited;
  - `design_live_a_hire_stopped_before_its_checkpoint_still_spends_the_design`, which pins #712's fix for a hire cancelled between creating the agent and checkpointing it.

  With the fixes reverted in place, they fail: the refine keeps the link, the manual start is refused as stale, a set-aside files a bell row, and the design comes back for an agent that exists. New ui unit tests cover which input counts as typed, when a returned design is offered rather than taken in, the shared sentence, and the read after a manual start. A test that a discard returns before the read that brings a waiting design back fails with the old `await`. A new e2e spec, `ui/e2e/agent-design-handback.spec.ts`, ran in headless Chromium against this worktree's stack. It uses a stand-in hire that fails before create and lets the open modal's own poll settle it. In the first chapter, a description being typed stays on the describe step, and **Open it** then shows the returned design with its reason. In the second, a manual form's Role and Department stay; naming it saves it while the returned design waits in the hires with its reason, and **Discard design** brings the returned design back. On rc's modal both chapters fail where the typing was replaced: the describe step was gone, and Role read "Scout". A third chapter holds a manual start's save on the wire and clicks **Create** before it answers. The hire it sends names the design that save made. With `flush` not waiting for a save already sent, the hire went out first and named none. Not covered: a design started in another tab still replaces unsaved typing in this one, as before.

- **Fixed:** A desktop release's omapak submission can be re-run for the same tag. The workflow says a re-run replaces the submit branch, but the push could only create one. The job's omapak checkout fetches `main` alone, so a branch an earlier attempt had pushed had no remote-tracking ref, and `--force-with-lease` read that as "expected absent" and refused the push as `stale info`. A submission that failed after its push, or a re-dispatched release, could not be retried without deleting the branch by hand. The job now fetches that branch before it pushes, so the lease compares against what is really there. A first attempt has no branch to fetch, and that failed fetch is allowed. Verified: under bash against a local bare remote set up the way the job's checkout is (a shallow `main` fetch, then the step's own fetch line pulled from the workflow file). A first attempt pushed. A re-run of the same tag replaced the branch, where the unpatched step had refused with `stale info`. The case came up while `desktop-v0.12.0` was submitted by hand (outcrop-labs/omapak#309), after its automated push got a 403 on the old `OMAPAK_SUBMIT_TOKEN`.

- **Fixed: the orphan sweep can no longer close a reply that this process is still writing. It now reads which replies this process holds after it reads the rows, not before.** The sweep built its one statement with this process's holds already read, and the statement read the rows only when it ran. A reply held between the two, and quiet past the lease by the time the statement ran, was in neither list. The sweep closed it as an orphan (`error`, "this reply stopped being saved partway through") while its writer still held it. The sweep now reads the quiet replies first, drops the ones this process holds, and closes the rest with the same guarded close. That is the order `reply_fate` and `active_streaming_assistant` already used. In production a reply is held as soon as it is made, while it is fresh, so the window needed a sweep to stall for most of the two-minute lease. It showed in CI instead: `orphan_live::lease::a_reply_this_process_writes_is_never_its_orphan` failed on #712 and on rc at d9023155 (`orphan_live.rs:196`, `left: None`), because a sibling test's sweep took the row the test held.

  Verified: reproduced on rc d3aedf96 against a worktree Postgres migrated the way CI's live-tests job migrates it. The old code failed 172 of 1,700 suite runs, one process at a time: the crate's ignored tests at CI's four threads failed 8 of 300 (7 of them CI's own `orphan_live.rs:196`); `orphan_live` alone failed 50 of 500 at four threads, 37 of 300 at eight, 44 of 300 pinned to two CPUs, and 33 of 300 at the default thread count. Every failure was a held reply closed to `error` by a sibling test's sweep. A new live test, `a_sweep_under_way_when_a_reply_is_held_leaves_it_alone`, forces that interleaving: the sweep's pool has one connection, checked out, so the sweep waits while the reply is held and goes quiet. It failed 20 of 20 runs on the old sweep and passes 50 of 50 with the fix. With the fix, the same schedules passed 3,600 of 3,600 runs (500 of them the crate's ignored tests at CI's four threads, on the commit as pushed). `bun run gate` passes, with `-p` cargo only. Not run: a booted api; `keep_replies`, which calls the sweep, is unchanged.

## 0.13.1 (2026-11-05)

- **Fixed: an agent design described in New agent now reaches the review step when the server finishes. Before, it said "Designing" until the page was reloaded.** There were two bugs. The design store started each new design's run on the plain object it had just built, not on the store's reactive copy. The modal and the roster's design row read the design straight away, so the run's answer, its error and its elapsed count were written where nothing could see them. The server answered in 20 to 30 seconds while the browser still showed "Designing" six minutes later on the owner's instance, and ten minutes later on another. The run now writes through the store, as a refine already did. Separately, the modal chose its step only once, when it opened, so a design that landed while it was open showed the describe form again rather than the review. It now moves to the review step when the design lands.

  Verified: in headless Chromium, against this branch's own stack (app :5304, the Rust api :5404) and a stand-in model that takes 20 or 60 seconds, the full New agent flow (describe, then Design agent) reached the review step with the drafted name at 20.7 s and 60.9 s. Closing the modal mid-design, then reopening it after the design landed, showed the review step; the roster row already read "Scout is designed and waiting for review". On the code before the fix, the same 20-second run still showed the "Designing" splash after 45 s. A new unit suite runs the design store under Svelte's client transform, which the existing suite did not use. Its four cases (ready, a derived reader moving to ready, the elapsed count and an error, each read while the run is out) fail on the old code and pass with the fix, and the existing store suite still passes. The transport is not the cause: through the real production server (`bun server-entry.ts`) proxying to a stand-in api that holds `POST /api/muse` like the Rust one, a 20-second and a 60-second answer both arrived whole, with status 200, at 20.0 s and 60.0 s.

- **Changed: in the web app, consecutive chat messages from one sender now read as one block, as in Slack. The first message shows the avatar, name and time. Later messages are continuation lines, and hovering one shows its own time in the avatar column.** This applies in Comms channels, DMs and ticket discussions, the thread panel, agent chat, and work, research and plan conversations. It is web only: the native mobile app's rows are unchanged. A new block starts when:
  - the sender changes;
  - more than five minutes pass between messages;
  - a message is stamped earlier than the one above it, so a header cannot move when a client-drawn row takes the server's time;
  - a new day starts;
  - an agent's scheduled run posts.

  In the thread panel, the root message always stands alone. The rules are one pure function (`ui/src/lib/message-groups.ts`). Each list maps its rows to that function's inputs through a small tested helper. A streaming message is grouped the same way it will be when it finishes, so arriving text never moves a header. Every message keeps its own `<time datetime>`, with the full date as its hover title. A continuation line shows a short "3:05" but gives a screen reader the header's "03:05 PM", plus a visually hidden author name, so assistive tech hears who sent each line and when even where the screen shows that only once. There is no API or storage change.

  Verified:
  - **Unit tests.**
    - The grouping rules: the threshold pinned at exactly five minutes; the same sender inside it; a sender change; a gap of exactly the threshold and one millisecond over; a negative gap and a clock-skew pair; a day boundary; a deleted message; a fresh row; a missing time.
    - Each surface's helper, through the real grouping function: the thread root standing alone; a scheduled run starting fresh; a row the client drew joining the viewer's own run; two people on a shared plan; status ignored while a turn streams and once it settles.
    - Seven deliberate mutations (thread rule `i === 0`, the scheduled-run rule removed, status read in either mapper, a negative gap grouping, a 10-minute threshold, no viewer fallback) each fail a test.
  - **Type check.** svelte-check reports 0 errors and 0 warnings.
  - **Browser run.** Headless Chromium, against a fresh worktree stack seeded with a channel, a DM and an agent conversation. Each had runs from two people and an agent, with a gap over the threshold. Checks covered:
    - grouped blocks, and the time shown on hover in the gutter;
    - reactions, including one added live on a continuation line;
    - a thread opened from a block, with grouped replies under the root;
    - a live edit of a continuation line;
    - an attachment and the `(edited)` mark inside a block;
    - two live sends: the first started a new block after the gap, and the second joined it;
    - deleting a block's first message, which moved the header to the next line;
    - the `interrupted` failed state, and an agent's tool-only turn inside a block.
  - **Themes and widths.** Both themes, at 1280 px and 760 px, with no horizontal scroll.
  - **Accessibility.** Playwright's accessibility snapshot of the channel, the DM and the agent chat lists a time with AM/PM for every line, and an author for every continuation line.

- **Changed: in Comms, one click on an agent opens a blank conversation with it, and every row in the sidebar has a menu of its own actions.** A click (or Enter) on an agent's name opens the fresh composer addressed to that agent and lists its recent threads under it. No thread is created until the first message is sent. The "new conversation" button stays, and a chevron over the avatar (or Right/Left) folds the threads away. Right-click, the Menu key, Shift+F10, a long-press on a touch screen, or the row's "…" button opens the row's menu, and the menu shows only what the person may do. A thread, channel, relay or DM offers Open, Copy link, Open in new tab (Open in browser on Talaria Desktop), Mark read or Mark unread, Pin, and for a channel or DM a Notifications submenu with levels and timed mutes. The owner also gets Rename, Archive and Delete. An agent offers New conversation, Copy link, View profile, Agent settings (for its managers), Pin, and Mute DMs for 1, 8 or 24 hours or until turned back on. Pins now live on the server (`/api/me/pins`), so they follow the person to every browser and to Talaria Desktop, and the rail's "Starred" section is now "Pinned". Stars already saved in a browser are moved to the server the first time that browser loads Comms. Three new endpoints back the rest: `POST /api/conversations/{id}/unread` and `POST /api/channels/{id}/unread` move the person's own read marker back one message, and `/api/me/agent-mutes` stores a timed mute of one agent's DMs: its replies in the person's chat threads with it and its own check-ins. While a mute holds, those rows still reach the bell, but quietly: no toast, push or mail. The agent's replies in a plan, a research run, a work session or a ticket are not its DMs and still ring. Mark unread only ever moves a marker back, never forward, so a click made against a stale count marks nothing read, and the badge then reads exactly 1; it is offered only where the person has a marker of their own, and it updates their other tabs and devices. Stars a browser could not upload (a server error, an expired session, no connection) stay in that browser and are tried again on the next load. A row's muted mark clears itself when the mute runs out. The menu itself (`ui/ContextMenu`) gained keyboard support: arrows, Home/End, typeahead, Right/Left through a submenu, and Esc or Tab to close, with focus returning to the row. It also gained a long-press on touch and placement that keeps the menu and its submenu inside the viewport. It also no longer removes a dialog that one of its items had just opened.

  Verified: `bun run gate` is green (svelte-check, the full vitest suite, and fmt, clippy and tests for the touched crates). In headless Chromium against this branch's own stack (app :5308, the Rust api :5408, its own Postgres), with two made-up people and two made-up agents. A click on Scribe opened `/comms/agent/scribe-documentation` with an empty composer and created no conversation row. Sending the first message created the row, and the thread appeared under Scribe. On a thread, Pin, Mark unread and Rename were each stored on the server and still showed after a reload. Copy link copied the thread's deep link, Open in new tab opened that link in a new tab, Archive retired the thread, and Delete asked first, then removed it. On #general, Mute for 1 hour, the Nothing level, Mark unread and Mark read each wrote the person's member row, and the muted mark showed after a reload. The DM menu had View profile and no Rename, Archive or Delete. A relay's owner could archive it. On Atlas, Mute DMs for 24 hours and Pin were stored, the profile drawer opened, and after a reload the row showed muted and the menu read Unpin. Using the keyboard only: Enter on an agent opened the blank composer. Shift+F10 opened the menu with Open focused. The arrows, typeahead, Right into the Notifications submenu and Esc back out all worked. A second Esc closed the menu and returned focus to the row. The Menu key opened the menu and Tab closed it. Tab reached the row's "…" button, and Enter on it opened the menu. Right and Left unfolded and folded an agent's threads. At 390×844 with touch: a tap on an agent opened the blank composer, a long-press opened the row menu, and the menu and its submenu stayed inside the screen. The "…" buttons showed without hover, and tapping one opened the menu. With a channel and an agent muted for 25 seconds, both muted marks cleared on their own at expiry without a reload, and a Mark unread in one tab showed its 1 in a second tab without a reload. Four new live-DB tests pass: pins in order, per person and capped; a muted agent's chat reply filed as `feed` while its plan reply still filed as `banner`, and a chat reply filed as `banner` again after unmuting; mark unread on a thread and on a channel, landing the badge on exactly 1 with a thread reply counted, and never moving a marker that was already behind; and the notify level on the channel listing. The existing agent-reply, conversation-read, unread-count and thread-read suites still pass. New unit suites cover the menu for each row kind and permission, the agent click, the menu keyboard and placement, and the controller's keyboard, focus and long-press handling.

- **Fixed: a Developer Agent's tickets progress in parallel instead of one at a time behind a single long build.** Talaria and Hermes already ran each ticket's session concurrently. The bottleneck was the agent's own container. Every ticket's clone, build, test suite and Oh My Pi run executes inside it, and a chassis seeded from an older template still gives it `cpus: ${AGENT_CPUS:-2}`, so up to 16 tickets' builds shared two cores. On the owner's instance three tickets ran on those two cores at a load average of 15, on a 32-core host. A cold `cargo build` ran past Hermes' 420-second tool ceiling, was killed and started again from cold, and two of the three tickets spent 40 minutes without reaching their harness. A developer agent's container now gets its own CPU settings instead of the chassis's. Its `cpus` is the host's cores less an eighth kept back for the platform, at least 2 (28 on a 32-core host). It stays a ceiling rather than no limit so that cargo, Go and the JVM, which size their parallelism from the cgroup, do not each assume the whole host. Its `cpu_shares` is 512, half the default, so sixteen builds yield to the app and Postgres under contention. Operators can override both in `fleet/.env` with `AGENT_WB_CPUS` (0 means no limit) and `AGENT_WB_CPU_SHARES`. A chassis `AGENT_CPUS` no longer reaches a developer agent. Its config now sets Hermes' `gateway.api_server.max_concurrent_runs` to the live-job cap plus 8, which is 24. Hermes' default of 10 counts chats and crons too, and would have refused the eleventh ticket's turn with a 429. A def that set its own larger cap, or no cap, keeps it. The Oh My Pi skill now says to run steps that may pass five minutes in the background and wait on them with `process_manage`, never through the foreground ceiling. Each job gets its own `--session-dir`. Applies to any repository a workbench runs. **Existing Developer Agents get this only when they are rolled, which recreates the container.** Upgrading Talaria re-renders their config, but a running container keeps its CPU limit and Hermes reads its run cap only at start. Roll each Developer Agent from Agents (the agent's Roll control, or Roll all), or with `POST /api/fleet/agents/{id}/control` and `{"action":"roll"}`.

  Verified: render unit tests cover the CPU block on outcrop's chassis (`cpus: ${AGENT_CPUS:-2}` and no `cpu_shares`) and on a quota/period chassis. They also cover the core-count default (32 → 28, 4 → 3, 2 → 2) and the run cap: a def's larger cap, or 0, negative or quoted no-cap, stands, and a smaller or junk value is raised. The whole `talaria-fleet-render` suite passes. `docker compose config` with the rendered lines gives `cpus: 4` for `AGENT_WB_CPUS=4` and drops `cpus` for `AGENT_WB_CPUS=0`. With no override, a created container reads `NanoCpus=28000000000`, `CpuShares=512`. Before this follow-up, the first version of the change dropped the quota outright. On a worktree stack whose chassis carries outcrop's `cpus: ${AGENT_CPUS:-2}`, the Developer Agent (Hermes v0.22.4) then came up with `NanoCpus=0` and `max_concurrent_runs: 24` in its config. Three tickets assigned to it were dispatched in the same second, and the agent ran their steps at the same time. Six live tickets then ran a stand-in build (two CPU-bound jobs each) every turn. Uncapped, each build took 8–11 s. After `docker update --cpus 2`, which is the quota the old render kept, the same builds took 46–55 s. Once the quota was lifted they were back to 8–10 s. All 335 of the agent's model calls were booked to their tickets.

- **Changed: an agent design is the server's, so a reload, a closed tab, another tab or a restart no longer loses it. New agent resumes where the design stands, and a design that finishes while you are away rings the bell.** "Describe it" used to run inside the browser: the page awaited the muse call itself and held the chat, the draft and the elapsed count in memory. Now a describe or a refine is an `agent-design` run on the runs runtime (`talaria-agent-design`). The record lives in Redis for 72 hours: the instruction and chat, the validated draft, the status, the error, and the start and finish times. Any api process can serve it, and a process that dies mid-design is reclaimed. `/api/fleet/agent-design` reads (GET), starts or refines (POST), saves the person's edits (PATCH) and discards (DELETE), all under `agents.manage`. A hire that names the design (`designId` on `/api/fleet/create`) claims it first, so two tabs cannot hire two agents from one design. The design is used up when that hire finishes. The design leaves New agent as the hire starts, so you can design the next agent while it runs. It is used up once the hire has created the agent, whatever fails after that (a download, a boot): the hiring strip's **Retry** or the agent's **Start** finishes those. A hire that fails before the agent exists (a department taken in a race, say) hands the design back with its reason. It goes onto the review step when New agent is empty. If you have started another design meanwhile, it waits and never overwrites that one: the bell says "The hire of <name> did not finish", New agent shows a line about it with **Discard it**, and the design comes back once the open one is hired or discarded. A **Retry** on the hiring strip takes the design along, so it is used up when the retried hire finishes. There is still one design per person: a describe while one is generating returns that one, and a describe over an idle design replaces it. Opening New agent shows the splash with the time since the server started, or the review step. Hand edits are saved as you type. An edit made just before you close the modal is saved as an ordinary save, at any size. One made just before the page closes rides a `keepalive` save, which browsers cap at 64 KiB. A larger edit (a long soul) sends its small fields, or nothing if even those over the saved soul are too big. The edit itself is kept in this browser for this person and offered back once, when New agent next opens on that design, unless the design has been saved since. It is never reported as saved. Signing out clears it. A Create that meets a newer design (another tab) stops and shows the current one. Each save and refine names the design it edits, so a tab that missed a discard elsewhere is refused and shown the current design, never written over it. **Duplicate** opens its own form and leaves a waiting design alone. **Discard design** stops a design that is running and throws it away. A design that lands with no modal open on it (none for the last 12 seconds) files an **Agent design ready** (or **The agent design failed**) row in the bell, under Work finished, linking to `/agents?design=open`; hiring, discarding or replacing the design marks that row read. While a design is generating or waiting for review, the **+** on the roster carries a dot.

The record is as durable as Redis: the stack's Redis keeps RDB snapshots and no append-only log, so a Redis crash, though not a clean stop, can lose a design written in the last minute or so. A design whose api process dies mid-run resumes when the run's lease runs out, up to five minutes later.

  Verified: headless Chromium against this branch's own stack (app :5304, api :5404), with a stand-in OpenAI-compatible model held for 3 to 20 seconds.
  - **Reload:** reloading 6.6 s into a design showed the dot on **+** (generating) and the roster row "Designing A research analyst…". Reopening New agent showed the splash with the same purpose, and the review step came up at 21.0 s.
  - **Refine and reload:** a refine reloaded mid-run came back on the review step with the refined name and the "Refine applied" receipt.
  - **Closed modal and bell:** with the modal closed and the tab moved to Inbox, the design landed and filed one unread bell row, "Agent design ready: Scout", linking to `/agents?design=open`. Clicking it opened the review step. A renamed field was on the server 1.2 s later.
  - **Hire:** **Create agent** queued the hire. The design was then gone and its bell row read.
  - **Second tab:** a second tab opened on the same generating design, and both tabs reached the review step.
  - **Discard and start over:** **Discard design** left the server with no design and the describe step empty. A new describe then landed.
  - **Live tests:** six `#[ignore]` tests against Postgres and Redis (`cargo test -p talaria-agent-design --lib -- --ignored`) pass. They cover a design that finishes after its client is gone and is read from a fresh session (run `done`, one bell row, TTL over 24 h); a second start that follows the first; an edit, a refine and a discard; a discard mid-run, which cancels it and drops the answer; a landing with a watcher, which rings no bell; a failure that lands its sentence; and a record whose run is gone, which reads as stalled.
  - **Unit tests:** 15 cover the state machine. 14 ui tests cover resuming after a reload: the opening step, the elapsed count on the server's clock across tabs, and each verb's request.
  - **Fix-verification round (NS1–NS4):** in headless Chromium against a parked stand-in hire, New agent opened on "Hiring Scout". A describe and a manual save each answered 409 "an agent is already being hired from this design". When the hire failed, the open modal moved to review with the hire's reason. A hire failed with a real input and was retried through `POST /api/fleet/hires/{id}/retry`: the design followed the retry and was used up when the retry created the agent. A stale tab clicking Create after another device discarded its design and started a manual one: with or without a pending edit, the tab showed the current design, no hire went out from its form, and the newer design was untouched. Live tests pin each case (`design_live_new_agent_waits_while_a_hire_holds_the_design`, `design_live_a_retried_hire_takes_the_design_with_it`), and four `gate_hire` tests pin the hire route's claim → enqueue → release order.
  - **Fourth round (NS5–NS8):** headless results are in the PR. Live tests: `design_live_the_design_gates_the_hire_and_new_agent_stays_open` covers a second claim refused, an empty slot during the hire, design B started meanwhile and never overwritten, A waiting with a bell row and coming back when B is discarded, and a hire that made the agent before its boot failed using the design up. `design_live_a_waiting_returned_design_can_be_dismissed` covers dismissing a waiting design, and `design_live_a_retried_hire_takes_the_design_with_it` covers following a retry. Two route wiring tests fail if the hire route stops going through `gate_hire`, or if the retry route stops calling `follow_retry` before it enqueues. The modal's close, pagehide and once-at-open wiring is pinned at the source.

- **The knowledge sidebar tree now remembers which folders you had open.**
  Doc rows and KB-space sections start collapsed — the tree is deep, and
  "everything visible" was never the shape you left it in — and expansion is
  remembered across navigation: leave to a board and come back, switch spaces
  and switch back, and every branch you opened is still open, every branch you
  closed still closed. KB-space sections get their own collapse chevron, so
  the sidebar folds up one more level; clicking a space's name still selects
  the space and now also opens its doc list, the way it always felt like it
  should. Creating a nested doc or dropping one inside a folder opens that
  folder, and a remembered document is visible in the tree when you come back
  to it — no more landing on a selection hidden behind a collapsed branch.

  Verified: `bun run test src/lib/knowledge-tree-state.test.ts` (9/9),
  `bun run typecheck` in `ui/` (5732 files, 0 errors), `bun run check` at the
  repo root — all green.

- **@-mentions resolve for every email shape again.** A mention stopped
  resolving for anyone whose email localpart carried a dot, an underscore or
  a plus sign: the composer inserted the raw localpart while the server's
  token scanner reads a grammar of letters, digits and dashes, so `@j.siegel`
  scanned to `@j` and nobody was ever notified (Jon's report, TALA-93). Both
  sides now speak the same normalized grammar — lowercase, every char
  outside `[a-z0-9]` mapped to a dash, runs collapsed, edges trimmed — and
  the agreement is pinned by tests on the notify crate (token shape plus an
  end-to-end picker-to-scan assertion), the mentions crate and the UI.
  Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-notify` 63/63 and `-p talaria-mentions`
  and `-p talaria-tasks` green from `api/`; `bunx vitest run
  src/components/chat/mentions.test.ts` 5/5 from `ui/` — the two
  implementation tests red before the fix, green after; the stale
  `ada.l` pin in talaria-mentions re-pinned to the normalized token it now
  correctly produces.

- **Changed: a live ticket shows what its agent is doing now, on the board and in the ticket.** A work session used to say `turn 2 of 12 — waiting on doug-engineering` from the moment the turn was sent until it ended. On the owner's instance that was the same for a session forty minutes into a build and one its agent had not started, and the ticket strip printed the turn twice. Each watch-tail frame is now stamped with its arrival time, and each turn records when it began. The ticket and board reads return the session's live status:
  - whether it is running a step, thinking, quiet, queued, waiting for a person, or still waiting for the agent to take the turn. The run row decides first, so a queued run never reads as sent, and a run picked up again after a restart never shows the dead turn's step. A status that could not be read says "unknown".
  - the step and how long it has run, the last output or sentence, and recent failures with the last one's text.
  - the tokens and cost booked to the ticket since the session started. A partly priced total says what it leaves out (`$1.20 + 3 unpriced`).

  When nothing is booked to the ticket, the read says why, and only when the reason belongs to this agent in this session's window: its own calls carried no session tag (Hermes before v0.22), or none landed under its name while shared-key calls arrived. Hermes crons are not counted.

  Board cards and list rows show the same in two lines. A queued ticket names the tickets it waits behind only on boards the reader can see, and counts the rest. A failed session's row in the Work log shows why it ended. A workbench job shows its provisioning step, or the step it failed at and why, from the `provision` the job read returns once the workbench provisions jobs itself (#706). Board polls reuse a session's pulse while its tail is unchanged, or read within the last 2 s. Everything comes from the server, so a refresh or a second tab shows the same.

  Verified: unit tests for the tail reader cover the shapes on the owner's instance:
  - a terminal call inside an execute_code cell, and a build killed at the 420-second ceiling;
  - the events plugin reporting a call before the stream does;
  - parallel calls, where one finishing leaves the other as the step;
  - a plugin-only tail, a cut window, and a refused workbench tool;
  - a command that mentions `"at":`.

  Unit tests also cover the cache rule (same turn and length, or under 2 s), the state word against the run row (queued, re-queued with a dead step, awaiting), each attribution reason and when it stays silent, the behind split, and the labels including partial pricing. A live-database test (`work_wait_behind_live`) puts one agent's sessions on two boards with different members and checks each reader sees only their own board's ticket by name. `svelte-check` reports 0 errors.

  The first version was exercised on a worktree stack with a real Hermes v0.22.4 Developer Agent and a mock model. With three, then six, live tickets, the board read and the screenshots showed each one `running` with its own shell step and clock, 5.3k tokens booked to each ticket, and `quiet` with its age while the agent was slow to take turns. After a failed turn, the Work log row showed the session's error.

- **Fixed: a Developer Agent's job now starts with a working coding harness. Before, the agent had to repair the harness itself first.** On the live engineering agent, the five work sessions of 3 and 4 November spent 13 to 75 turns each, about 12 to 18M tokens in all, on harness repair before their first coding step. TALA-83 took 55 minutes to reach one. The agents hand-downloaded bun 1.4.4 because `npx …@latest` omp refused the repo's pinned bun 1.4.0. They copied the shared, root-owned `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` into private dirs, and TALA-93 then ran on the dir made for TALA-92. They also pasted the persona's key into `models.yml` to get past a 401. Now `start_job` provisions the job before it hands out a single command, as the agent's user inside its sandbox, in five steps: sandbox, clone, toolchain, harness, preflight. It clones the job's branch, installs the repo's toolchain, installs a pinned Oh My Pi (`OMP_VERSION` 18.16.0) once per volume, and gives the job its own harness dir and launcher (`/opt/data/workbench/harness/jobs/<jobId>`). The launcher runs omp on the harness's bun by path, so a repo that pins an older bun no longer breaks it. The preflight then checks, without a model call, that the launcher starts omp, its dir is writable, the model is in omp's catalog and the gateway accepts the workbench key. It checks the model the job's lines will actually name: the ticket's pinned plan, else the agent's, else the org default. The harness lines are handed out only after the preflight passes. A clone, toolchain or harness step that fails quickly is retried once. The clone goes to a temp dir that is renamed into place only once it has a HEAD. omp installs are swapped in by symlink, under a lock that never falls through, so a running job's install is never deleted; an install is pruned only two days after it was retired, and only when no process maps it. A provision stops as soon as its job ends. A failure goes on the job (`workbench_jobs.provision`: the failing step, its error and the tail of its output), in the `start_job` / `job_status` answer, on the ticket's activity, on the ticket strip and in `GET /api/workbench/jobs`. Its output is scrubbed first, string by string: credential-shaped text, and the secret values the sandbox was given (never a `CI=true`). The agent never discovers it by running the harness, and is told to retry once, then comment and call `report_outcome` with `errorMessage`; it never moves the ticket. `job_status` provisions a job that started from the queue or after approval (a resumed revise round starts with no provision), takes over a provision whose run died, rebuilds one whose model moved after its preflight, and provisions a failed one again when asked (`retry: true`); `prepare_env` provisions again. The Work view recognizes the new launcher line as a harness turn. Also: the stale-sandbox token now lives in the container's env (`TALARIA_SANDBOX_SHAPE`), because the old file sat in a live bind and so called a container from 22 September current. A failed sandbox command now reports its exit status and output, so doctor no longer prints `the probe could not be run in the sandbox: .`. The workbench image no longer bakes in an unpinned omp. The `oh-my-pi` and `workbench-driving` skills say to run harness turns in the background, which avoids the terminal's 420 s foreground cutoff.

  Verified: on this branch's own stack (app :5305, the Rust api :5405) with a real Developer Agent (Hermes v0.22.4, Z.ai GLM 5.3 through the gateway) on a local Forgejo fixture repo that pins bun 1.3.14 (`mise.toml`). The agent was given a ticket. It called `start_job`, got `provision.state: ready` (sandbox, clone, toolchain, harness, preflight all ok), and its next tool call was the given launcher line, run in the background. That was its first coding step, with zero install, PATH, auth or harness-dir calls before it. omp added `multiply` and its test, and `bun test` passed (2 pass) on the repo's own bun 1.3.14. In the same checkout, the old `npx -y @oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent@latest --version` printed `error: Bun runtime must be >= 1.4.4 (found v1.3.14)`. A fixture that pins `node = "0.0.1"` failed provisioning at `toolchain`. `start_job` returned no harness lines, the error read `mise ✗ node@0.0.1 … failed: HTTP status client error (404 Not Found)`, the output carried mise's log, and the ticket got the line `Workbench provisioning FAILED at toolchain: …`. Tests that run the real thing: the runtime script with a stand-in bun (an install swapped in beside the old one; the old one, days old, kept because it was retired just now, and pruned once retired two days; the fallback lock reclaiming a dead or pid-less holder); the retry policy (once, not for a slow or taken-over step); the scrub (secrets out, `true`/`main`/`production` kept, a JSON boolean never touched); the launcher (workdir, agent dir, project env, a refusal without the key or the install); the harness layout refusing an ended job; the preflight failing on a missing key, an old bun, a model id that is only a prefix of a listed one, and a 401; teardown removing the harness dir and refusing a hostile id; and a real `git clone` that keeps an existing checkout, moves a no-HEAD one aside and leaves nothing behind on a failed clone. Against a live database (`cargo test -p talaria-api --test it -- --ignored workbench_provision_live::`): the claim (one run at a time, a dead run taken over, an ended or cleared job never claimed), the lines withheld until ready, `job_status` provisioning a failed job again only with `retry: true`, the lines naming the model the preflight checked (and a moved role provisioning the job again), and a resumed revise round — queued or approved — provisioned afresh instead of handing out the last round's lines. Also the Work view's vitest, with the real launcher line. Not verified: a push and PR from the rig. The fixture's Forgejo is plain http on loopback, and Talaria hands out git credentials over https only, so `git push` was refused by design. The agent reported that and blocked the ticket rather than working around it.

- **Fixed: an agent design being hired can no longer come back twice, nag from the bell, or turn into a manual copy in another tab.** Each write to a design held for a hire is now a compare-and-set on the hold as it was read. That covers marking it returned, using it up, following the hiring strip's Retry, dismissing it, and handing it back into New agent. When two reads settle one failed hire at the same moment, or a read races Retry, the design ends up in exactly one place: never both back in New agent and still waiting, and never handed back over a retry that is making the agent. The "The hire of <name> did not finish" row is filed once per hold, so reading it no longer files it again with another toast or push. When a design leaves New agent for a hire from another tab, the modal open on it resets to an empty describe step and says "<name> is being hired from another tab" instead of keeping its fields, where the next keystroke would have saved them as a manual copy. A conflict that finds no design resets the same way. Smaller edges:
  - A bell row about a design that is gone, expired or ended elsewhere, is marked read.
  - **Discard it** finds a waiting design even if it moved into New agent in the same moment, and a failure to discard is shown.
  - A hire stopped between creating the agent and checkpointing it counts as having created it, because the agent is under the hirer's management.
  - Editing a handed-back design ends its link to the failed hire, so a later Retry of that hire does not use up the edited design.

  Verified: against this worktree's Postgres and Redis, `cargo test -p talaria-agent-design --lib -- --include-ignored` passes 40 tests. Four live tests are new. `design_live_two_reads_settle_one_failure_once` runs two reads at once, over five rounds, and the design lands in New agent and nowhere else, with no "waits" row about it. `design_live_a_read_racing_the_retry_follow_cannot_undo_it` runs a read and the Retry follow at once, over five rounds, and the design ends on the retry and is used up when it finishes. `design_live_the_waiting_bell_row_is_filed_once` checks that the row is filed once, unread, and that after it is read three more reads file nothing. `design_live_a_bell_row_about_a_design_gone_is_read` covers the expired design's row. The ui tests pin the reset helper and the modal's reset wiring.

- **Fixed: assigning a ticket no longer moves it or starts work.** Before, assigning an agent (or a person) to a ticket in intake moved it into the board's agent column ("promoted by assignment") and started the agent on it at once. A ticket created already assigned was born in that column and started straight away too. Now an assigned ticket stays where it is. A new ticket starts in intake unless its creator chooses a column (a new optional `status` when creating, for people; agents' tickets still land in intake). Work starts only when a ticket is in an agent column: a person moves it there, creates it there, or assigns an agent to a ticket already sitting there. Assigning an agent to a ticket anywhere else starts nothing. Agents still move their own tickets while they work, to In progress, Quality review or Blocked, exactly as before. A plugin change request (Manage → Apps) and a plugin upkeep ticket are a person's or the plugin's own ask for the maintainer's work, so they are still created in the board's agent column and start the maintainer, as before. Separately, a person's Stop on an agent now lifts when that person moves the ticket again.
