  is `kind='work'` (a plan can no longer be *started*; existing plans keep their
  prompt and their living document until the harness prompt lands), the
  research rail's own empty/error copy (one rail, one voice), per-surface
  remembered state (collapse key, sticky agent — one surface now), and
  `claimViewTitle` naming a run rather than its thread (inert today: nothing
  reads it).

  Verified: `bun run check` clean (911 files, 15 rules, **0 duplicate-body
  clusters** — the three views, `RunView`, and both Home tabs are deleted, not
  left beside their replacements); `bun run typecheck` 0 errors over 5,483
  files; **1,531 ui tests in 99 files** green, 29 of them new (selection,
  the badge sum, the tab store including `labelTab`, the surface list); scoped
  cargo across `talaria-conversations`, `talaria-research`, `talaria-plan-doc`,
  `talaria-routes-boards`, `talaria-routes-comms`, `talaria-harness-defs`, clippy
  clean. The merge was built by a fan-out, then **adversarially reviewed against
  the deleted originals** (45 behaviours preserved, 16 lost, 14 changed), and the
  lost ones fixed and re-reviewed: 13 fixed, 2 partial on the server side until
  the template and delete-together changes above landed, which they now have.

- **Stop stops, and you can talk to an agent while it works.** Stop used to
  abort the browser's read and nothing else: the Hermes run kept going behind
  a frozen transcript until it ran out of things to do. And there was no way
  to say "not that — this" mid-turn; a correction typed over a streaming reply
  could only wait for the reply to finish being wrong.

  Both now reach the run, through the run id a pinned session lands on the
  row (`#542`): the stop tile posts `/api/conversations/{id}/stop` before it
  aborts, and Hermes hard-interrupts the agent. The turn lands **complete**,
  with whatever it managed to say and a `· stopped` note — not an error row
  with a retry affordance on a turn nobody wants retried — and the chain
  behind it stays quiet unless somebody has spoken since. (A turn on the
  full-history path has no run to interrupt; the route says `hermes: false`
  and the client's abort is, as before, the whole of it.)

  **Send now.** While a reply streams, Enter still queues your message for the
  next turn. ⌘⏎ — or the *Send now* control beside the stop tile — hands it to
  the turn already running: `/api/conversations/{id}/steer` writes the user
  row **first** (what you said mid-run is part of the thread whether or not
  the agent could take it), then steers Hermes. `steered` means the run took
  it, and the row is stamped so the completing turn's chain does not answer
  it a second time; `queued` means the run was past taking it and the row
  waits like any queued message. The row wears a small "sent mid-turn" note.

  **The doom-loop guard.** Over the API, Hermes' own loop breaker is a TUI
  prompt nobody sees. Talaria now counts identical calls — same tool, same
  arguments, one count per call however chatty its progress frames — inside
  one turn. At **3** a `notice` chip lands on the reply ("Repeating the same
  call") and a steer tells the agent to change approach or say what is
  blocking it; at **5** the run is stopped and the reply says why, after its
  last word. The decision is pure (`loop_verdict`) and fires on the exact
  count, so a pair stuck at twelve repeats earns one nudge and one stop, not
  a nudge per frame.

  On the way: a session's tool rows now carry one id **per call** — Hermes
  names no call id on its session frames, and three runs of one tool in one
  reply had been merging into a single row rewritten three times.

  Verified: 78 tests in `talaria-gateway` (+4: `run.cancelled` lands the
  words said before it and ends the turn as *stopped*, `run.steered` lands
  nothing, the steer body is sealed, three calls of one tool are three
  rows); 17 in `talaria-chat-persist` (+5: the guard's thresholds, a repeat
  that warns then stops, different arguments never counting as a loop, pairs
  counted apart, unlabelled calls never counted); 639 UI tests (+18: send-now
  vs queue, the ⌘⏎ key, the notice chip, the two new client calls);
  svelte-check clean; `bun run docs:api` regenerated (two routes); a new
  `#[ignore]` live module `run_control_live` proves the Hermes-free half
  against Postgres — both routes refuse with 409 when nothing streams and
  write nothing, a full-history turn's stop answers `hermes: false`, its steer
  lands as a stamped queued row, and a stranger gets the same 403 as the read.

  Live, against the hired Hermes agent from `#542` (GLM-5.3 Flash via Z.ai):
  a turn told to sleep twice in the terminal, **stopped mid-sleep** — Hermes
  answered `stopping`, the row landed complete and stopped with the partial
  text, `GET /v1/runs/{id}` read `cancelled`, no chain re-fired, and a second
  stop answered 409. A second turn **steered mid-run**: Hermes accepted it
  (`200 steered`), the row landed stamped — and the turn then died on Z.ai
  answering **429 `1113`, "Insufficient balance"**, which also kept the
  doom-loop turn from ever reaching a tool call. Those two live halves — a
  steer carried through to the reply, the guard tripping on a real run — wait
  on the account; the guard's decision and the routes' Hermes-free half are
  the tests above. On the way: Z.ai's `1113` now reads as the account limit
  it is at the gateway's boundary ("out of credit or over its usage limit")
  instead of a generic 429.

- **Talaria Mobile releases itself, in its own tag namespace** — a `mobile/`
  push to `main` builds the Android APK, mints `mobile-vX.Y.0` and opens a
  GitHub prerelease with the APK attached. Starting at **0.1.0**.

  **It is a deliberate sibling of `desktop-package.yml`, not a second scheme.**
  The question is identical — a surface that produces something a person
  installs needs a version an installer can compare — and that answer is
  already load-bearing in this repo: auto-minor on a surface push, a manual
  door for a major, artifacts-only on a pull request. `mobile-v*` sits beside
  `desktop-v*` for the same reason that namespace exists.

  The one place the two differ is what they count. Desktop's auto-minor reads
  **both** `v*` and `desktop-v*`, because desktop tracks the platform's version
  line. Mobile reads only `mobile-v*`: it is its own artifact on its own
  cadence, cutting versions far faster than the platform cuts its, which is
  also why its first mint is `0.1.0` rather than wherever the platform happens
  to be.

  **The version is injected, never committed**, so
  [`RELEASING.md`](./RELEASING.md)'s rule survives intact — releasing never
  edits a file. `-PmobileVersion=X.Y.Z` arrives from the workflow and is
  stamped for that build only.

  **`versionCode` is derived, not maintained**, because it is the one number
  Android actually enforces: a device *refuses* an APK whose code is not
  greater than the installed one, so a non-monotonic scheme makes an upgrade
  silently impossible to install — and two humans editing one integer is
  exactly how that invariant breaks. `maj*10000 + min*100 + patch`, checked
  across 0.1.0→100, 0.2.0→200, 1.4.7→10407, with a floor of 1 for the
  `0.0.0-sha…` builds that mint nothing.

  **Three traps the logic is written against, two of which bit during
  testing.** A lexical sort puts `0.10.0` below `0.2.0`, so the tenth release
  would mint a version that already existed — the sort is numeric per field. A
  tag pushed with `GITHUB_TOKEN` starts no workflows, so the build and the mint
  have to live in one run rather than hand off to a tag trigger, which is why
  `attach` escalates to `contents: write` instead of delegating. And
  `printf '%s\n' $tags` depends on word-splitting, which bash does and zsh does
  not — so the first version of the logic test was green while the logic was
  wrong; `gh` emits one tag per line and is now piped straight through.

  **Every mobile release is a prerelease, deliberately.** The APK is
  debug-signed with the keystore that ships inside every Android SDK on earth:
  installable with `adb install -r`, and not distributable. `/releases/latest`
  must never resolve to one. A Play-signed build is a second job in that
  workflow once store credentials exist — not an edit to the one that is there.

  **Two things that had to be true before an APK was worth building at all.**
  Android has blocked cleartext HTTP by default since API 28 and this app
  targets 37, so a build pointed at a self-hosted instance on `http://host:port`
  could not reach it — and the symptom is indistinguishable from the server
  being down: the launcher says "could not reach" and nothing mentions that the
  platform refused to dial. A debug-only manifest permits it; release builds
  keep the secure default, because the session cookie rides those requests. And
  "unsigned" is not a thing Android will install: `assembleDebug` signs with
  the debug keystore, which the workflow verifies with `apksigner` alongside
  asserting the cleartext allowance survived the manifest merge. Both checks
  *find* their inputs rather than hardcoding paths — AGP writes more than one
  merged manifest and has moved the spelling between versions, and a check
  pinned to one path becomes a check that silently stops checking.

  **iOS is `continue-on-error` and off the required-checks list** until it has
  ever been green. Android is being tested on real devices first, and a macOS
  job that has never passed must not hold that up; it still runs and still
  reports. The same posture `judge.yml` already holds.

  **Verified.** Both workflows parse; the version-resolution logic checked
  against six tag sets (none → 0.1.0, 0.1.0 → 0.2.0, 0.10.0 → 0.11.0,
  1.0.0 → 1.1.0, malformed tags ignored); the injected version read back out of
  AGP's own output metadata for five inputs; `assembleDebug` green; the merged
  manifest carries `usesCleartextTraffic="true"`; `apksigner` confirms a V2
  debug certificate; `bun run check` clean.

- **A conversation can put its agent on a clock, and the answers come back
  into the conversation.** An agent's cron already existed, on the fleet page:
  you gave the agent a schedule and a prompt, it fired on time, and it answered
  itself. The turn went into the container's own session and reached no Talaria
  surface at all — `api_server` is a non-push origin, so the gateway had
  nowhere to deliver to, and the one hook that fires at the end of a session
  carries no text. A daily digest you could not read is spend nobody sees.

  A schedule created **from a thread** is that thread's standing request, so
  `POST /api/conversations/{id}/schedule` records the conversation that is
  waiting on the job, and every run of that job posts its final text back as an
  ordinary assistant turn in the same thread — the unread pill moves, the
  agent-reply bell rings for whoever was away, and the next question you ask
  reads the digest as context because it is a message like any other.

  **Two gates, asking different questions.** Seeing the thread answers 404 for
  a thread you cannot reach (a thread you may not read must not be confirmed to
  exist by the way scheduling it fails); then the agent's own manager rule,
  keyed by the model the thread names, because a schedule writes to the agent's
  scheduler and spends its budget on a timer. Being able to read a thread is
  not enough to make its agent work while nobody is watching.

  **The row is written only after Hermes reports a job id**, and if that write
  fails the job is taken back out of the container: a job with no row pointing
  at a conversation fires forever, finds no listener, and is dropped.

  **`conversation_schedules` is keyed `(agent_model, job_id)`**, not by job id
  alone — a job id is unique only inside one agent's own `jobs.json`, and the
  model is both how a conversation names its agent and what the agent's own
  authenticated call back carries. The listing keeps the two halves apart: the
  stored half (name, schedule, when, which job) is always there, and the live
  half (`enabled`, `state`, `nextRunAt`, `lastRunAt`, `lastStatus`) comes back
  null when the container cannot be read, so a rolling agent does not look like
  a vanished schedule.

  **The delivery door is agent-authenticated and idempotent on the execution.**
  `POST /api/agents/cron-output` takes the plugin's `cron:<job>:<execution>`
  task id, refuses anything outside that grammar, finds the listening
  conversation by `(the caller's own model, job)` — never by job alone, so one
  agent's key cannot post into another agent's thread — and clamps and
  secret-scrubs the text at the boundary, the same distrust `/api/agents/
  tool-events` shows the same plugin. The stored turn's marker names the
  execution rather than the clock, so a re-delivered run answers with the first
  message id and writes nothing.

  The `talaria-events` plugin grew a third hook, `post_llm_call`, and forwards
  **only** `platform == "cron"` turns: every chat and work-session turn already
  reaches the platform through the gateway's own stream, and reporting them
  here would double every reply. One bounded queue still serves both doors —
  an event now names its own path, defaulting to the tool-events one, so a tool
  event's URL, body and headers are byte-for-byte what they were.

  A schedule can be taken away again — `DELETE /api/conversations/{id}/
  schedules/{jobId}` removes the job from the agent and the listener row
  together, behind the same two gates; a slug rename carries the rows with
  the agent; a blank delivery is refused rather than landed as an empty
  turn; the listing reads by conversation through its own index.

  Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-agent-crons -p talaria-routes-comms -p
  talaria-routes-fleet -p talaria-fleet-render -p talaria-personal-agent` — 5
  / 13 / 21 / 20 / 5 passing (new: the task-id grammar's eight cases, the
  turn marker's spelling, the UTF-16 clamp at the boundary); clippy
  `-D warnings` clean over those plus `talaria-api-routes`; `bun run gate`
  green; `docs:api` regenerated (316 routes); migration replay + snapshot on
  a throwaway Postgres (427 statements); svelte-check 5476 files, 0 errors;
  `ui/src/lib/schedules.test.ts` 5 passing. **Live** (`#[ignore]` module
  `conversation_schedules_live`, 9/9 against a fresh database): a thread the
  caller cannot see is 404, an 81-character name is 400 and writes nothing,
  a member who does not manage the agent is 403, an agent with no running
  container answers the crate's sentence and never a 500, the stored
  schedule lists for its thread with the live half null, the agent door
  takes no session, a key-shaped span is scrubbed before it lands, an
  unheard or unparseable task id is refused, and a cron turn lands in the
  thread exactly once — the replayed delivery answers the first message id.

  **Not yet exercised end to end**: no run of this has gone plugin → route →
  thread against a real container firing a cron. The header button that
  opens this to a person lands separately; the client
  (`ui/src/lib/schedules.ts`) is in place and speaks the wire.

- **A delegating agent now shows what it handed out, and what came back.** An
  agent that hands work to a child goes quiet. The child runs under its own
  session id, so the tool events the `talaria-events` plugin already reports for
  it carry a correlation the parent's reader has no way to join — and the
  parent's stream shows a minutes-long gap that reads, to the person waiting on
  it, exactly like a hang. Nothing in the chat said work had been delegated at
  all, let alone to whom or how it went.

  Hermes fires `subagent_start` and `subagent_stop` around every child
  `delegate_task` spawns, and the plugin now registers both. They go to their
  own door — `POST /api/agents/subagent-events`, agent-authenticated with the
  agent's own key, the same door shape as tool events — which lands **one chip
  per child** on the turn the parent is speaking in: *"reviewer · check the bind
  casts"*, running, then done with the child's summary and the tools it used.

  **The stop overwrites its start in place.** The chip id is the child's session
  id, because that is the only handle both hooks carry, and `subagent` joins
  `todo` and `question` as a snapshot kind — a kind whose content is the current
  state rather than a record of something that happened. Stacking a second chip
  would read as two children; keeping the start would leave a finished child
  reading as still running, which is the one thing the chip exists to say. A
  stop whose start never arrived **still lands**: the start is best-effort
  observability and can drop under queue pressure, and a result with no
  beginning is far better than a child that silently never finished.

  That rule turned out never to have been enforced against the database.
  `snapshot_kind` existed and `merge_chips` honoured it, but nothing in
  production called `merge_chips` — the write did its own merge in SQL as a pure
  first-wins append, so a plan rewritten mid-turn kept its *first* version in
  the row too. The merge is now one statement that states both rules: every
  incoming chip appends when its id is new, and the snapshot subset **replaces
  the chip already sitting at that id, in its place** — with ordinality, so a
  plan that rewrites itself does not jump to the end of the row and drag the
  reader's eye with it. `todo` and `question` get the behaviour they were always
  documented to have.

  **And a cap, because delegation is the one agent capability that multiplies
  itself** — a child may delegate too, so without a number somewhere a single
  request can fan a managed box out into as many concurrent sessions as the
  model feels like asking for. `agent_defs.max_children` (default **3**: useful
  out of the box, small enough that nobody discovers the cap by running out of
  memory; **0** is a real setting and means this agent delegates to nobody)
  renders into the agent's `config.yaml` as
  `delegation.max_concurrent_children`. It is written from the column every
  render, so a def cannot author its way past it — and every *other* delegation
  key a def set is left alone, because the rest of that block is the agent's to
  tune. `PATCH /api/fleet/defs/{id}` takes `maxChildren` 0..16, audits it as
  `agent.max_children`, and **rolls the agent exactly as the Developer switch
  does** (one roll even when both change — the render it picks up carries
  everything).

  The platform trusts the plugin's clamps no further here than it does for tool
  events: kind, child session id, role, goal and summary are re-validated,
  re-clamped and secret-scrubbed **at the boundary**, scrub before clamp so a
  key cut in half cannot slip its prefix into the row. `childStatus` arrives as
  the harness words it and is mapped here, not in the container — anything
  error-shaped (`error`, `fail`, `timeout`, `abort`, `cancel`) is an error,
  everything else finished — because a container that already holds this plugin
  file cannot be re-taught one harness version's vocabulary.

  Verified: `talaria-chips` 13 tests (2 new: a stop replacing its start in place
  beside an untouched link chip, and only snapshot kinds reaching the replacing
  leg of the write), `talaria-routes-fleet` 22 (3 new: the two kinds and the one
  required field, a start that runs against a stop that carries the harness
  verdict, and the label's clip with a key scrubbed out of the goal),
  `talaria-fleet-render` 21 (1 new: the cap lands alone on an empty map, an
  authored block's own keys survive while a def's `max_concurrent_children: 99`
  is overridden, and the emitted YAML carries it unquoted and parses back
  identically), `talaria-agent-defs` 5. Clippy `-D warnings` clean across those
  four plus `talaria-api-routes`. The exact merge statement the macro emits was
  run against a real Postgres in a rolled-back transaction: the snapshot
  replaced at its own index, the approval left as its first version, the new
  chip appended last. The plugin was exercised in process against a stubbed
  `urlopen` — four hooks registered, a 64-entry mixed tool history clamped to 40
  names, and the tool event still posting its same eight keys with no `url`
  among them, so that wire is byte-identical. Four `#[ignore]`d live tests in
  `api/tests/it/subagent_events_live.rs` **ran, 4/4, against a fresh
  database**: start then stop is one chip that turns done, an orphaned stop
  still lands, the bogus kind and the unkeyed caller land nothing, and the cap
  refuses 17 while keeping 4. Migration replay + snapshot on a throwaway
  Postgres (426 statements); `bun run gate` green. `bun run check` green — 902 files / 15 rules, 596 docs / 835 links, 313
  routes / 503 method rows / 25 generated files all current; svelte-check 5474
  files, 0 errors.

  Not yet: the chip has no renderer. `ChipKind` admits `subagent` and the
  chip's fields are typed, but `ChatChips.svelte` has no branch for it, so the
  chip is stored, merged and fanned and draws nothing — and the Summary-tab
  control for the cap waits on #542, which owns that file. Until both land,
  delegation is visible through the api and the row, not the chat. The child
  id is bounded in UTF-16 units, the same measure the clamp uses.

- **Conversations can be pinned, grouped and ordered — by each person, for
  their own rail — and an agent can file the session it is in.** The rail
  was one list, newest activity first, and the only organisation it knew was
  Archive. A plan you keep coming back to sank under every new chat.

  Three things a row can now carry, per viewer: **pinned** (first in the
  list), a **group** (a short name, 1–40 characters), and a **position**
  (an explicit order among the rows that have one). They live in a new
  `conversation_layout` table keyed by *(viewer, conversation)*, not on the
  conversation — a shared plan sits in every member's rail and each of them
  organises their own; the owner's pin is not the collaborator's. The list
  left-joins the viewer's row and orders `pinned, position, then newest
  activity`; `PATCH /api/conversations/{id}` takes the three (`null` clears
  a group or a position), and a row whose three values are all default is
  deleted rather than kept.

  **`organize_session`** — the agent's door, with no conversation parameter
  for the same reason `todo` has none: the agent is speaking in a
  conversation right now and Talaria knows which. `{title, pinned, group,
  archived}` → `POST /api/agent/organize` renames, pins, files under a group
  or puts away *this* conversation, writing the **owner's** layout row, so
  "move this to Done when you're finished" is a sentence an agent can act
  on. Never archive unasked — the description says so, and that sentence is
  the only guard behind it. The full tool contract rides along: the MCP
  registration, the catalogue entry (85 tools), the sandbox arm, the
  exposure list.

  The rail itself — pinned first, collapsible groups, drag to reorder, a
  ⌘K palette over sessions — lands on top of the merged Work harness (#541);
  this is the server half it stands on, and the wire already carries the
  three fields on every row.

  Verified: 5 tests in the new `talaria-conversation-layout` (bounds, trim,
  absent-vs-cleared, an empty patch refused, a non-boolean pin refused); 10
  in `talaria-fitness-talaria-tools` (the catalogue carries every tool
  exactly once, at 85); 77 in `talaria-fitness-toolbox` (+1: the sandbox
  organises the session and refuses a call that asks for nothing); 13 in
  `talaria-routes-comms`; `bun run docs:api` regenerated (313 routes);
  migration snapshot updated (426 statements); svelte-check and the MCP
  typecheck clean. Live, against the worktree database (`#[ignore]` module
  `conversation_layout_live`, 5 tests): pinned-then-position-then-recency
  ordering with the three keys on every row; a patch merges rather than
  replaces and an all-default row is deleted; a collaborator's pin is
  invisible to the owner; 41-character and blank groups, `-1` and `100001`
  positions and an empty body are 400s, a stranger 404; an agent mid-turn
  renames and groups the conversation through the door and the owner's list
  shows both, while an agent with no live turn is told 409.

- **An agent can show you the page it saw, and an operator decides which
  toolsets it gets at all.** Hermes turns every built-in toolset on by default
  and `agent.disabled_toolsets` in the rendered `config.yaml` is its last word
  on availability, so until now the only names Talaria closed were the two it
  hardcoded (`todo`, `clarify` — its own versions are the ones a person can see
  and answer). `agent_defs.disabled_toolsets` is the operator's list on top of
  that pair: a jsonb array, empty by default, set whole through
  `PATCH /api/fleet/defs/{id}` as `disabledToolsets`, read back on the def wire
  (list and get). Only Hermes' 28 governed built-ins pass — a typo would reach
  the rendered config and be ignored *there* in silence, leaving a toolset the
  operator believes closed — and the refusal names the first stranger, because
  one mistyped name among a screenful of checkboxes is otherwise a 400 nobody
  can act on. The renderer merges three lists in one order that is itself the
  meaning: the floor Talaria always suppresses, then what the operator closed,
  then whatever the def's authored config already carried, deduped. A reader of
  the rendered file can tell the three apart by where they sit, and a re-render
  of the same three emits the same bytes. The change rolls the department, and
  a PATCH that also flips Developer Agent is still **one** roll. The change is
  audited as `agent.toolsets` with both sides on it.

  **The first toolset this governs is `browser`**, because a browsing agent
  costs real money on every roll. Chromium is not in the hermes-agent image;
  `hermes tools post-setup agent_browser` downloads it, which takes minutes,
  and the image points `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` at `/opt/hermes/.playwright`
  — *inside the container layer*, so the install is gone with the next roll and
  the following browser turn fails on a missing executable. Every agent's
  compose env now carries `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/data/.playwright`, on
  the department's state volume, which outlives the roll (a def whose chassis
  extras name their own path keeps it; the Developer Agent's harness dir still
  wins, on the same volume). The install itself runs at the two places a fresh
  container becomes real — after `wait_healthy_slot` in the roll, and after the
  `up`'s health wait — detached, only when the department's agent still holds
  `browser`, and guarded by a marker file on the volume so the second call
  costs nothing. It is best-effort by contract, like the bundled-skill prune
  beside it: an agent whose browser never landed cannot browse, which is not a
  fleet that cannot serve. The marker is written only on success, so a failed
  download never looks installed.

  **And the screenshot now reaches the person.** `browser_vision` writes a PNG
  inside the container and reports its *path* — a path that means nothing to
  the platform and is gone with the container. The `talaria-events` plugin
  (1.1.0) reads the file the tool named, bounded at 5 MiB, and posts the bytes
  to a new agent-authenticated door, `POST /api/agents/uploads`: base64 in a
  JSON body, three image mimes, both size bounds re-decided server-side because
  the platform does not trust the plugin's clamps. The image rides *after* its
  own tool event, so several MB of base64 never stands in front of the record
  the run watch reads, and the tool-event wire is byte-identical to before. The
  door's two writes are ordered, and the order is the point: the attachment is
  stamped on the turn's message row *before* the chip is surfaced, because
  `can_access_upload` answers "may this reader see these bytes" by probing the
  attachments JSON of rows the reader can reach — a chip ahead of its stamp is
  an image that 404s for everyone but the owner, and the chip write is also the
  realtime nudge that sends a browser to fetch it. No live turn to land on is a
  409, asked before a single byte is stored: a screenshot with nowhere to go is
  a blob nobody will ever open, and the next tool call is one screenshot away.

  Verified: 61 unit tests across the six crates this touches, all green —
  `talaria-agent-defs` 6 (+1: trim, dedupe keeping the first, the cap, and the
  refusal naming the *first* stranger, including a real Hermes platform toolset
  Talaria still refuses), `talaria-fleet-render` 23 (+2: the operator's list
  merging between the floor and the authored names with dedupe against both,
  idempotence over a previous render, `browser_enabled` over three defs, and
  the browsers path landing unless a def named its own), `talaria-fleet-docker`
  5 (+1: the install is marker-guarded on the state volume and `&&`, never
  `;`), `talaria-routes-fleet` 24 (+5: the mime list is the whole list, the
  filename trimmed and bounded, both size bounds — the wire's and the decoded
  one, each proved at its own ceiling — a non-object body, and the image chip's
  shape pinned whole), `talaria-conversations` 3, `talaria-fleet-reconcile`
  compiles. One existing expectation moved: a def whose authored config said
  `[browser, clarify]` now renders `[todo, clarify, browser]` where it rendered
  `[browser, clarify, todo]` — the merge order is the new contract, and nothing
  was loosened. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean on those six
  plus `talaria-api-routes`; `cargo fmt` clean. Three `#[ignore]`d live tests
  in `api/tests/it/browser_toolsets_live.rs` link clean and assert from
  Postgres rather than from the handler: the stored column, the wire field and
  the audit row; a real 1×1 PNG landing as one attachment *and* one image chip
  on the live streaming row, with `can_access_upload` then true for the
  conversation's owner through the attachments probe alone (the def owns
  nobody, so the owner shortcut cannot be what answers); and the four refusals
  — unsigned, dead turn, bad mime, oversized body — each leaving the live row
  and the `uploads` table untouched. Plugin behavior exercised out-of-band:
  both result shapes resolve a path, prose merely mentioning a `.png` does not,
  an oversized or unreadable file yields nothing, and a `browser_vision`
  success enqueues exactly two events while every other tool enqueues one.
  `bun run typecheck` 5475 files, 0 errors; `bun run docs:api` regenerated
  (315 routes, agents 25→26); `bun run check` exit 0 — 903 files/15 rules, 837
  doc links, gen-docs all current, mcp-routes, changelog and sweep clean.

  The install has an operator's brake — `TALARIA_BROWSER_INSTALL=off` skips
  it, with a line in the log — because a Chromium download per department is
  real network and disk, and a dev stack rolling agents to test something else
  should not pay it.

  Not here yet: the Svelte renderer for the `image` chip (`chips.ts` carries
  the kind and the `uploadId`, and `fleet-defs.ts` the `disabledToolsets`
  field, as types only), and the manage-modal checkboxes that set the list.

- **Added:** Blueprints — the asks somebody sends again — get a table and an api. A blueprint is a named piece of text a person keeps and pastes into the composer: `blueprints(name, body, owner_user_id, surface, sort)`, where a NULL owner is the whole access model in one column. A row with an owner is that person's and nobody else lists it; a row without one is the org's, readable by every member and writable only with `templates.manage`, the permission that already governs the org-wide skeletons everyone starts from. `GET /api/blueprints` answers the caller's own plus the shared ones, ordered `sort` then name; `POST` creates one (personal with a session alone, shared with the permission); `PUT` edits — including crossing the line in either direction — and `DELETE` removes. Somebody else's personal blueprint answers 404 and never 403, because a row you cannot see does not exist and a 403 on an id would confirm it is real; a shared row refuses with 403, because everybody can see it and what they are missing is a permission. Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-api --test it blueprints_live:: -- --ignored` 4 passed (a personal blueprint created, listed in sort-then-name order with its camelCase wire shape and its bounds refused at 400; a stranger's list without it and 404 on PUT/DELETE of it; a shared create refused at 403 without the permission, written and read org-wide with it, and refused at 403 to the member who may not edit it; delete gone from the list and from the table), run against a scratch postgres:16-alpine the migration pass had just built; `cargo test -p talaria-routes-knowledge` 7 passed, clippy `-D warnings` clean, `cargo fmt`; `bun scripts/check-migrations.ts --update-snapshot` applied 441/441 with the schema snapshot regenerated; `bun run docs:api` and `bun run check`.

- **Added:** Three ways into a session and one way out of it. A "/" at the start of a line in an agent-facing composer opens a command menu over the skills every agent ships with and over your blueprints — prompts you keep to send again; picking a skill inserts the command, which travels to the agent as "Use your `name` skill. …" (what you sent is the sentence, and so is what the transcript shows); picking a blueprint fills the well with it; "Save as blueprint" keeps the draft you are holding, and a blueprint of your own can be removed from the menu. Blueprints are personal, or shared org-wide by whoever may manage templates. An empty session stage offers starter cards — plan a sprint, research a question, draft tickets from a discussion, put the agent on a clock — that start a session with the chosen agent. An Export action in the session header turns the transcript into a document artifact (turns, who spoke, stamps, attachments, secrets scrubbed, a message's own headings never read as structure) with a Word download beside it, and the artifact surfaces offer Download as Word or Excel for any document or sheet. Verified: ui vitest 113 files / 1748 tests (command rules incl. a command on a later line and a trailing token, transcript, starter cards, office export), svelte-check 0 errors; `talaria-routes-knowledge` 7 unit tests, clippy clean; the blueprints live module 4/4 on a fresh database; `bun run docs:api` and `bun run check`; an adversarial review round over the diff with its blocker (starter cards mounted where no agent is ever selected) and three majors (a saved blueprint keeping the trigger token, a command on a later line reaching the agent raw, Escape re-arming the menu) fixed and re-tested.

- **Added:** The MCP gateway now keeps a record of every tool call it answers, so "which agent called which tool, how often, and did it fail" has an answer that is not a log grep. Each `tools/call` through `/api/mcp/gw/{server}`, and each refusal (no access to the server, a tool outside the allowed set, or a refused batch), writes one `mcp_tool_calls` row: the agent, the acting person when the caller is a personal assistant, the server, the tool (capped at 200 characters), an outcome (`ok`, `error`, `denied`, `not_connected`, `upstream_error`, `spend_error`, `cancelled`), the HTTP status answered, the latency, and the error sentence the caller or the upstream was given, capped at 300 characters. A row never holds the call's arguments, its result, a header or a token. An upstream's error sentence can quote an argument back, so two rules keep arguments out of the error column: a call the spend boundary put a credential into keeps only the JSON-RPC code and a fixed sentence, never the upstream's text, and on every other call each argument string the agent sent (6 characters or more) is replaced with `«argument»` before the row is stored. A tool that reports `isError: true` is recorded as an error under a fixed sentence, because its own text is a result. A caller that hangs up before the answer finishes is recorded as `cancelled`, which does not count against the server's errors. Handshakes, `tools/list`, pings and notifications are not recorded. A failure inside the gateway before access is known (the access lookup failing) is recorded as an error, so an outage shows up in the record instead of as silence. The record is written by a background task, so a tool call never waits on it: each row is one insert statement with the owner and server lookups inside it, at most four inserts use a database connection at once, past 10,000 waiting rows new ones are dropped with a warning, and a failed insert only logs a warning. A streamed answer is recorded when its stream ends: the relay passes every byte through unchanged and classifies the call from a bounded tail, so the latency covers the whole call and the outcome is what the upstream actually replied. Admins read the record at `GET /api/mcp/calls`, newest first, filtered by `server` (id or name), `agent`, `tool`, `outcome` and `since` (epoch ms), with `limit` (default 100, max 500). `GET /api/mcp/calls/summary` reports, over `since` (default the last 24 hours) and optionally one `server`, each server's calls, errors, denials, not-connected answers, p50 and p95 latency and five busiest tools, plus each agent's calls and errors. The percentiles leave out refusals and not-connected answers, which the gateway answers itself in a few milliseconds. Observability has a new MCP tab with a summary strip, a by-server table and the call table (time, agent, server, tool, outcome, latency, error). Its filters are server, agent, outcome and a 1h / 24h / 7d window, and they live in the URL. Each server card on the MCP page gains one line, "Last 24h: 142 calls · 3 errors · 1 denied", which opens that tab filtered to the server. The leased `mcp-calls-prune` job runs every six hours and deletes rows older than the retention, default 30 days, in batches of 5,000. Admins set the retention from the MCP tab ("Keep for") or with `PUT /api/mcp/calls/retention` `{days}` (a whole number from 1 to 3650; `GET` reads it). It is stored as `app_settings` `mcp_calls_retention_days`; a stored value that is not a positive whole number falls back to 30 days, so a bad value can never prune everything. Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-mcp --lib calls::` (21 passed: all seven outcomes round-trip; errors exclude refusals, missing connections and cancellations; percentiles exclude what the gateway answered itself; truncation to exactly 300 characters, by character, with an ellipsis; a 2 MB tool name is cut to 200; only a single `tools/call` is recorded, and each `tools/call` member of a batch is its own member; a batch carrying tools/call or tools/list needs refusal, a batch of pings does not; JSON-RPC errors, house errors, `isError` results and code-only errors classify, and `isError` text never reaches the row; a spent call's error keeps only its code through the reply, dispatcher, SSE and pump paths, tested with a Zod-style "received 'ghp_…'" message; echoed argument strings are scrubbed, longest first, short ones left alone, the copy bounded; in-process answers classify by body and then status; JSON and SSE answers classify, including a reply to another id and a truncated SSE tail; broken, cancelled and reply-less streams; the tap keeps a bounded tail; the tapped stream passes bytes through unchanged and records when the upstream finishes; filter parsing and its 400 sentences; limit clamping; summary ranking, top-five tools and totals; an empty window; stored retention parsing and the stricter asked-for retention; the prune job's spec); `cargo test -p talaria-routes-fleet --lib mcp_` (14 passed, including a batch hiding `delete_repo` refused with a -32600 for each member that has an id); `cargo test -p talaria-jobs` (the job-table completeness test now also requires `mcp-calls-prune`); `cargo clippy -p talaria-mcp -p talaria-routes-fleet --tests -- -D warnings` clean; `cargo check -p talaria-api-routes`; against the dev Postgres inside a rolled-back transaction: the single-statement insert resolving a refusal's server id by name, naming a personal assistant's owner, naming none for an unproven caller, and inserting nothing for an unknown server, plus the filtered percentiles (ok 12 ms and error 40 ms beside a denied and a not-connected row give p50 26; a refusal-only server gives none); ui `svelte-check` 0 errors; vitest for the panel's helpers, 30 passed (latency, the card line, URLs, windows, error rate, outcome tones including `cancelled`, retention choices and labels). The end-to-end script drives three ok calls, a gate denial, an access denial, a not-connected call, an upstream 401, a tool-level error, a refused batch that never reaches the upstream, and unrecorded protocol calls, then checks the list, the filters, the summary, the retention route, and that no row contains the arguments. It runs once the stack is rebuilt with this change.
- **Fixed:** A JSON-RPC batch carrying a `tools/call` or a `tools/list` is now refused at the MCP gateway with a -32600 for each member. The tool allow-list, the credential spend boundary and the tool-list filter only read a single-request body, so a batched call used to reach the upstream unchecked and unrecorded. Each `tools/call` inside a refused batch is recorded as its own denied row. Batches of other requests (pings, notifications) still relay as before, and current MCP clients do not send batches. Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-routes-fleet --lib mcp_gw_server` (a batch hiding `delete_repo` behind a notification and a `tools/list` gets two -32600 replies and is not relayed; an all-notification batch gets one; a ping batch and a single call pass through); `cargo test -p talaria-mcp --lib calls::` (batch membership and the refusal rule).

- **The MCP marketplace hides servers that no longer answer, and admins edit the featured
  shelf.** The catalog mirror carries every hosted entry the registry lists (~28k of ~42k), and
  a good share are gone — weekend demos, expired tunnels, hosts that 404 — so an install failed
  at discovery after the person had already chosen it. A new leased job,
  `mcp-library-liveness` (every 5 min, first run 3 min after boot), POSTs one JSON-RPC
  `initialize` to up to 300 hosted entries a run (never-checked first, operator stand-ins ahead
  of registry rows, then the oldest verdict; 8 in flight, 6 s each, at most 3 redirects, through
  the SSRF guard's resolver) and records `ok` (a JSON-RPC result or SSE data), `auth`
  (401/403/407 — alive, wants credentials), `dead` (404/405/410, 5xx, DNS/connect/TLS failure,
  timeout) or `unknown` on the row (`live_state`, `live_checked_at`, `live_detail`; appended
  migration). Search sorts dead rows last and leaves them out by default, answering
  `hiddenDead` — the picker shows "12 unreachable servers hidden · show" (`includeDead=1`), and a
  shown dead card says "Unreachable when last checked 3h ago" with the reason on hover and still
  installs. Every server carries `live: {state, checkedAt, detail}`; the featured shelf never
  shows a dead row; the status line adds "N checked · N unreachable · N to go"
  (`catalog.liveness`, partitioned on the verdict so unreachable never exceeds checked). Search
  runs the page and the hidden-dead count as two statements side by side (a partial index on
  the dead rows; appended migration), so the filter-only view costs what it did before. A row the sync rewrites with a changed entry is re-asked on the next run
  (and loses its verdict when its endpoint changed). Admins can run a batch now:
  `POST /api/mcp/library/liveness`. The featured shelf was a Rust constant; it is now the
  built-in list merged with the admin's edits (`app_settings.mcp_featured`: added domains,
  hidden built-ins, and stand-ins `{domain, title, url}` that win over the registry and the
  documented map for their publisher), edited from the marketplace's **Edit featured** link
  (`GET`/`PUT /api/mcp/library/featured`, admin only, bare hosts and https URLs validated —
  a stand-in URL with a user name, password, query string or fragment is refused, since every
  member is served it — audited as `mcp.featured`); a save shows on the shelf at once. `TALARIA_MCP_REGISTRY_URL`
  points the mirror at another registry list endpoint (an e2e stub). Verified: cargo tests for
  `classify_liveness` (every status class and failure kind), the merged featured list (add, hide
  a built-in, stand-in override, validation), the shelf picker and search ordering with dead
  rows, the status and hit wire shapes, the job timings and an unbound loopback port judged
  dead; the transport-error mapping and SSE framing under a non-SSE content type; a panicking
  batch not wedging the in-flight flag; `#[ignore]`d live-DB tests (`catalog_live`, run against
  the worktree database in a throwaway schema, and failing when the dead-last key is flipped,
  the dead filter dropped or `checked` counted by stamp) for search's dead-last order, the
  hidden-dead count under limit/kind/tier filters, the all-dead empty page, the shelf passing
  over dead publisher rows, and the status counts through a same-URL and a changed-URL rewrite;
  the new search statements timed against the worktree mirror with 1 in 5 hosted rows marked
  dead (empty query, kind=hosted: page 81–98 ms as before, dead count 3 ms; "git": page
  ~855 ms against 940 ms before, count 12 ms); vitest for the liveness sentences and the editor's chip logic; svelte-check; every new
  query run against a copy of the worktree mirror (187 hosted rows probed in 10 s: 80 ok, 64

- **Added:** The MCP surface has an end-to-end suite (`ui/e2e/`, Playwright; [docs/E2E.md](docs/E2E.md)). It drives a real app, api and browser against a stub world in one stdlib process (`scripts/e2e/mcp-stubs.mjs`, HTTPS with a throwaway CA, since the catalog keeps only https remotes). The stubs are a paging registry (cursor, `version=latest`, `updated_since`, `search`), an open server, a key server that answers 401 until it is sent `X-Api-Key`, an OAuth 2.1 server (client registration, an `/authorize` that 302s straight back, PKCE-checked `/token`), a dead entry and a package entry. Seven chapters: the catalog syncs and the marketplace finds the entries; an open install lands ready with its 3 tools; the key server opens the credentials editor and connects once the key is set, and the key never comes back from the api; the OAuth server is detected and connects through the popup; an agent's MCP tab assigns the server, narrows it to one tool, shows on the registry card's count and comes off again; the gateway, called with the agent's own key, echoes the allowed tool, refuses the other with -32602 before it reaches the upstream, and answers 401 with no credential; the custom form registers a raw URL. A failed chapter does not skip the rest: each one rebuilds what it needs. The suite never starts a container (the agent tab's edits go out with `apply: false`) and removes everything it made. `bun run test:e2e` runs it, and the new `e2e` CI job runs it when the ui, the stubs or the MCP crates move. That job seeds the fleet chassis a hire needs, keeps its logs beside Playwright's output (which Playwright wipes), and uploads results, report and logs on failure. Verified: against the worktree stack (the rc api, started with the stub env), `E2E_MARKETPLACE=0` (registration by URL, chapter 1 skipped) gave 6 passed, 1 skipped. With the five stub entries written into that stack's mirror by hand (an rc binary cannot follow `TALARIA_MCP_REGISTRY_URL`), all 7 passed, twice in a row. Each run left no server, agent, endpoint, fleet key or container behind. Chapters 2–4 also passed through the marketplace UI. The sync half of chapter 1 runs at integration. actionlint 1.7.7 on ci.yml: clean. `tsc -p ui/e2e`: clean. ui svelte-check: 0 errors. ui vitest: 1614 passed. check-docs and check-invariants: pass.

- **Added:** An hourly MCP health check. Until now a server's status changed only when someone pressed Discover, so a revoked key, a dead host or an OAuth grant the provider stopped refreshing kept reading "ready" while every agent call failed. The `mcp-health` job (talaria-mcp `health.rs`; hourly, leased, first run two minutes after boot) re-asks every enabled external server, and `POST /api/mcp/health` (admin) runs the same pass on demand and returns `{checked, changed, down, recovered, notified, servers}`. Header-auth org servers get `initialize` + `tools/list` with the sealed org headers. This is the same conversation discovery has (it is now one shared function), and no audit row is written. When the tool *name* set changes, the cached catalog is replaced. Assignments whose tool subset names a tool the server no longer offers are recorded in the probe as `staleAssignments: [{agent, missing}]`. Org OAuth servers have their grant refreshed first. A grant that was connected and that the provider then refused to refresh gets the new `reconnect` probe state, and the card offers Reconnect; Discovery (Check now) reports it too, and says the token endpoint did not answer (rather than "not connected yet") when a refresh simply went unanswered. The refusal is recorded where it happens: `oauth_token_for` drops the grant and flags it in the new `mcp_oauth_reconnect` table in the same step (the token row itself is deleted on refusal), so a grant the gateway lost in the middle of an agent call still reads as Reconnect at the next pass, and a fresh sign-in clears the flag. The refresh is now single-flight per grant: it runs under the token row's lock and re-reads the row once it holds it, so the gateway, the health pass and a second pass refreshing one grant at once make one refresh instead of having the loser spend a rotated refresh token, get 400, and delete the winner's fresh grant. Per-user servers get an unauthenticated reachability probe, where a 401 counts as up. Then each person's stored OAuth grant is refreshed, so a refusal surfaces within the hour even when the person's agents are idle. `GET /api/me/mcp` then answers `needsReconnect` and Settings → Connections shows Reconnect; a disconnect clears the flag. Builtin, app and Workbench servers are not probed. An oci-http package server is asked at its container (resolved, and started if it stopped, the same step the gateway's first call takes); a stdio package has no address and is not asked, and its card shows no "Checked" line. Passes in one process run one at a time, each server's conversation gets at most 45 seconds whatever its own timeout, and each verdict is written as it arrives, so one hung server delays only its own line. When a server the last pass saw `ok` is found unreachable, erroring, refusing credentials or needing a reconnect, every admin gets one in-app notification (`mcp_server_down`, routed to the capability-gaps class). It fires once per transition: the pass compares against a new `mcp_servers.health_state` column (what the last *pass* saw), so a person's Check now cannot swallow the transition, and the read-and-write is one locked update, so two overlapping passes cannot both notify. A recovery writes the probe only. While any external server's last probe is not ok, admins see one "N MCP servers need attention" warning in `/api/alerts` that names the servers and links to `/mcp/external`. The agent's MCP tab answers `assignedToolsMissing` per server (computed live against the cached catalog; the tab's copy of the probe leaves out `staleAssignments`, which names every agent on the server) and shows a warning chip with a one-click **Drop missing tools**. That re-posts the assignment without those tools, or asks to remove the assignment when none would remain, because an empty subset grants nothing and a null one would grant every tool. Every server the pass asks shows "Checked <when>" from the probe with a **Check now** action, plus a line when assignments name tools the server no longer offers; the others keep the time on their failure detail. A per-user server the check cannot reach shows unreachable instead of "per-user accounts".
  Verified: `DATABASE_URL=… cargo test -p talaria-mcp-oauth --test refresh_live -- --ignored` against the dev Postgres (2 passed: two concurrent `oauth_token_for` calls on an expiring grant, against a loopback provider that rotates refresh tokens and answers a spent one 400, make one refresh, both get the fresh token, the rotated refresh token is kept and nothing is flagged; a provider answering 400 leaves no token row and a `mcp_oauth_reconnect` flag), and with the row lock removed the first test fails (the second caller got None), so it tests the lock; `cargo test -p talaria-mcp-oauth` (staleness and token-document reads); `cargo test -p talaria-mcp` (65 passed, including the health tests covering: which servers the pass asks, with pulled oci-http packages in and stdio, unpulled and unparseable package rows out; the transition rule from every state to every state; missing-tools in subset order, deduped, and nothing claimed against an empty catalog; stale assignments, which skip all-tools and intact subsets; catalog drift wording; the probe document's key order with `staleAssignments` and the `reconnect` state; and the report's camelCase wire); `cargo test -p talaria-alerts` (the attention alert's singular/plural wording, severity and href); `cargo test -p talaria-notify kinds_route` (`mcp_server_down` → `gap_reported`); `cargo test -p talaria-jobs register_all` (now asserts `mcp-health` is registered); `cargo test -p talaria-routes-fleet` (34 passed, including the agent tab's probe never carrying `staleAssignments`); `cargo clippy -D warnings` clean on talaria-mcp, talaria-mcp-oauth, talaria-alerts, talaria-notify, talaria-scheduler, talaria-routes-fleet, talaria-routes-integrations, talaria-jobs, talaria-api-routes and talaria-api-facades; every new SQL statement (the locked probe swap answering the previous state, the reconnect flag upsert and its reads, the alert's server query, the admin and role reads) run against the dev Postgres in a rolled-back transaction; ui svelte-check 0 errors; vitest `mcp-status.test.ts` 23 passed (which servers show "Checked" and Check now, new cases for the reconnect verdict, reconnect outranking OAuth-app setup, a stale reconnect after a fresh sign-in, a per-user server that is unreachable or erroring, "Checked …", missing/stale tools and the drop helper), and the full ui suite passed (1627). The end-to-end script (DeepWiki and a dead URL probed; ok → down notifies once across two passes and survives a manual check; a never-ok server notifies nobody; recovery is silent; a bogus tool in a subset appears as `staleAssignments` and `assignedToolsMissing` and Drop clears it; the alert; `needsReconnect`; an OAuth org server reading `reconnect`) was written for the integrated stack and runs there.

- **The MCP marketplace searches a local mirror of the official registry; credentials,
  OAuth app setup and per-agent MCP are first-class.** Search queried the registry live on
  every keystroke, and the registry stalls: measured 2026-10-16, one search took 9.7s and the
  next three timed out at 15s, which the picker rendered as "No servers match"; its search was
  also a name-substring match, so "google drive" found nothing. The scheduler now mirrors the
  registry into `mcp_library_entries` (`/v0.1/servers`, latest versions, full cursor walk once,
  `updated_since` incrementals every 30 min, resumable, "Sync now" from the picker) and search is
  Postgres full text over title/publisher/name/description with tier and hosted/package filters;
  the live registry answers only while the first walk runs. Marketplace package installs were
  filed under the Built-in tab (a `talaria-pkg://` URL failed the http scheme test) and could not
  be removed — they are External now. Servers that need an API key the registry never declared
  had no field for it anywhere: discovery now records a probe (`last_probe`: ok, auth-required,
  unreachable, error, with the server's own words), the card says "needs credentials" and opens a
  credentials editor (declared fields, or free header rows; `mergeHeaders` sets and removes keys
  without ever echoing a value; saving re-tests), installing from the marketplace asks for the
  key in the same step when discovery answers 401, and the custom form takes any number of
  headers. OAuth: the callback URL shown for manual apps came from `window.location` while the
  authorize request used the verified hosting domain — providers rejected the mismatch; the api
  now computes the one canonical callback and the card shows it, with the provider's developer
  portal and the steps that matter there (two dozen providers, `guides.rs`), an explicit scope list for
  manual apps, **Re-detect auth**, and automatic OAuth detection when a header server starts
  answering 401. The agent settings MCP tab attached RAW URLs to the Hermes config, bypassing the
  gateway, with no marketplace and no registry toggles; it is now the registry scoped to the
  agent (`GET`/`POST /api/fleet/defs/{id}/mcp`): what it carries and why, a tool subset per
  assignment, one-toggle assignment of what exists, add-from-marketplace that installs and
  assigns, leftover raw entries listed for removal, raw `add` refused. A personal assistant's
  rendered config also stops listing a server its owner's team denies (the gateway already
  refused it), and hosted servers registered through the api no longer carry a jsonb `null`
  in `package` that every `is_some()` reader took for "is a package" (the insert binds SQL
  NULL; a migration clears the rows already written). Verified: cargo tests for the library (sync bookkeeping, domains, tiers), oauth
  (guides, meta), and the registry crates; vitest for the status matrix and the external/internal
  split; `bun run gate`; and in the worktree app: catalog sync from empty to the full registry,
  search for brands the old path missed, install → needs-credentials → set key → tools discovered,
  the agent tab assigning and narrowing, and the canonical callback on an OAuth-app card.

- **Changed:** An MCP server's org-level headers — the API key or auth header an admin types into its Credentials form — are now sealed at rest like every other secret (`mcp_servers.headers_sealed`, SecretBox, one JSON object per server) instead of plaintext jsonb. One module in `talaria-mcp` (`org_headers`) is the only code that opens them, for the gateway's upstream call, discovery and the platform's own tool calls; every write (register, replace, the Credentials editor's merge) opens, applies, re-seals and empties the plaintext column under the row lock, so two concurrent saves cannot lose each other's key. Header values no longer leave the api at all: the registry answers `headerKeys` (names only) in place of the masked `headers` map — the register response used to echo the values back unmasked, and now cannot — and the register audit records the key names. A seal the instance cannot open (a database restored onto other key material) lists no keys, and the next Credentials save replaces it instead of failing with a 500. Rows written before this change are sealed once the instance has been up past a self-update's drain (`TALARIA_ROLL_DRAIN_SECONDS` + 180s — the old slot still serving reads only the plaintext column, so sealing under it would send its calls upstream without the key), idempotently and safely across instances (each row's update is conditioned on the plaintext it read), and the same sweep re-runs on every registry read after that; DEK rotation now re-seals the new column with the rest. An agent that calls a server it may use but whose account nobody connected yet no longer gets the same 403 as a refusal: the gateway answers the handshake itself (so the harness keeps the server), lists the cached catalog filtered to the agent's allowance (a `connection_required` stand-in when there is none), and answers every call with JSON-RPC -32001 and one sentence the agent can repeat — "Your Notion account isn't connected to Talaria. Connect it at <instance>/settings/connections, then try again.", "The workspace's Linear connection isn't set up yet. An admin connects it on the MCP page at <instance>/mcp/external.", or "Notion is a per-user server; only a personal assistant can use it." The link uses the verified hosting domain, else `AUTH_PUBLIC_URL`, else the request origin as a browser opens it (an agent reaches a host-run app as `host.docker.internal`, which the link turns into `localhost`). The in-house answers keep JSON-RPC's rules: no `id` is a notification (202, no body) whatever the method, a batch gets an array, and an unknown protocol revision is negotiated down instead of echoed. Such servers now stay in the agent's rendered config (an org agent carries a per-user server only when granted to it by name), and a personal assistant no longer carries a server its owner is denied, connected or not. The agent's MCP tab now shows a server as carried exactly when the rendered config lists it, and says why a granted server is left out (`withheld`: the owner is denied, or a per-user server needs a direct assignment on an org agent). Connecting an org account, or any other registry change, now also rolls agents that carry the server through a team grant, so they leave the in-house answer for the live upstream. Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-mcp` (30 passed — seal/open round trip through the helper, an unreadable seal is an error to readers yet replaced by a merge, the sealing grace outlasts the drain, the no-id notification, batch, revision-negotiation and browser-link cases, legacy plaintext read and overlay, merge set/remove/keep against a sealed value, `server_wire` carries no header value, the three sentences, the in-house initialize/ping/notification/tools-list shapes and the -32001 call/other-method answers); `cargo test -p talaria-routes-fleet mcp` (13 passed, including the existing gateway tests, the not-connected framing against the gate's with a batch, and the connect link never naming `host.docker.internal`); `cargo test -p talaria-mcp-apply`; the widened carriers query run against the dev Postgres; `cargo test -p talaria-secret-rotation`; `cargo clippy -D warnings` clean on talaria-mcp, talaria-mcp-apply, talaria-routes-fleet, talaria-jobs, talaria-fleet-render, talaria-secret-rotation, talaria-api-facades; `cargo check -p talaria-routes-integrations`; ui svelte-check 0 errors and the full vitest suite (1614 passed); the end-to-end script (register with headers, GET and DB show no value, merge set/remove, legacy plaintext sealed by the sweep, the three gateway sentences against Notion) was written for the integrated stack and runs there.

- **Office files, both directions: a .docx you attach is read, and an artifact
  you want to send becomes one.** Two halves of the same gap. An attached Word
  document reached the agent as a mime type and a byte count — the attachment
  pipeline could only read what `TEXT_MIME` admitted, so the format most of the
  business world writes in arrived as nothing at all, and the model answered a
  message whose subject was missing. And an artifact the agents had written
  could be read in the app but not sent anywhere: no file to attach to a mail,
  hand to a lawyer, or open in Word and edit. The only existing way out was
  `/export/google`, which needs a connected account and a round trip to Drive
  to hand you a file you already had.

  **A new leaf crate, `talaria-office`, with no `talaria-*` dependencies.**
  Nothing in it knows about a request, a database, an artifact or a user — it is
  bytes in, text out and text in, bytes out, which is exactly what lets the
  uploads path and the export route both depend on it without depending on each
  other. `office_kind(mime, filename)` names the document, `extract_text` reads
  one, `markdown_to_docx` and `grid_to_xlsx` write one. OOXML is a zip of XML
  parts, so the whole job is the zip crate plus a pull parser.

  **Reading keeps the structure a reader can act on and drops the rest.** docx:
  one line per `w:p`, tabs and breaks as themselves, table rows as tab-separated
  cells, field codes and tracked deletions excluded (they are text nodes too,
  and they are not words anyone wrote). xlsx: every sheet in **workbook order**,
  `## <sheet name>` then one row per line — shared strings, inline strings,
  numbers and booleans all read, sparse columns padded from the cell reference.
  pptx: `sldIdLst` order, `## Slide N`, every `a:t` run. Formatting, numbering,
  merges and drawings are dropped silently rather than approximated.

  **The mime is a claim and an extension is a guess, and the rule follows from
  that.** A `.docx` posted from a browser routinely arrives as
  `application/octet-stream`, so a generic mime (octet-stream, zip, empty) falls
  back to the filename. The reverse is deliberately *not* symmetric: a mime that
  specifically says `text/plain` beats a `.docx` on the end of the name. Every
  file `TEXT_MIME` already admitted still takes the same lossy-utf8 path it
  always did — the two sets cannot overlap.

  **Every byte reaching the reader came off an upload, so nothing there trusts a
  header.** Each part is refused above 20 MiB on the central directory's
  *declared* size — before a byte is inflated — and again afterwards if that
  header lied. Malformed XML comes back as `Malformed(detail)` rather than an
  unwrap; a column reference past Excel's own XFD is rejected, because padding
  out to it would be the whole attack; per-sheet text is capped because column
  padding is an amplifier. The caller still clips.

  **An export that cannot be opened is not an export**, so the writers emit the
  parts Word and Excel actually look for: `[Content_Types].xml` first with an
  override per part, `_rels/.rels`, the main part's own rels, a style sheet, and
  `docProps/core.xml` carrying the title. Lists are `ListParagraph` with their
  bullet or number written into the text — real numbering definitions are
  several times the file's size and buy a renumbering behaviour nobody asked an
  export for. Cell references run past Z properly, sheet names are sanitised to
  what Excel accepts, numbers that parse stay numbers so the sheet sums, and all
  text is escaped. Same input, same bytes.

  **`GET /api/artifacts/{id}/export?format=docx|xlsx`** is the twin of the
  Google export without Google: the same read gate on both arms, owner arm
  included, but no connected account, no network and nothing recorded — the
  bytes are built in process and answered as an attachment, with the RFC 6266
  filename pair so an accented title saves under its own name. A **sheet**
  becomes a one-sheet workbook from the grid the app renders it from; every
  other text kind becomes a .docx of its markdown. Which file an artifact can
  become is its **kind's** answer, not the caller's: a `file` artifact has no
  document to export (its bytes already download through `/api/uploads/{id}`),
  and a format the kind cannot take is a 400 with a sentence rather than a 200
  with an empty file.

  Verified: 34 tests in the new `talaria-office` crate — every fixture built by
  hand in the source, because a fixture you can read in the diff is worth more
  than one you have to open in Word. `office_kind` by mime with parameters and
  case, by extension under each generic mime, and the cases that must stay
  `None`; docx paragraphs, tabs, breaks and tables; two sheets in workbook order
  with one absolute rel target; two slides whose parts sit in the zip in reverse
  order; entity and character references (a separate parser event — a walk that
  handled only text would silently drop every ampersand and em dash, and that
  test is the regression); a 21 MiB entry refused as `TooLarge` with the fixture
  asserted under 200 KB, so nothing inflated; malformed, truncated, non-zip and
  empty bytes; every part of both writers re-parsed as well-formed XML; column
  names to XFD; sheet-name sanitising (an apostrophe on either end included);
  characters XML cannot carry dropped rather than written; a table nested in a
  cell staying inside that cell; a cut sheet saying `[truncated]`; and both
  round-trip properties. Extraction and the writers run off the executor
  (`spawn_blocking`), so a 20 MiB document never stalls the request thread. Plus 5 in
  `talaria-uploads` (one new: office files admitted by mime or by extension, a
  specific non-office mime beating a `.docx` name, and a ref chip never
  qualifying) and 5 in `talaria-routes-knowledge` (two new: the filename stem
  and the disposition pair). `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean
  across the four touched crates; `bun run docs:api` regenerated (312 routes →
  313); `bun run check` green; `bun run gate` green. **Live** (`#[ignore]` module
  `office_export_live`, 5/5 against a fresh database): a doc exporting as a
  .docx that reads back, a sheet as an .xlsx whose rows come back in order, the
  three refusals, a stranger getting the read gate's answer, and a .docx uploaded
  through the real `POST /api/uploads` becoming prompt text with no raw zip in
  it. Not yet opened in Word or Excel themselves — the fixtures and the
  round trips are the proof of the packages until somebody double-clicks one.

- **Research has dials, knows when it has enough, and can start inside the
  conversation you are already in.** A research run was one of three presets
  — recon, brief, expedition — and a preset was all or nothing: somebody who
  wanted an expedition's rounds over a brief's handful of angles took the
  whole shape or none of it. Every run also spent its full budget, round
  after round, whether or not the second round had already answered the
  question; and a run always opened its own thread, so research commissioned
  from a plan or a work session reported somewhere else.

  **Three dials, 1–3 each: effort, breadth, sources.** Effort is rounds
  (1/2/3), breadth is angles per round (1/3/4), sources is how many
  citations the report may stand on (6/12/24). The presets are the dials
  with names — recon 1/1/1, brief 1/2/2, expedition 3/3/3 — and **a mode
  nobody has dialled costs exactly what it always did** (1×1, 1×3, 3×4; the
  maps are pinned to the old budget by test). `POST /api/research` and the
  `research` tool take any of the three beside `mode`; the run records
  them as `dials` and the wire carries them back.

  **`research-enough`** — a new census site (noul, lean 0.75, on). When a
  round completes with rounds still to spend and something citable found,
  the judgment reads the ask, the scoper's read and the findings so far and
  answers "do these answer it at this depth?" — yes writes the report now,
  with the phase saying *enough after round N*; the budget's own "keep
  going" is the shadow baseline. It is never asked on the last round or on a
  round that found nothing. A follow-up's inherited sources sit outside the
  cap (the cap counts what *this* run read), and a marker the cap took off
  the report is not counted as a fabrication — only a number no source ever
  carried is.

  **The scoper acts, one way.** `research-scope` has been measured against
  the scoper's own verdict since it was declared; it may now override a
  *vague* verdict with a confident *crisp* — proceed on the read, ask
  nothing — and never the reverse (a confident "vague" with nothing to ask
  is not an answer). Off by default, and the judgment is not even made
  while it is off.

  **`conversationId`.** A run started with one discusses and reports into
  that conversation — a plan, a work session — rather than minting a
  research thread. The caller must be able to open the conversation (a
  conversation they cannot see answers "not found", never "forbidden"), and
  one live run per thread: a second start while one is working answers 409
  with the run it would duplicate. The conversation-keyed readers follow the
  newest run.

  Verified: 45 tests in `talaria-research-def` (+11: the dial maps and the
  presets' unchanged cost, an old checkpoint without the new fields still
  deserializing, the cap keeping the lowest indices, the sources dial end to
  end, and the loop — enough after round one writes the report and never
  plans round two, a no runs both, the last round is never asked, a round
  with nothing citable is never asked); 100 in `talaria-decide` (+8:
  `enough` state clamping, the one-direction override, the census's
  consistency tests over 12 sites); 19 in `talaria-routes-workbench` (+6,
  the body's validation); 8 in `talaria-research`; the catalogue and sandbox
  parity tests (10 + 77); `bun run docs:api` regenerated; migration snapshot
  updated; svelte-check and the MCP typecheck clean; a new `#[ignore]` live
  module `research_dials_live` (a dial off the scale is a 400 naming it; a
  conversation the caller cannot see is 404; a valid body on a workspace
  with no search path answers the no-search sentence as a 4xx, never a 500).

  Not changed, on purpose: the Plan/Search stages keep their names — a
  3,000-line driver with checkpoints older deploys wrote, for a cosmetic
  rename. A live run needs a search backend and a model; the Z.ai account
  is out of balance, so the loop's live proof waits with the others.

- **`talaria setup` on a checkout that is already set up regenerates nothing — it refreshes the `talaria` PATH shim and the git wiring, and adds only what is missing.** Re-running setup used to re-pull all six infra images and rebuild the toolkit and the auth bridge on every run, so nobody re-ran it, and installs ended up with no `talaria` on PATH at all (the shim was also the LAST step, behind every pull and build that could fail). Now the shim and the `git wt` / pre-push hook wiring come first, before anything slow; images are pulled only when the daemon lacks them (compose is asked what the stack resolves to, the daemon which of those it holds); `mcp/dist` and `omp-auth/dist` are rebuilt only when missing or older than their sources — the same predicate `talaria dev` runs on every boot, now shared rather than re-spelled; and `ui/.env`, `fleet/chassis.yml` and `fleet/.env` are left exactly as they were (the one write that stays is the existing pin of `TALARIA_SECRET_KEY` on a pre-key install, which never generates a value). From a linked worktree the shim keeps pointing at the primary checkout, because a `talaria worktree` is gone the day its pull request merges. A fresh clone gets the full bootstrap as before.
  Verified: `bun run gate` green; `cd cli && bun test` (the new `runSetup` cases: a complete install makes no pull, install or build call and leaves `ui/.env` byte-identical; a fresh root generates everything; a root missing only `mcp/dist` builds only mcp; only the images the daemon lacks are pulled; a linked worktree's shim names the primary). Exercised for real in a `talaria worktree` checkout: the first run found every image present and pulled nothing, built the missing `mcp/dist`, and warned-and-continued on the auth bridge (its dependencies were not installed there); two further runs spawned no docker pull, no bun install and no build, `sha256sum ui/.env` was identical before and after all three, and the shim it wrote names the primary checkout and runs `talaria --help` from another directory.

- **Added:** Three windows into what a pinned agent still holds. At the top of a pinned session's transcript, a row says when the agent compacted earlier messages — how many were folded, at least how many when the session runs past one page, and since when the thread now starts — and never claims a summary it cannot show, because Hermes sends none over the wire; the api answers `GET /api/conversations/{id}/session` from the agent's own session door in one control window, decides server-side whether the row applies, and says nothing for a thread the viewer cannot see. On an agent's Config tab, a Compaction section holds the threshold ratio and the token ceiling, written into the agent's authored `compression` block, versioned like the rest of the config, rolled only on Save & apply, with the note that Hermes raises a threshold under 0.75 for models with less than 512K of context; only a knob you touched travels, so an ordinary save never clears a value the form could not show. The Memory tab gains an entry view beside the whole-file editor: the agent's memory and its user profile as cards you can search, edit, remove or add to, every write applied to the file as it is on disk now and written back as the clean §-delimited list the agent's own memory tool requires, with a lone marker line inside an entry escaped so it can never split one. Verified: `talaria-gateway` 86, `talaria-agent-defs` 11, `talaria-routes-fleet` 35, `talaria-routes-comms` 14, `talaria-agent-memory` 2, `talaria-routes-knowledge` 8 unit tests and clippy clean; the `session_overview_live` module 4/4 on a fresh database (a stranger's 403, an unpinned agent, a pinned agent with no manifest row, a legacy thread); ui vitest 110 files / 1725 tests, svelte-check 0 errors; `bun run docs:api` (the edit route's `compression` member and the session route documented) and `bun run check`; an adversarial review round over the diff with its findings fixed — the reads run concurrently, the answered session id is checked, a partial page reads as a floor, an unreadable date is dropped, `reachable` is null when nothing was asked.

- **Fixed:** A browsing agent could not browse. The toolset switch, the uploads door and the screenshot chip from "an agent can show you the page it saw" were right, but the premise under the roll-time install was not: the hermes-agent image already ships Chromium under its own `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` (in the image layer, which a roll keeps because a roll is the image), and `hermes tools post-setup agent_browser` inside Docker does not download a browser at all — it installs the browser-use CLI onto the state volume and prints a pull hint when it cannot see Chromium. The renderer's override of `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` to an empty directory on the volume therefore hid the bundled browser, and every browser turn failed with "Chromium is missing". The override is gone; the post-health setup keeps running once per volume behind a marker (`/opt/data/.talaria-browser-setup`), for the CLI it does install, and `TALARIA_BROWSER_INSTALL=off` still skips it. The Developer Agent overlay's own Playwright path (its Oh My Pi harness dir) is untouched. Verified: `talaria-fleet-render` 23 and `talaria-fleet-docker` 5 unit tests, clippy clean on the four fleet crates; live on the worktree stack, the first run reproduced the failure (marker written, `/opt/data/.playwright` empty, the agent reporting Chromium missing while `/opt/hermes/.playwright/chromium_headless_shell-1243` sat in the image), and after the fix the rerun's result is recorded in the pull request.

- **The bundled SearXNG sidecar is gone from every stack; fleet agents search with Hermes's own web tools, and the Talaria-side `web_search` MCP tool that duplicated them is removed.** Hermes Agent ships a web-search provider registry of its own (searxng, brave, ddgs, exa, firecrawl, parallel, tavily, perplexity, keenable, xai, with keyless public tiers as the floor), so every agent was getting two `web_search` tools and Talaria was running a metasearch container, an init service to render its settings, DNS pins and a canary query to notice when its engines were CAPTCHA-walled — which on a fresh instance was most of them.
