The org floor stored `["safe"]` as `image_gen, vision, web`, and the admin checklist (screenshot) and the roster's `toolsets.governed` both list the 22 governed names with no composites. CI is the compile and test proof line for the rest of the workspace and the chassis smoke.

- **Changed:** An app's server owns every path under `/api/apps/<slug>/` and gets a fuller request context: the sub-path decoded once as `ctx.segments`, `ctx.api()` to call the platform API as the caller, `ctx.secret(name)` for the workspace secrets an admin gave the app, `ctx.origin`, and `ctx.signal`, which aborts when the caller disconnects. App documents with a malformed id now return "not found" instead of crashing the app, and an app needs `app.ts` only when its manifest declares a surface. The store's `get` and `update` return `null` and `remove` returns `false` for an id that is not a UUID, where Postgres used to refuse the cast and the request came back as a 500 "app crashed". The request path is no longer decoded twice. `%25` used to 500 before the app ran, and it now reaches the handler as a literal `%`. An encoded slash (`%2F`) used to split one segment into two. It is now refused with a 400, so a segment never holds a `/`, and a malformed escape is a 400 rather than a 500. In production a malformed escape on a GET used to get no answer at all, because the static-file check threw on it. The grants example in `docs/sdk/server.md` now checks `ctx.segments[0]`, because a `ctx.path` prefix check missed the bare `admin` path. The host's rebuild route moved from `/api/apps/<slug>/rebuild`, where it took that path from every app, to `/api/app-host/<slug>/rebuild`, a TS resident listed in the generated API reference. Manage → Apps calls the new path, and no caller of the old one remains. `ctx.api(path, init)` sends only the caller's session cookie to the Rust api, so the caller's permissions apply. It returns parsed JSON and throws an `HttpError` carrying the status and the server's sentence. It refuses `/api/apps/`, `/api/app-host/`, the app MCP gateway and `/api/internal`. Reads time out after 30 seconds and writes have no deadline. `ctx.secret` resolves only a workspace vault secret, not expired, whose allowed hosts list `talaria-app://<slug>` exactly, the same entry that lets agent handles reach the app's MCP tools. An unrestricted secret is not readable by app code. Each read spends any use limit and writes a `secrets.spend` audit row (actor `app:<slug>`, plus the reading person's id), and the reason for a refusal goes to the host log. `server-entry.ts` and the vite dev middleware abort the request's signal when the response closes unfinished. The proxy now cancels a read once its caller has gone, and still lets a write run to completion. A read cut because its caller left answers 499 and is not logged: it is not reported as `[rust-proxy] … unreachable` or answered 502, so that log line still means the api is down. A real upstream failure, or a read the 30-second deadline cut, is still a logged 502 even when the caller leaves at the same moment. `ctx.api` follows the same rule: the caller leaving cuts a read and never a write, so a write an app started finishes after the tab closes. A `signal` the app passes still cuts any call. A server-only or MCP-only app with no surfaces builds without a client and enables. Verified: `bun run check`; svelte-check 0 errors; new vitest suites for the route matcher, the store, `ctx.api`/origin/segments (including its read/write split on a caller leaving), the secret rule, the gateway context, the proxy's read/write split and its quiet 499 for a caller who left (with a logged 502 kept for a refused connection or a deadline that fires as the caller leaves), and clientless builds and probes, which `build.test.ts` builds and probes for real. Live on a worktree stack, under `talaria dev`, two scaffolded apps were enabled through Manage → Apps, whose Enable click called `POST /api/app-host/<slug>/rebuild`. Each check below ran as the admin and as a member granted the work view. `GET`, `PATCH` and `DELETE items/123` answered the app's own 404, and a real id worked. `echo/files/100%25` reached the app as `["echo","files","100%"]`, `%2F` and a lone `%` answered 400, and `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE rebuild` all reached the app's own handler. `ctx.api('/api/auth/session')` returned the caller's own id and role. `/api/boards` listed only the caller's own boards. `/api/admin/users` returned the admin's list and threw `HttpError(403)` for the member. The allowed secret resolved for both callers and wrote audit rows naming each person. Secrets locked to another host, unrestricted or unknown returned null, with the reason logged. With forwarded headers `ctx.origin` was `https://talaria.example.com`. A 15-second handler cut by curl at 2 seconds logged `aborted` at about 2,000 ms with no crash, and the uncut control finished at 15,002 ms. The server-only app (no `app.ts`, no surfaces) built and enabled, answered its admin and refused the member (no surface to grant). Then `bun run build` and `bun server-entry.ts` on the same stack. The server-only app built `server.js` and `mcp.js` and no `app.js`. Its boot probe first refused it, because it reused the dev build made without them (the shared build key, noted on #583), and Enable in Manage → Apps rebuilt it. The same probe gave the same answers for both callers. `HttpError` from the built SDK passed `instanceof` for the member's 403. A malformed `GET /api/healthz%` answered 400, where it used to hang. The slow handler cut at 2 seconds logged `aborted` at about 2,000 ms under Bun, and the member's work surface loaded the built `app.js` and added an item with no page errors.

- **Fixed:** A workchain step whose predecessor is still open is no longer dispatched to its agent, and the dead mission-control heartbeat contract is gone. The only code that kept an agent off a blocked step was the heartbeat's `assigned_work`, and nothing called the heartbeat: the `plugin/talaria` plugin that would have was mounted nowhere. So a blocked step sitting in a pickup column with an agent assigned got a work session while the step before it was still live. Now `maybe_dispatch_ticket` asks the chain order (`talaria_tasks::workchain_blocked`, over `talaria_workchains::chain_readiness`) once per ticket before any per-agent side effect. The sixty-second sweep asks it once per pass and logs held steps as `waiting on an earlier workchain step` instead of counting them as re-offered. The work-session loop asks the new `agent_work_refusal` on every turn, so a session whose predecessor a person reopens stops with "agents cannot work this ticket yet: an earlier step of its workchain is still open". A sign-off that makes successors ready offers each one to dispatch straight away, rather than waiting up to a minute for the sweep. The agent cannot start a waiting step by hand either: its own status move into a working column or review (a terminal move included, since it lands in review) is refused with the same sentence, and so is a workbench `start_job` or repo request whose `taskId` names the step. Everything else stays open: agents still comment on, edit fields of, report problems against and triage a waiting step, including moving it to an open column or raising Blocked. The toolkit's `triage_ticket` and `report_outcome` descriptions, the workbench `taskId` descriptions and `whoami`'s guardrails say so. Deleted: `plugin/talaria/`, `POST /api/agents/register`, `GET /api/agents/{id}/heartbeat`, the `talaria-agents-registry` crate, `assigned_work`, Rust `fleet_caller`/`check_fleet_key` and their TS twins, and `TALARIA_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS` from the render and the chassis template. `GET /api/fleet` status is now plain container state (`idle` running, `offline` otherwise), which is all it ever reported, and `lastSeen`/`lastActivity` are gone from the response. The `fleet_agents` table stays until a contract migration drops it. Verified: `bun run gate` green (check, ui typecheck and tests, fmt, clippy `-D warnings` and tests for every touched package). `workchains_live` 13/13 against a live worktree database, including the rewritten ordering test. That test drives the real dispatch assembly: no work-session row for the blocked step, the work question refuses it, a field edit lands, the agent's moves to `in_progress`, `quality_review` and `done` are each refused with the chain's sentence, a workbench `start_job` through `dispatch_workbench_mcp` is refused with it, the sign-off hands B back for dispatch, and one row once step 1 is done. With the dispatch gate switched off (rc's behaviour), the same test fails with `left: 1, right: 0`. With the patch's chain clause switched off it fails at the `in_progress` move (`left: None`), and with the workbench binding asking only the write question it fails because `start_job` gets past the ticket gate to `GitHub is not connected`. Each switch-off was restored byte for byte (sha256 checked). Live on a worktree stack with a Hermes v0.22.4 agent (pinned digest), a person moving step 2 into "assigned" for the agent started no session, and the next sweep logged `(1 waiting on an earlier workchain step)`. Signing step 1 off dispatched step 2 62 ms later, and the agent took the turn through the gateway. Reopening step 1 ended that session on its next turn with the chain's reason, and once the settle window passed the sweep held step 2 again with no new session. `GET /api/fleet` answered 200 with `idle`, `offline` with the container stopped and `idle` again after a restart. The Agents page showed `1/1 online` and Comms showed the agent's green dot. Both deleted routes answer 404 to the agent's own key, and the container env carries no `TALARIA_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS`. On the same stack, with the agent's own key against the real api, `PUT /api/tasks/{step 2}` answered 403 with the chain's sentence for `in_progress`, `quality_review` and `done` while step 1 was in progress. A tag edit and a comment answered 200, and a move to `inbox` answered 200. After a person signed step 1 off, the hand-off push created step 2's run 66 ms later, and the same `in_progress` move answered 200. With step 1 reopened and the agent switched to a Developer Agent with one granted repo, `start_job` through `/api/mcp/gw/workbench` with step 2's `taskId` answered "agents cannot work this ticket yet … Ticket CGE-2 starts once the step before it is signed off — until then, omit taskId". Once step 1 was signed off, the same call got past the ticket gate to "GitHub is not connected", and no job row was written. `whoami` lists the new guardrail. The full workspace compile and test run is CI's.

- **Fixed: one broken file in an app's `harnesses/` no longer fails the app's build and switches the app off, one malformed app harness no longer drops every app's harnesses from Models → Fitness, and Manage → Apps' harness lines follow the enabled set.** Since #589 the harness build sat in the same try as the client, server and MCP builds, so a syntax error, an import that does not resolve, or a shared package bundled into one harness file failed the whole build, and reconcile disabled the app (build recipe 3 rebuilt every installed app on upgrade, so an app with a stray harness file was switched off at boot). The build now compiles `harnesses/` on its own terms: when the combined build fails, each file is compiled alone to find the ones that break it, the rest are built into `harnesses.js`, and each file left out is named in its new `skipped` export with the compiler's sentence (one line, the app's own path, no code frame). If even that fails, the app still builds, with no harness. The host reads `skipped` and reports each file as "it failed to compile: …" on the app's row. Build recipe 4. The load probe's checks now cover every field the listing puts on the wire: a JSON harness's `repair` must be a whole number from 0 to 5 (NaN and Infinity reached the api as null, and past a u32 the api failed the whole listing and fell back to the builtins), the `model` spec's pin, role and chain must be names and a list (`chain: 3` threw inside the listing route, which answered 503), and `floor.suppliable` and `widen.requires` must be lists. A definition whose checking throws is a problem on that harness. On the api side, `talaria-app-harnesses` decodes the listing one entry at a time: an entry it cannot read is skipped with a warning and reported on its app, and the others still register. The harness reports in Manage → Apps are rewritten for every enabled app whenever the enabled set changes: after each live load probe, when a failed app is switched off, and when the api enables, disables or uninstalls an app (a new `POST /api/app-host/harnesses`). So when an app that sorts first is enabled and claims the same id, the app that held it now shows the skip, and gets the id back when that app is switched off. A disabled app's chip reads "N harnesses · not registered". A skipped harness is logged once per distinct app, file and problem per process, in the host and in the api, instead of on every listing the fitness matrix's polling triggers. The fitness sweep's skip for an app harness that wants its own tool loop now names the real reason (an app harness cannot be dry-run in the api's sandbox) instead of saying the model can neither run its own loop nor be handed tool definitions. Verified: `bun run gate` exited 0 — check, svelte-check with 0 errors, the full ui suite (2347 tests), and `cargo test` plus clippy `-D warnings` on talaria-app-harnesses (9), talaria-fitness (423) and talaria-routes-admin (16). New tests: a real app build with one good and two broken harness files (a syntax error, an import that does not resolve) builds ready, the good harness registers and each broken file is reported with a one-line, app-relative sentence; one with no file that compiles still builds ready; the 12 new malformed-wire definitions (NaN, Infinity, negative, fractional, over-u32 and string `repair`; non-list `chain`; non-string `pin` and `role`; non-list `suppliable` and `widen.requires`) are each refused by name, and a listing with three such harnesses in one app still lists the other app's and serialises every `repair` as a u32; the api decodes a listing holding an overflowing `repair`, a null `repair`, a missing floor and a non-object, registers the one good entry and reports the rest; the report refresh moves a contested id to the app that sorts first and back, through the probe and `failHealth` on real build pointers; a skip is warned once over five listings; the sweep's app tool-loop skip carries its own sentence. Exercised with the real host shim (`bun run build`): a scratch app with a good harness and three broken files (a syntax error, a missing module, a bare `svelte` import) built ready with `harnesses.js` holding the good chunk and a `skipped` export naming the three, and the production loader and listing reported them. Live on this branch's worktree stack under `talaria dev`, with two scratch apps both shipping `fx:triage`: zeta-fx (plus a `model: { chain: 3 }` harness) enabled showed "2 harnesses" and the chain file skipped; alpha-fx (plus a file with a syntax error) rebuilt `ready` instead of failed; enabling alpha-fx through `PUT /api/admin/apps` rewrote zeta-fx's report to name `app "alpha-fx" already registers "fx:triage"`, and the fitness matrix showed both apps' remaining columns; disabling it gave zeta-fx the id back and Manage → Apps showed alpha-fx's chip as "1 harness · not registered". Over repeated fitness polls the host logged each of the three skips once.

- **Fixed:** **Kept app data goes back only to the repository it was kept from, opening Manage → Apps no longer spends a workspace secret, and an update keeps its record true when it fails.** These are the review findings on #588. (1) The automatic update check no longer asks a source that is read with a workspace secret. Each check spent a use of the secret and wrote a `secrets.spend` row, so viewing the page could use up a limited secret and leave the app unable to update. Such an app now shows **update not checked**, and Update fetches with the secret. Sources read with a GitHub-minted token, and public ones, are still checked. (2) Install now writes the repository into the app's data directory (`app-data/<slug>/source.json`), and an uninstall that keeps the data keeps that record too. For an app installed before this change, uninstall writes it from the source record. A reinstall from the same repository adopts the data as before. A different repository installed under the same slug, or kept data with no record, is refused with a 409 that names both repositories, until the request says `keptData: "adopt"` or `"wipe"`. Before, it silently got the old app's store and database password. Manage → Apps shows both choices as buttons. (3) A host typed with capitals (`https://GitHub.com/…`) now gets its credential. Git is pointed at the parsed URL with the host lowercased, so askpass answers for it. Before, the token was minted and git never received it. (4) Install now takes the same per-slug lock as update and uninstall, so it cannot race either one. (5) When the new version fails and swapping the old one back also fails, the answer now says `rolledBack: false`. The UI says that `apps/<slug>` holds the new commit, and the record follows. (6) A failed update no longer deletes `apps/.<slug>.prev`. The version an update replaces stays at `.next` until the new one is live, so `previousSha` always names what `.prev` holds. (7) A released update now discards the build its stage made. On a platform without the atomic swap, update is refused before it fetches anything. (8) The published schema and both validators now agree on `triggers`. A trigger has exactly one of `cron` or `event`, and that one is a string that is not only whitespace. Verified: new `#[ignore]`d live tests in `talaria-apps` (`lifecycle::live`) run against a freshly migrated scratch database. They use local bare git repositories and a mock app host over HTTP. They drive install → update (lands, fails to build, the stage call errors, fails to load, swap back fails) → uninstall (keep and wipe), and the trees and `app_sources` are asserted after every step. They also cover the kept-data refusal, adopt and wipe, the legacy record, and the slug lock: all 4 pass. Before this change, a new `git_credentials` test failed with git's own `could not read Username for 'http://LocalHost:…': terminal prompts disabled`; it passes now. There are new unit tests for the passive check, which must not touch credentials when a secret is named, and for the kept-data decision. The shared manifest fixture has new trigger cases that both hosts assert. A schema test reads `triggers.items` case by case against the validator, and it fails on the old schema. `update.test.ts` has a release test. `cargo test`/`clippy -D warnings` pass on `talaria-apps`, `talaria-app-manifest` and `talaria-routes-admin`, and `bun run gate` is green.

- **Fixed: an app tool call now matches what production does in five places the #587 review found.** First, the gateway no longer starts an app tool's handler when the agent has already left: an agent that disconnected while its access resolved or its credentials were spent used to get the handler run anyway, with its side effects, on a call recorded as cancelled. Second, the call record no longer keeps a refused result's own keys. When a result failed its `outputSchema`, the -32603 sentence the record keeps quoted zod's report, keys and paths included (`✖ Unrecognized key: "secretKey"`). It now names only zod's issue codes and counts (`1 × invalid_type, 1 × unrecognized_keys`). Third, the app gateway's -32700 answer now agrees with the Rust gateway's serde_json. Nesting deeper than 127 arrays or objects, a lone surrogate escape (`"\ud800"`), and an overlong or encoded-surrogate UTF-8 sequence used to be accepted or reported at offset 0. They are now refused in serde's words, at serde's line, column and offset. In `@talaria/sdk/testing`, `callAppTool` with `caller: { proven: false }` now gives the null `id` the gateway sends, where it used to give `"test-agent"`. A call cut by `signal` now says the caller disconnected rather than claiming the time limit passed, and the result's new `cutBy` field says which cut happened (`"deadline"` or `"caller"`). `cut` is unchanged. Verified: new tests for each case, all failing on `rc` and passing here. The -32700 answers were compared with serde_json 1.0.151 (the api's `Cargo.lock` pin) through a standalone probe: the 34 review cases agree, and so do 30,000 mutated request bodies (679 of them disagreed on `rc`). The vitest suites for the app MCP call, gateway and SDK testing pass, and `bun run gate` is green.

- **Fixed:** **`bun run check` no longer dies in a checkout where an app has run its database, and a worktree cut from a newer ref gets that ref's chassis and says when an older CLI set it up.** The doc-link walk in `scripts/check-docs.mjs` read every directory under the checkout. `app-data/<slug>/pg` belongs to the app database container's user, so once any app had started its database the walk threw `EACCES` and the whole check chain failed. The walk now lives in `scripts/markdown-walk.mjs`. It skips `app-data/` and `app-builds/`, the app platform's dev state, and it skips any other directory it cannot read and names it, where before it crashed. Both directories are now gitignored, and `.dockerignore` keeps them out of the image's build context (an app's `db.env` is a password file). `talaria worktree` runs the CLI of the checkout it is invoked from, usually the primary on `main`, not the base ref's CLI. It seeded `fleet/chassis.yml` from that checkout's template too, so a stack cut from `rc` got `main`'s chassis, with an older Hermes image line and env lines `rc`'s renderer had dropped. The chassis now comes from the worktree's own `scripts/chassis.template.yml`, and from the invoking checkout's only when the base ref has none. When the running `cli/src/cmd/worktree.ts` differs from the base ref's, the command now ends with a warning that names both. On 2026-10-22 a stack was cut this way with no `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT`, because the primary's CLI predated that line. `rc`'s CLI writes `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT`, `TALARIA_RUST_API_URL` and the chassis on every path: `ui/.env` is always written fresh, and a second run against an existing worktree dies before it writes anything. Verified: on `rc`, an unreadable `app-data/repro/pg` failed `bun run check` with `EACCES, scandir`, and with the fix the same tree passed the whole chain. An unreadable `docs/` subdirectory was skipped and named. New check-docs tests cover the exempt runtime directories, an unreadable directory (which fails the old walk with `EACCES`), and a missing root, which still throws. A new worktree test plants a base-ref checkout with its own template and `worktree.ts`: the chassis is the base ref's, and exactly one warning names the base ref. That test fails without the fix. `setupDiffers` is covered for the same file, a different one, and a base ref without one. Live: this branch's CLI cut `fx-dev-traps-probe` from `origin/rc`. Its `fleet/chassis.yml` was byte-identical to the probe's own `rc` template, its `ui/.env` carried `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT`, `TALARIA_RUST_API_URL` pointing at its own api port, and its other ports, and the run ended with the warning. The probe was then torn down. `scripts/cleanup-sweep.test.mjs` passes, and a dry-run sweep kept `talaria-wt-fx-dev-traps`. `bun run gate` is green.

- **prepare_env's toolchain block now reaches the shell the agent's terminal actually runs.** Hermes v0.22.4 runs terminal commands with `HOME=/opt/data/home`, not the agent user's passwd home (`/opt/data`), where the mise block was the only one written. A new terminal session still picked the block up, because Hermes sources the gateway's own `~/.profile` before it snapshots a session. A shell the agent opened before calling prepare_env did not: following the advice to run `. ~/.profile` read the empty terminal home and left the repo's toolchains off PATH. The block also found mise through `$HOME`, which under the terminal's HOME named an empty data dir and no global bun pin. prepare_env now writes the block into both homes and carries mise's data dir and global config as absolute paths. The `usage` text also says shims resolve from inside the repo. Verified: before and after on the pinned `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a69…a4cf`, driving Hermes's own terminal tool through its API server with a stub model. The model asked for one terminal call before prepare_env ran and one after, in the same session; on rc `. ~/.profile` found no file and `jq` (pinned by the repo's mise.toml) did not resolve, and with the fix it did. The new devenv tests run USER_SH with a stub mise and source the terminal home's profile. `bun run gate` is green; CI is the full-workspace proof line.

- **Fixed:** A credential sealed out of an agent's own config no longer reaches the agent's `execute_code` scripts. Since federation started sealing inline config credentials as `CONFIG_*` per-agent secrets (#579), and the render started listing every per-agent secret in `terminal.env_passthrough` (#572), the two together handed a platform token or a named provider's key to every script the agent ran: Hermes admits a credential-looking name into `execute_code` only by passthrough, and the list now named them. `passthrough_names` leaves out the `CONFIG_` prefix, so only the secrets a manager gave the agent for its own tools are listed; the sealed ones still reach Hermes through `secrets.env` and the config's `${CONFIG_…}` handles. The plain terminal still inherits the container env as before: Hermes strips only its own names there, and the same literal sat in the agent's readable `config.yaml` before #579. Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-agent-secrets` (28 passed, including a new test that runs `plan_config_seal` and checks every minted name stays out) and `bun run gate`. Exercised on this branch's own stack with the pinned `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a69…a4cf`: a federated roster with an inline `providers.acme.api_key` and `platforms.telegram.token` sealed to `CONFIG_PROVIDERS_ACME_API_KEY` and `CONFIG_PLATFORMS_TELEGRAM_TOKEN`, plus a manager-set `FIGMA_TOKEN`. The rendered `terminal.env_passthrough` is `[FIGMA_TOKEN]`. Inside the running container, Hermes's own `_scrub_child_env` gave `execute_code` only `FIGMA_TOKEN`; with the list `origin/rc` renders it gave all three. Hermes's `load_config()` still resolved both handles to the original literals. CI is the proof line for the rest of the workspace.

- **Fixed:** Two worktree stacks running agents at once no longer collide. Every stack used to hand its first agent gateway port `8770` (each allocates from its own database, and every database starts with none), so the second stack's hire failed with `port is already allocated`. Every stack's api also spawned its toolkit MCP on `:5280` and its omp auth bridge on `:5276`. Both probe their port first and adopt whatever answers, so the second stack's agents had their tool calls served by the first stack's toolkit, which refused their keys (`401` from `/api/mcp/gw/talaria`). Now `talaria worktree` gives each slot its own toolkit port (`57xx`), omp auth port (`58xx`) and a hundred agent gateway ports from `20000 + slot·100`, written to the worktree's `ui/.env` as `TALARIA_MCP_PORT`, `TALARIA_OMP_AUTH_PORT` and `TALARIA_GATEWAY_PORT_BASE` and lifted into the api by `talaria dev`. A slot is free only when all of those are. The api allocates agent gateway ports from `TALARIA_GATEWAY_PORT_BASE` (default unchanged at `8770`), still continuing past the highest port ever assigned. The worktree seed clears the gateway ports copied from main's agents, so a worktree never publishes onto main's live fleet. Separately, the built-in Talaria toolkit row in `mcp_servers` now has its url rewritten on every boot: it was insert-only, so a seeded database, or any install whose `TALARIA_MCP_PORT` changed, kept pointing the MCP gateway at a stale toolkit port. Devboxes do not share the problem (their agents are dialled by container name and their api's children bind inside the box), so they are unchanged.
  Verified: `bun run check` green; `bun test src/cmd/worktree.test.ts src/cmd/dev.test.ts` 44/44 (slot math, the range-overlap sweep over all 89 slots, the generated env lines, the seed's port clear running after the restore and only against the worktree's database, the api env lift); new Rust unit tests for the base parse, the allocator floor and the upsert's conflict arm. `bun run gate` green (check; cli tsc + 262 tests; fmt, clippy `-D warnings` and tests for talaria-fleet-layout, talaria-fleet-render and talaria-mcp — the three new Rust tests confirmed by name). Live, two worktree stacks at once on this branch: `hx-wt-ports` (slot 5, its ui/.env given the three new lines by hand because the old CLI cut it) and `hx-wt-ports-b` (slot 6, cut by this branch's `talaria worktree`, which printed `gateway ports from :20600 · toolkit :5706 · omp auth :5806`). Each hired an agent on `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a6920…` through `POST /api/fleet/create`; both came up healthy together on `127.0.0.1:20500->8642` and `127.0.0.1:20600->8642` (`agent_defs`: `porta:20500`, `portb:20600`). Each stack's toolkit listened on its own port with its own api (`:5705` with `TALARIA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:5405`, `:5706` with `:5406`), each `mcp_servers` talaria row named its own (`127.0.0.1:5705/mcp`, `127.0.0.1:5706/mcp`), and from inside each agent container an MCP `initialize` + `tools/list` through that stack's `/api/mcp/gw/talaria` with the agent's own key answered 200 with the 84-tool toolkit. A stale `http://127.0.0.1:5280/mcp` planted in stack A's row was rewritten to `:5705` when its api restarted. The seed's clear statement nulls a populated `agent_defs` (checked inside a rolled-back transaction) and runs clean on a database with no `agent_defs`. CI is the full-workspace proof line.

- **New: every app harness has a model setting of its own, `app:<slug>/<harnessId>`, that an admin assigns in Admin → Models → Fitness.** An "App harness models" list under the fitness matrix shows each app column's setting and saves a pick at once (`PUT /api/admin/app-harness-models`; `GET` lists the assignments and the slots an enabled app registers). The new `ModelSpec.slot` is set by the host on every bound run, never by the app, and the new `slot` chain step resolves it before `role` in any chain, from an `app_harness_models` setting both resolvers read (`ui/src/server/app-harness-models.ts`, `talaria-harness-model`). Like a platform pin it is not gated by the member allowlist and wins only while its model routes; the run records `step: 'slot'`. The route refuses a slot no enabled app registers and a model the gateway does not serve, and always lets a stale assignment be cleared. `ticket-relevance` was already a platform agent id on both sides. Verified: chain tests in TS and Rust (the slot before the role in default, custom and empty chains; a pin still first; fallthrough when unassigned or stale; not allowlist-gated; `chain_with_slot` and `chainWithSlot` agree), the registry test for the slot on an app harness def, and live: the matrix payload carried the app column's assignment, the route refused a non-admin, a non-app slot, an unregistered harness and an unknown model, and a pick in the fitness page through Playwright saved, audited as `app_harness.assign`, and moved the next run onto the new model with `step: 'slot'`.

- **New: an app harness can declare a tool loop the runner holds, `loop: { tools, maxTurns? }`, and the fitness sweep dry-runs it when every tool has a `simulate`.** Each tool is a `ToolDefinition` plus exactly one road: `handler(args, ctx)` (the app's code), `mcp: '<tool>'` (the app's own MCP tool, through the same dispatch an agent's call takes) or `org: '<server>/<tool>'` (an org MCP tool, through the MCP gateway as the agent that called the app, presenting that agent's own key, so its grants, its owner's allowance and the call record apply; a request or a trigger has no agent, and the model is told so). The loop lives in the TS runner, because the tools are app code, and keeps the rules of research's tool-search loop and the fitness dry run: at most three calls a turn, a last turn's calls still dispatched, failures and unknown tools answered as tool results, calls on the tool channel, a closing turn with the tools taken away when the turns run out, a repair turn that continues the conversation. Results gain `toolCalls`, `calls` (the `EvalContext.calls` shape) and `exhausted`, and the guard is grounded in what the tools returned. Every field is optional: a harness with no loop runs exactly as before, `toolDefs` still only offers, and a loop does not stream. The app host checks a loop at load (one road per tool, real names, no clash with `toolDefs`, `maxTurns` 1–12) and lists each tool's road and `simulate` on the wire; the sweep sends a loop harness's fixtures to the host only when every tool simulates and the candidate takes tool definitions, the host replays with every tool answered by `simulate`, and the case keeps the calls. A loop with an unsimulated tool keeps #595's skip, naming the tools. `runHarnessOffline` scripts tool calls and runs handlers for real (or everything through `simulate`). Verified: `bun run gate`; the new `loop.test.ts` (dispatch and the tool channel, three calls a turn, an unknown tool, a failing tool, exhaustion and the closing turn, repair, mcp and org roads with and without a host, a dry run touching nothing real, grounding firing on an uncited link and not on a returned one, no streaming, no loop fields on a plain run); load checks, the wire and a simulated replay in `app-harnesses.test.ts`; the runner's per-context roads; Rust tests for the loop on the wire, `app_loop_skip_reason`, and a sweep that dry-runs the simulating harness through the host and skips the other. Live on a worktree stack with a mock gateway model and a mock org MCP server: a member's request ran a handler and the app's own MCP tool (which saw the harness run as its caller and the member as the person acted for); the org tool from a request answered the model that it needs an agent; an agent calling the app's MCP tool on its own key ran the org tool through the Rust gateway, recorded in `mcp_tool_calls` as that agent, and narrowing the agent's tool subset turned the same call into the gateway's refusal; `stream` refused the loop; an evals sweep scored the simulating harness through `simulate` (pass, its calls kept) and skipped the org one naming `search_docs`.

- **Changed: an app runs its harnesses through `ctx.harness`, a runner the host binds to the caller it authenticated, and the free `runHarness` no longer takes `deps`.** `ctx.harness.run(def, input, options)` and `ctx.harness.stream(def, input, { onDelta })` are on the request context and the MCP tool context, built by one factory (`appHarnessRunner`, `ui/src/server/app-harness-runner.ts`) that the trigger context will call too. The host now decides what the app used to: every run is recorded as `app:<slug>:<harnessId>` and booked to ledger source `app` (new in TS and as `LedgerSource::App` in Rust; gateway rows carry it, and now the run's `refId`/`taskId` too when they are UUIDs), the definition is held to the platform's harness rules (the JSON floor included, even for one built without `defineHarness`), and nothing an app passes reaches the guard, the transport or the recorders. **Pinning is gated:** from a request, an agent only if the signed-in member may use it (the api's `usable_agent_gate`, asked through `GET /api/agents` with their session) and a gateway model only if the member model allowlist opens it to them; from an MCP tool, only the calling agent, and only when it called on its own key; from a trigger, no agent. A refused run makes no model call and follows the harness's `onFailure`. **Breaking for app tests:** `deps` is gone from the SDK's `RunContext` and is dropped, with a warning, if passed anyway; the free `runHarness` also warns when it pins an agent, since it checks nothing. Test a harness offline with the new `runHarnessOffline` in `@talaria/sdk/testing` (scripted replies, capabilities on record, every request returned). Verified: `bun run gate`, the new `app-harness-runner.test.ts` (stamping, ledger, slot, deps ignored, JSON floor, rule refusal, `onFailure: 'throw'`, every pin case for request, MCP and trigger, streaming, signals, the free runner's warnings), the SDK doc tests moved onto `runHarnessOffline`, and `cargo test`/clippy on the touched crates. Live on a worktree stack with a scratch app and a mock OpenAI-compatible endpoint registered through the gateway: runs and streams came back booked `app:w4probe:w4probe:triage`, source `app`, with the ticket id on the row and a non-UUID `refId` dropped with a warning; a member pinning an agent they cannot see, or a model outside the allowlist, was refused with the sentence above and no call; their usable agent and an allowed model passed; an admin's pin passed; an agent calling the app's MCP tool on its own key ran the harness, and its pin of another agent was refused; the free runner logged both warnings.

- **Changed: every model call an app makes goes through the Talaria gateway on the app's own key, and the app host's second gateway is gone.** An app's harness runs (from its `server.ts`, an MCP tool, or a fitness replay of its fixtures) used to reach providers from inside the app host: the host decrypted provider keys, built and sent the request, learned parameter rejections, checked a budget and wrote its own ledger rows. That copy recorded no provider-reported cost, left a reply without usage unmetered, filed the spend under whatever caller name the app passed (so an app could spend under another app's name), checked the budget on one call path of three, read capability probe facts the api had already retired (json-strict below probe revision 1), and filed app spend as `chat` or `gateway`. A harness turn on a fleet agent was metered twice: once by the host, and again at the relay, where the agent's own calls landed as `unattended` because no turn was recorded. A `refId` that was not a uuid, which the SDK doc example passes, dropped the host's ledger row. Now every call the host's runner makes is a POST to `/api/llm/v1/chat/completions` on a per-app key named `app:<slug>`. The api mints the key when the host first asks (the new internal route `POST /api/internal/apps/<slug>/llm-key`), seals it in `app_llm_keys` (rotated by the secret rotation, listed in Admin → Secrets), and revokes it when the app is disabled or uninstalled; the host keeps it in memory and app code never sees it. The relay trusts the key only while that record holds its id, and `POST /api/keys` refuses names starting with `app:`. The host decides which app is calling, not the app: every boundary where it runs app code (`isolateApp`, an MCP tool handler, a replay) marks the app, and a model call outside one is refused. The relay books each call with ledger source `app` under the run's caller stamp, kept inside the app's namespace (`fitness:x` becomes `app:<slug>:fitness:x`, and `app:other:…` becomes `app:<slug>:app:other:…`). It records the provider's cost, estimates a reply without usage, and books the run's ref and ticket only when they are uuids, never at the cost of the row. It enforces the app's budget (`app:<slug>` in Admin → Security → LLM budgets, summed over every stamp under it) on every call. A model that is a live fleet agent is driven for one turn through the persona door with the turn recorded as `app` spend, so the agent's own calls are its only meter. The relay runs no guard pass of its own for an app's key, because the runner's pass with the harness's own rule set is the one of record. Fitness replays of app harnesses now report the provider's own token counts instead of the chars/4 estimate. Deleted from the app host: the upstream builder and fetcher, the parameter learner (`harness/gateway-params.ts`), the budget check, the gateway stats ring, the ledger writer (`usage.ts`), `completeViaGateway`, `recordGatewayUsage`, `guardCompletion`, `meterPersonaTurn`, `personaProbeTurn` and the direct agent proxy (`proxyChat`). What stays in `llm-gateway.ts` is the model catalog and the routing read the runner resolves models and capability keys with. Verified: `bun run gate` exited 0. That covers check, svelte-check with 0 errors, the full ui suite (2310 tests), and `cargo test` plus clippy `-D warnings` on the eight touched api packages. There are new Rust tests for the key vocabulary, the stamp namespace, the budget family, the persona base, the key record and the stale-key sweep, plus a live-DB test (run against the worktree's Postgres) that an app row keeps a uuid ref, drops a non-uuid one without dropping the row, and that the app's budget sums its stamps and nothing beside them. New ui tests cover the transports against a stubbed relay (signed with the key of the app in scope, refused outside one, a 401 re-asks once, the relay's own sentence on a failure, real usage on a plain completion, the persona turn's hold and refs), the scope at each boundary, the key cache, the replay's stamp, and the probe-revision rule. Exercised on this branch's worktree stack with a mock provider registered as a gateway endpoint: a scratch app's harness run from its server landed one usage row, `app:gwprobe:triage`, source `app`, the run's uuid ref, 111/22 tokens not estimated, and the provider's $0.000321 cost. A non-uuid ref booked the row with no ref; a caller of `app:billing:x` booked `app:gwprobe:app:billing:x`; a streamed call on the app key relayed with `x-talaria-transport: gateway` and booked its row. A replay through `POST /api/app-host/gwprobe/harnesses/gwprobe:triage/cases/…` passed with 111/22 tokens and `estimated: false`, booked as `app:gwprobe:fitness:gwprobe:triage`. A budget of 500 tokens on `app:gwprobe` (665 spent across its stamps) refused the next run with the gateway's budget sentence and no provider call. A harness pinned to a fake fleet agent went through the persona door: the agent's own inner call on its `agent:` key was the turn's only row, booked under the agent with source `app` and the run's ref, and the host wrote none. A key named `app:gwprobe` that the record does not hold got 401, and `POST /api/keys` refused the name. Disabling the app revoked its key (the held copy got 401, and the internal route answered 404). Re-enabling it minted a new key, and the host's next run swapped its stale copy on the relay's 401 and succeeded. Uninstalling revoked the key too.

- **Added:** An app's code can now run with nobody calling it, and drive a fleet agent. The `triggers` an app declares in `talaria.json` run: a `cron` schedule (five fields or `@daily` and friends, read in UTC) fires the handler its `server.ts` names in `defineAppServer({ triggers })` within 30 seconds of its minute, through the api's one scheduler (`app-triggers` job, leased), and an `event` trigger fires on `ticket.created` or `ticket.moved`, the two changes the tasks engine already announces, with a payload of ids and column keys only. A triggered run acts as the app with no user: its context has the store, the secrets an admin gave the app and the cause, no `ctx.user`, no `ctx.api`, and it may not drive an agent. Every run is recorded (`app_trigger_runs`: queued, running, ok, failed or skipped, with the handler's own line or the error) and shown on the app's row in Manage → Apps; a failing trigger never turns the app off. Only an enabled app with a ready build fires; disabling an app or a failed build disarms its schedules, and turning it back on re-arms them rather than catching up. Install now refuses a schedule that does not parse, an event the platform does not emit and a reused trigger id, with the reason. Separately, `ctx.agents.turn({ agent, message, session?, watch? })` on the request and MCP tool contexts sends one turn to a fleet agent through the fleet's own chat door (`POST /api/internal/apps/agent-turn`), on a Hermes session the app keys (the agent keeps the transcript; Talaria stores none) or fresh, streaming the agent's words and tool calls to `watch` and resolving with the reply. The api decides who may drive whom from what the host authenticated: from a request only an agent that person may use, from an MCP tool only the proven calling agent, from a trigger none. The turn's spend is booked to the agent under ledger source `app`.
  Verified: `bun run gate` green; cargo fmt, clippy `-D warnings` and tests for the nine touched crates (talaria-platform-events, talaria-app-manifest with its new cron grammar, talaria-app-agents, talaria-app-triggers, talaria-scheduler, talaria-tasks, talaria-jobs, talaria-routes-admin, talaria-api-routes); the shared manifest fixture gained the events list and nine trigger cases, asserted by both hosts; ui tests for the trigger runner, the agents client and the server-module probe; `migrations:check` replayed all 481 statements on a fresh Postgres and matched the regenerated snapshot (additions only), then applied 0 in a second process. Live on a worktree stack with a scratch app declaring `tick` (`* * * * *`), `flaky` (`*/2`, throws), `on-new` (`ticket.created`) and `on-move` (`ticket.moved`): `tick` ran every minute with its line recorded, `flaky` was recorded failed each time with its sentence while the app stayed enabled, creating a ticket and moving it inbox → in_progress → done recorded three event runs whose payloads carried the ids, column keys and `closed: true` and none of the ticket's title or description, and `on-new`'s attempt to drive an agent was refused with the trigger sentence. Disabling the app stopped every run (a ticket created meanwhile queued none) and emptied `app_trigger_state`; re-enabling re-armed it at 16:35:31 and fired first at 16:36, not the two minutes missed; editing `flaky`'s schedule re-armed that trigger alone. Manage → Apps showed each trigger's schedule, last run and line, the failure in red (screenshot via Playwright). Agent turns ran against a Hermes-shaped stand-in registered in the stack's fleet manifest (this stack has no model provider to hire a real agent with): two turns with `session: "notes"` landed on one session id, the second answering with the first message in its transcript; a turn without a key went the completions way; `watch` received the tool start and finish and the words as they streamed; `usage_attributions` recorded the session's key under source `app`; driving another person's personal assistant, an agent not in the fleet, an MCP actor that was unproven or not the calling agent, or any agent from a trigger was refused with a 403 and its sentence, before any turn started.

- **Plugins are kept maintained: the workbench job sweep reads each plugin's PRs and puts its maintainer back to work, a merged change waits for an admin as an update approval, and a broken build, a host-upgrade break or an eval regression becomes a ticket for the maintainer.** The `workbench-job-sweep` now runs a plugin pass after its workspace passes. It never merges, pushes, comments on GitHub or edits a repository: its GitHub calls are all GETs.
  - **PR pass.** For each open PR on a GitHub plugin's repo it reads the checks verdict and the review decision (the `pr_status` read). Failing checks or a change request is a comment on the PR's ticket naming the failing checks and the reviewers. On a PR a workbench job opened, the maintainer is then assigned, the ticket moves out of review into the board's working column, and the ticket is offered to dispatch, which honours a person's stop. A PR somebody else opened is said on the plugin's ticket, and nobody is put on it. Checks are reported once per head commit and a change request once per review, so a fix pushed under a standing review does not wake the agent again. A PR that merges is a line on its ticket.
  - **Update pass.** When the plugin's branch moves past the installed commit, the sweep raises an `app_update` approval (admin-only, bounded to the plugin's board). It announces the approval at once, says so on the plugin's ticket naming the merged PRs, and keeps one waiting update per plugin. **Update** in Manage → Apps → Plugin updates runs `update_app`, which builds and probes the new version beside the live one, swaps it in and rolls back on failure. **Reject** takes a reason. A plugin set to `auto` is updated by the sweep itself. Each outcome is a line on the plugin's ticket, and a commit an admin rejected, or one that failed to apply, is not raised again.
  - **Notice tickets.** A failed build, a talaria.json this host refuses, a break after a host upgrade, and a worse band in the plugin's harness columns in Models → Fitness each become a ticket on the plugin's board, assigned to its maintainer. There is at most one open ticket per plugin per kind. A host-upgrade ticket names the `sdk` range the app needs and the version this host provides.
  - **Request a change and `app_harness_fitness`.** Every plugin card has **Request a change**, which files a ticket for the maintainer, created by the person asking (`POST /api/admin/apps/change-request`, for board editors and admins). A read-only `app_harness_fitness` tool returns the plugin's fitness columns and the host's harness report.

  Verified:
  - **Unit tests.** `cargo test`: talaria-plugins 13 + 3 ignored, talaria-approvals 19, talaria-workbench-mcp 54, talaria-routes-admin 16, talaria-jobs 2. The unit tests pin these rules:
    - checks are news once per head commit;
    - a change request is news once per review, not per push;
    - the comment names failing checks and reviewers and never offers a merge;
    - an SDK refusal and a new host build each read as a host-upgrade break;
    - only a worse band counts as a regression.

    Clippy `-D warnings` and fmt are clean on every touched crate.
  - **Live test.** The ignored test passed against a freshly migrated postgres 16 (486 statements; snapshot regenerated). It drove `upkeep_pass` against a loopback GitHub serving recorded PR answers, a `file://` repository and a mock app host:
    - PR #7, with a failing `test` check and ann's change request, produced one comment on its ticket. The ticket moved from review to `in_progress` with the maintainer assigned.
    - PR #8, opened by ann and failing `lint`, was said on the plugin's ticket with nobody put on it.
    - A second pass said nothing new.
    - After the merge and a new commit, `plugin PR #7 merged into main` and `… is on its default branch (merged: #7) — the update from … waits for an admin's approval` landed on the ticket, with one pending request, announced, carrying `prs: [7]`.
    - `decide_update` ran stage and activate and recorded `approved update: updated plugin … from … to …`.
    - A build pointer that was ready on host h1 and failed on h2 filed one host-upgrade ticket for the maintainer, and only one.
    - A fitness cell that went from ready to unfit filed an eval-regression ticket.
    - Every GitHub call was a GET.
  - **Worktree stack, real scheduler and app host.**
    - The first sweep applied the waiting update of `notes-plugin` (policy `auto`) from 2884e42 to 33b3a0e. It wrote `automatic update: updated plugin "notes-plugin" from 2884e42 to 33b3a0e` on PLUG-1, plus an audited `app.update` and an already-decided request row.
    - With the policy back on `approve`, a third commit pushed, the live manifest's `sdk` set to `^9.0`, and the plugin's fitness cell turned unfit, the next sweep logged `raised 1 plugin update approval(s), filed 2 plugin ticket(s)`. It filed PLUG-5, "broke after the host upgrade", naming `this app needs @talaria/sdk ^9.0; this host provides 1.0.0`. It filed PLUG-6, "harness evals regressed", naming `notes-plugin:summarize on gpt-oss-120b: ready → unfit`. Both were assigned to Nora Dev.
    - `app_harness_fitness` returned the column, and refused a missing slug.
  - **Chromium at 1440×900.**
    - Manage → Apps → Plugin updates showed `notes-plugin 33b3a0e → 412b790`. **Update** answered `applied`, swapped the tree to 412b790 (restoring `sdk: ^1.0`) and wrote the line on PLUG-1.
    - **Request a change** filed PLUG-4, assigned to Nora Dev and created by the admin, and linked to it.
    - At 390×844 the open form does not scroll sideways.

- **A Developer Agent can ask for the app it built to be installed, and the installed app remembers who maintains it, who it is for and where its tickets go; repos Talaria creates get their default branch protected.** A new `plugins` record links an installed app (through its existing `app_sources` row, so repo, branch and installed commit are never repeated) to the maintaining agent, the person it was built for, the board of the ticket that started it, a git host (`github`) and an admin-set update policy (`approve` by default, or `auto`). The workbench gains `request_app_install(repo, ref?, why?, taskId)`: the repo must be one the agent is granted, the ticket is required, and a repo already installed or already requested is refused. It raises a new `app_install` approval (admin-only, its text bounded to the ticket's board like `repo_request`). Manage → Apps → Installed lists the requests: **Install** runs the same credentialed install as Install from Git, records the plugin and lands the app disabled (enabling and granting stay admin steps), kept data from another repository asks adopt or wipe first, and **Reject** takes a reason. Every outcome is one line on the requesting ticket. A read-only `plugin_status` tool reports the installed and latest commits, the repo's open PRs with their checks and review decision, the app's enablement, build and manifest refusal, and its harness report. A plugin's card shows its maintainer, owner, board and ticket, and an admin changes its update policy there (`PUT /api/admin/apps {app, updatePolicy}`, audited). Approving a `request_repo` now adds a ruleset that blocks force-push and deletion on the new repo's default branch (no required reviews or checks); the approver can untick it, and when GitHub refuses (a private repo on a free plan) the repo is still created and the answer, the request row and the ticket line say why. Verified:
  - `cargo test`: talaria-github 21 pass (a loopback-GitHub test pins the ruleset body: `~DEFAULT_BRANCH`, `deletion` and `non_fast_forward` only, no bypass list, minted on the creating installation's token, and a free-plan 403 carried back without failing the creation), talaria-plugins 5 + 2 ignored, talaria-approvals 19, talaria-workbench-mcp 53, talaria-routes-admin 16, talaria-routes-workbench 23. Clippy `-D warnings` is clean on every crate touched.
  - The two ignored live tests passed against a freshly migrated postgres 16 (480 statements; the schema snapshot was regenerated from that replay): an approved request installed a `file://` repo through a mock app host, recorded the plugin with the agent, the ticket's assignee and its board, wrote `approved installing acme/<repo> — installed as "<slug>" at <commit>; it built. It is not enabled yet: …` on the ticket, refused a second request for the installed repo, and its plugin row went with its source on uninstall; a repo with no talaria.json and a rejection each left their own line.
  - On the worktree stack, as a Developer Agent through the real MCP gateway: `tools/list` lists both tools; `request_app_install` refused an ungranted repo, a missing ticket, a `-upload-pack=x` ref and a duplicate, and filed PLUG-1's request with Ada as owner. The admin received the `approval_pending` notification. Approving through `PUT /api/admin/apps/install-requests` installed `notes-plugin` from a local bare repo and built it through the real app host, disabled. The first build failed on a stale Docker container name, and the ticket line reported that error; after the container was removed, a Rebuild from the app host built it. `plugin_status` reported `updateAvailable: true` after a second commit was pushed, and refused a slug the agent does not maintain. The update-policy PUT was audited both ways; an unknown policy got 400 and a non-plugin 404. A rejection with a note landed on the ticket, and a second decision on the same request got 404.
  - In Chromium at 1440×900 as the admin, Manage → Apps listed the pending request with its agent, ticket and owner chips. The plugin card showed `maintained by Nora Dev · for Ada Admin · tickets on Plugins · PLUG-1`, and switching its select sent `{"app":"notes-plugin","updatePolicy":"auto"}`. **Reject** with a reason removed the request and showed the ticket line. At 390×844 the card wraps and nothing scrolls sideways. In Admin → Org, with the GitHub status and the decision intercepted because the stack has no GitHub, **protect default branch** was ticked by default and the two approvals sent `"protect":true` and then `"protect":false`. The free-plan answer rendered as "its default branch is not protected: …".

- **Added: an app can be checked, built and evaluated outside the host — the instance serves an SDK kit and a `talaria-app` CLI, and a workbench job on a Talaria app gets them from `prepare_env`.** `@talaria/sdk` resolved only inside a Talaria checkout, so an app in a repo of its own — a Developer Agent's plugin repo above all — had its first compile on the host, after a merge and an install, where a failure turned it off. `GET /api/sdk/kit.tgz` now serves a kit built with the ui and versioned with the host build (`x-talaria-kit-version`: the host build stamp, then a digest of the kit's contents): declarations for `@talaria/sdk`, `/server` and `/testing` generated from the host's own SDK (so `ctx.harness`, `ctx.agents` and `triggers` included), the shared-module list, `talaria.json`'s schema, the host's own build recipe, load probe and harness replay bundled to run with no host and no database, and `talaria-app scaffold | check | build | eval`. `scaffold` writes the skeleton `talaria app new` writes (one source; `talaria app new` gains `--harness` too). `check` holds `talaria.json` to the host's rules, typechecks against the kit's declarations (only what an app may import resolves) and runs the app's own tests. `build` runs the host's recipe and probe and reports per surface, per MCP tool and per harness, skipped harnesses named as Manage → Apps names them, on the host's own build key. `eval` replays every harness fixture against replies recorded in `harnesses/recorded/`, or through the instance's gateway with `--gateway --model <id>` (`--record` keeps the replies). A signed-in member or an enabled agent on its own credential may fetch the kit. For a repo with a `talaria.json` at its root, `prepare_env` fetches the kit as the agent, installs it once per version on the department volume, links `talaria-app` onto the terminal's PATH, gives the repo a node for the checkers, and records an eval session; the relay now books a workbench-key call that carries a recorded session to that job and its ticket. The host's build recipe now refuses, by name, a bare import it does not share (`"zod" is not shared with apps: …`) — the same failure as before on the host, said the same way in the kit even where the package would resolve. Verified: vitest suites for the kit (arguments, scaffold, the slug an install would take, the declarations' rewrite, a reproducible tar, the checkers' configs, both eval transports, the eval run over recorded, failing and gateway replies), the kit route, the build guard and the proxy; the client-docs typecheck compiles the starter harness; `cargo test` for the workbench MCP (the kit block run in a shell against a stub instance) and the relay; and, on a stack running this branch merged with rc, the whole loop — the kit fetched with a session and with an agent key (and refused without either), an app scaffolded with a harness in an empty repository outside any checkout, checked (typecheck, its own MCP test), built, evaluated against its recorded reply, a trigger using `ctx.harness` typechecked and built, the app installed from a local bare repository on the same build key the kit reported, enabled, served and rendered; then `prepare_env` for a workbench job in a sandbox container running the agent image, which installed the kit and node, after which `talaria-app check`, `build` and `eval --gateway --record` ran from the agent's login shell and the gateway turn showed on the job's ticket usage.

- **Fixed: an app harness whose `model.pin` names no platform agent now says so.** `pin` takes a platform agent (`muse`, `judge`, `titler`, …), never a model id, and `pin: 'mockep/mock-1'` read like "pin this model". A harness like that loaded with no warning, and every run returned only "no model available". It still loads, and runs on the rest of its chain. Now the app harness registry warns at load, logged once and written to the build status: the harness, the pin, and the two ways to choose a model (`model.role`, or the app's own model slot `app:<slug>/<id>` in Admin → Models → Fitness). Manage → Apps shows the warning on the app's row, and `talaria-app build`, which runs the same check, prints it under the harness line and in `--json`. A run that finds no model names the pin in its error instead of "no model available". Verified: `bun run gate`; registry tests (a stray pin registers with the warning, a platform agent's pin does not warn, the probe's report carries it), a pointer round-trip test, a runner test for the error. Live: the demo app's build status and Manage → Apps carried the warning, the host log printed it once, a run of the harness returned the new error and `harness_runs` recorded it, and the kit's `talaria-app build` printed it.

- **Added: when an MCP server a Developer Agent uses asks to confirm an action (for example "Delete record 42?"), the request becomes a card for the person whose chat it is, and the allowed action lands. Hermes' other human-only gates (an untrusted MCP server's write tool or spend limit, a saved card fill) would be carded by the same seam, but Talaria configures none of them today, so they do not come up. A protected-instruction write is never carded: it is refused at once and the agent is told why. Nor is an MCP server's request for fields to be filled in (a reason, an amount): a card can only allow or deny, so it is declined at once and the agent is told why. A reattached run's approval request now reaches the tap. In Comms, a conversation link you cannot open (it was deleted, you are not in it, or the link was cut short) now says "Conversation not found" instead of opening an empty thread.** Every agent's file-tool write root is now rendered (`HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/opt/data`, the agent's data volume), with `HERMES_HOME` pinned to the same folder, and Hermes exempts that folder from its protected-instruction gate, so the gate only ever asks about a write the root refuses whatever the answer. The door recognises that gate by Hermes' own words, answers `deny` without offering it to a card, writes `reason: outside_write_root` on the `agent.approval_denied` row, and then steers the run with the real reason, because Hermes' own BLOCKED text says the user denied it. The note quotes the file Hermes named in backticks, on one line, with no control or invisible characters, and at most 120 characters. An open card holds only its own conversation; the agent's other conversations carry on. A failed answer to the agent no longer writes the agent's dial URL into the audit row, and a refusal's row keeps the request's description redacted and clamped to 500 characters, as it keeps the command (an MCP form's description lists the server's fields in its own words). `GET`, `PATCH` and `DELETE /api/conversations/{id}` answer 404 for an id that cannot be a uuid, where they answered 500. In Comms, a plan or work session opened as `/comms/agent/<model>/<thread>` (your own, or one you are a member of) is restored when you come back through the nav rail, instead of a fresh thread: a thread outside your chat list is put to the server, which decides who may read it. Before this, the fleet chat door answered every Hermes `approval.request` `deny`. That left the gates Hermes never auto-approves (an MCP server's confirmation request and a write to a project's AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / SOUL.md, plus, where they are configured, an untrusted MCP server's write tool and a saved card fill) unreachable on any streamed turn. Now, on an *attended* conversation turn (sent from `/api/chat`, or chained or resumed from one: the new `TurnAttribution::attended`), the door first offers the request to a card seam (`RAISE_CARD`, wired to the new `talaria-approval-cards` crate). A card is raised only for a Developer Agent, and only when the conversation's owner manages that agent (a named manager, its personal owner, or an admin). Every other request is refused at once, as before: an ordinary agent's, a non-manager's, or one on a channel, ticket, research, app, workbench or harness turn. The card is a `chat_approvals` row of kind `hermes_approval` and an `approval` chip on the turn's message. Only the owner sees **Allow once** / **Deny**, with a countdown; anyone else in the thread sees it read-only. The answer goes through `POST /api/chat/chips/approvals/{id}`, which re-checks the rule and sends exactly `{request_id, execution_generation, choice}` with `once` or `deny`, never `session` / `always`. A 409 or `already_resolved` from Hermes marks the card expired (the route answers 409). A Developer Agent now renders `approvals.timeout: 120`; everyone else stays at 60. The card closes itself at 115 s, answers `deny` and reads expired, and a boot sweep re-arms or closes the cards a restart left open. A person's answer is audited as `agent.approval_allowed` / `agent.approval_denied` with that person as the actor; an expired card is `agent.approval_denied` by `talaria`; an answer that reached an agent no longer waiting took nothing and is `agent.approval_expired` by the person, never an allow. Cards stay out of the approvals census. Separately, `reattach_session_run` now raises the parked run's `pending_controls` approvals as `approval.request` frames, once each, through the same tap. A run parked on an approval after its stream dropped is refused (or carded) within a poll instead of waiting out Hermes' timeout with the session's FIFO held. The projection does not say when a prompt was asked, so each rebuilt frame carries the earliest moment it can have been (the lost stream's last bytes, or the poll before), and a card raised from one counts its 115 s from then; one with under 10 s left is refused instead. While a person's answer is on its way to the agent, a reattach that raises the same request leaves it to that answer rather than racing it with a `deny`. Verified:
  - **Gates.** `bun run check`, `bun run gate`, `cargo fmt`, and `cargo test -p talaria-approval-cards -p talaria-gateway -p talaria-chat-persist`, and clippy `-D warnings` on those three. The new tests cover card eligibility per policy and per `TurnAttribution.source` (and the unattended `chat` flows), the route's body shape for `once` and `deny`, the card payload round trip, the audit body, the projection-to-frame mapping (one frame across two polls; clarify prompts ignored), the reattached stream answered by the tap against a stub agent door, each rebuilt frame's earliest-asked bound against a stub run door (the lost stream's last bytes for a prompt the first read found, the previous read's send for one a later poll found), the card's closing time from that bound, the in-flight hold on a claimed card, and the audit action for an answer Hermes never took. `cargo check` covered the touched crates' tests. The chips vitest suite covers the card's per-viewer view, and svelte-check is clean. **CI's api job is the full-workspace proof line** (a new crate and `TurnAttribution` gained a field).
