- **New: the app marketplace reads a list of catalogs the operator fills, instead of one URL that defaulted to Outcrop's registry.** Manage → Apps → Discover gains a **Catalogs** panel — add (name + https URL), rename, change the URL, turn off, move up or down, remove — backed by a new `app_catalogs` table and `/api/admin/apps/catalogs` (GET for anyone with the Apps view; POST, PUT `{id,…}` or `{order}`, and DELETE admin-only and audited as `app.catalog-add|edit|reorder|remove`). Every enabled catalog is read at once through the SSRF guard; each app card names the catalog it came from, a slug two catalogs list is shown from the higher one (the lower one says it was shadowed), and a catalog that cannot be read shows its own error while the rest still list their apps. Adding a catalog reads it once and says how many apps it lists or why it could not be read. **The default is now a migration, not a fallback:** upgrading moves the old `apps_catalog_url` value in as the first catalog, or seeds Outcrop's registry when none was set, and no code ever re-adds it — an operator who removes every catalog gets an empty Discover tab that says no catalog is configured, and install from Git keeps working. `GET /api/admin/apps?catalog=1` now answers `catalog: {apps, catalogs}` (each app tagged `catalog: {id, name}`), and the `catalogUrl` field and `PUT /api/admin/apps {catalogUrl}` are gone (nothing else read them). Catalog URLs are https-only; a dev stack with `TALARIA_APPS_LOCAL_SOURCES=1` may also list `http://` to loopback (the SSRF guard still wants the host in `TALARIA_FETCH_ALLOW_HOSTS`). Verified: Rust tests for URL and name validation, index admission, the merge (list order, catalog tags, one card per slug, shadowed slugs, per-catalog errors, off catalogs not read) and two loopback catalogs read through the guard; an ignored live test of add/duplicate/edit/reorder/remove against a migrated database, ending in an empty list that stays empty; the migration on a fresh database (one Outcrop row) and on an upgrade from rc's schema with a custom `apps_catalog_url` (one row, that URL); and live on a worktree stack (whose database migrated from an older schema to one Outcrop row): every route over curl with minted admin and Apps-view member sessions (a member reads and is refused writes; a non-https or credentialed URL is a 400, a duplicate a 409, a partial order a 400), two loopback catalogs plus a 404 one merged on the Discover tab with a slug shown once and the error on its own row, a reorder moving that slug to the other catalog, an add and a remove through the panel in Playwright, the `app.catalog-*` audit rows, and screenshots of the tab at 1440 and 390 with no sideways scroll.

- **Fixed: an agent that hits its LLM budget now fails the turn in seconds and says when the budget reopens. Before, it waited ten minutes and then said "resets in ~5 min" about a 24-hour window. Agent transport errors no longer show the agent's internal address, and the gateway's dead agent-reported spend writer is gone.** A budget refusal now carries the real resume time: the moment enough of the rolling window's oldest spend ages out to bring the rest under the cap, if nothing more is spent. It goes out as `error.resets_at` (epoch seconds) and as the same minute, in UTC, in the message. An agent's own key gets no `Retry-After` with it. Hermes honours that header with waits of up to 600 s, so the old `Retry-After: 300` held the turn for two 300-second waits. Operator and app keys keep `Retry-After: 300` and also get `resets_at`. A failed call to an agent's API server (the Crons tab of a stopped agent, a steer, a stop, a turn whose reply broke after it was sent, a refused-turn withdrawal) now reads like "error sending request: Connection refused (os error 111)". reqwest's own text was "error sending request for url (http://…:<port>/…)": it showed the container's dial address and left out the cause. The full error, address included, still goes to the server log. `record_usage`, `UsageInput`, `classify_agent` and `classify_model` had no callers after the relay took over metering, so they are deleted. `nudge_if_unpriced` stays, because the relay's writer still uses it. The harness's TypeScript comments (`run.ts`, `transport.ts`, `run.test.ts`) no longer explain the tier slot by the TS ledger writer (`recordUsage`, `classifyAgent`), which was deleted with `ui/src/server/usage.ts`. They now say what is true: the relay prices the call it routed, books a tier's turn under its base agent (`persona_base`), and gets only `refId` and `taskId` from the harness. The harness's ledger attribution (`LedgerAttribution`, on every `TransportRequest`) now holds only those two refs. Its `agentModel`, `tier` and `source` rode on every request, but nothing in ui, mcp, api, desktop or the apps read them, so they are removed, along with the unused `ledgerOf`. `RunLedger.source` stays on the SDK type, marked deprecated and read by nothing, because apps written before `ctx.harness` still pass `ledger: { source: 'chat' }` to the free `runHarness`. The app runner no longer stamps it: the relay books every call on an app's key under source `app` anyway.

  Verified:
  - **Gates.** `bun run check` and `bun run gate` pass (cargo test and clippy for talaria-error, talaria-gateway, talaria-price-oracle and talaria-routes-fleet). New unit tests: the message names the minute, rounded up; the refusal sends no `Retry-After` on an agent key and keeps it on other keys; `resets_at` is left out when unknown; the error envelope's wire order; a refused agent's error names the cause and not the URL; a reply that breaks after the send gives a 502 body with no address in it. The new `usage::live_db` test passed against a migrated Postgres, with the other four live tests: rows 10 h, 5 h and 1 h old, and caps that need one, two and three rows to age out. CI's live-tests job runs it too.
  - **Live, worktree stack, pinned `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a6920…a4cf`** (digest read back with `docker inspect`). Every model call went to a scripted mock upstream (400 + 100 tokens per call) behind the stack's own gateway. No real model was called, and none was needed, because the refusal happens before the upstream call.
    - With `llm_budgets.agents["meter-metering"].tokens = 600` and 1,000 tokens booked, a call from inside the container on the agent's key got `429` with no `Retry-After` and `resets_at: 1793232403`. That is the oldest row's `created_at` + 24 h, the same value Postgres computed. The message said "around 2026-10-29 00:07 UTC". An operator key over its own cap got `retry-after: 300` and its own `resets_at`.
    - A chat turn into that wall ended in **8.9 s**. Hermes waited 2.5 s and 4.9 s ("Rate limited. Resets in ~23h 58m"). The turn was saved as an error message: "…its usage limit resets in ~24h…" and then the budget sentence with the time. The same wall on the same image on 2026-10-22, before this change, took 600.6 s and said "~5 min".
    - Hermes marked its one pooled credential (`custom:talaria`) exhausted until `resets_at`. After an admin raised the cap, the next turn still went straight to the model, with no rate-limit wait in the Hermes log, so the longer bench does not hold the agent back.
    - **Known limit, with a fallback model.** The same agent was given one fallback model (`mock-fallback`, through the same gateway). Into the wall, Hermes switched to the fallback at once ("Primary retry eligible in ~84751 s"). The fallback hit the same budget, and the turn ended after 8 s of retries inside Hermes. A second run of the same turn took 11 s end to end; the first took 60 s on a host under IO pressure. An admin then raised the cap. The next turn in that conversation was answered by the fallback model (the mock logged `model: mock-fallback`), because Hermes' cached agent for that session waits for `resets_at` before going back to the main model. A new conversation started right after the raise, and the walled conversation after an agent restart, were both answered by `mock-model`, even though the credential was still marked exhausted. Before this change that wait was 5 minutes. It now lasts until the window would have reopened, or until the session has been idle for about an hour (read from the v0.22.4 source, not measured). The docs say so.
    - With the agent stopped, `GET /api/fleet/agents/{id}/crons` answered "cannot reach meter-metering's scheduler: error sending request: Connection refused (os error 111)". The api log kept `…for url (http://127.0.0.1:21200/api/jobs?include_disabled=true): client error (Connect): tcp connect error: Connection refused`.
  - **The TS comments (comments only, no code).** `git grep -n "recordUsage\|classifyAgent"` finds neither name outside `docs/history/` and the changelog. Each new sentence was checked against the code: `relay()` in `transport.ts` sends only the caller, `refId`, `taskId` and hold headers. `llm_chat.rs` books every call it serves, and on an app key finds a tier's agent with `persona_base`. `turn_subject` registers a tiered turn under the agent. `git merge-tree --write-tree origin/wt/fu-sessions wt/fu-metering` (#610 also edits `transport.ts`) merges with no conflict. `bun run gate` passes, including the ui typecheck and tests.
  - **The dropped attribution fields.** Every reader of `agentModel`, `tier`, `source`, `ledgerOf` and `RunLedger` was grepped across `ui/`, `mcp/`, `api/`, `desktop/`, `cli/`, `mobile/`, `scripts/`, the docs and the two client apps (`apps/leadworks`, `apps/waypoint`, read only). The only reader of `TransportRequest.ledger` is `relay()`, which sends `refId` and `taskId` as headers. The Rust harness has its own `LedgerAttribution`, whose `agent_model` and `source` it does use, so that one is unchanged. Both client apps pass `ledger: { source: 'chat', refId: null }` to `runHarness`, which is why `RunLedger.source` is deprecated rather than removed. The tests that pinned the dead fields (`run.test.ts`, `transport.test.ts`, `app-harness-runner.test.ts`) now pin an attribution of refs only. The relay test still sees `x-talaria-ref-id` and `x-talaria-task-id` on the wire.

- **Fixed: `talaria reset` run in a worktree resets that worktree's stack, not main's, and every other CLI command that acts on a stack takes its targets from the worktree too.** `reset database|secrets|fleet` exec'd into `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER ?? 'talaria-postgres-dev'`. Nothing sets that variable in a worktree, so the reset worked on MAIN's database, and its fleet sweep removed every container whose name held `talaria-fleet-agent`, which only main's fleet produces. A new `cli/src/stack.ts` resolves the stack from the checkout's own `ui/.env`: a worktree's `talaria-pg-<name>`, `talaria-wt-<name>` and `talaria-wt-<name>-fleet`, with fleet containers picked by compose project label. `reset` prints those targets before its typed confirm. Before the first count, it checks that the postgres it would exec into belongs to the worktree's compose project, publishes `DATABASE_URL`'s port, and that `DATABASE_URL` names the `talaria` database and role that reset's `psql` runs as. It passes the fleet project to `compose down` with `-p`, and it refuses a rendered `fleet/docker-compose.yml` that names another project. Every command that acts on a stack now refuses, and says why, when the target would be a guess:
  - a shell variable naming another stack's container or worktree;
  - in a worktree, a shell variable that overrides a line its `ui/.env` owns with another value (`DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`, `PORT`, the api port and url, the gateway url, the fleet project, the toolkit, omp-auth and gateway ports), or a `TALARIA_PG_PORT`/`TALARIA_REDIS_PORT` that is not the URL's. `talaria dev` lets the shell win, so a stale `DATABASE_URL` from main's shell made the worktree's api a second server on main's database;
  - a worktree with no `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT`, or one that is not its own, whose agents would render into main's project. `dev` refuses it now, as `reset fleet` does;
  - in the primary, a `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT` that is a worktree's (`talaria-wt-*`), for `reset fleet`;
  - a linked git worktree with no marker;
  - the installed `talaria` shim run from inside another checkout. The shim always runs the primary's CLI, so in a worktree `talaria reset`, `dev`, `backup` and `restore` acted on the primary.

  More changes:
  - `talaria dev` no longer lets a shell `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER` override a worktree's own container.
  - `deploy` and `service` in a worktree need a `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` of its own instead of the production default `talaria`, and `service install`/`uninstall` refuse there. `deploy up`, `down` and `update` in a worktree need every multi-instance key CONTAINER.md lists (`COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`, `TALARIA_STATE_DIR`, `TALARIA_HTTP_PORT`, `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT`, `TALARIA_FLEET_NETWORK`) set to a value of its own and not a `talaria-wt-*` name. A project of its own alone still bound `/var/lib/talaria` and rendered into `talaria-fleet`.
  - `restore` in a worktree refuses blob restores into main's shared object storage, a bucket nobody named, a dir inherited from main's env, and, when no `--target` is given, a shell `DATABASE_URL` or a `TALARIA_ENV_FILE` whose `DATABASE_URL` differs from `ui/.env`'s. It reads the worktree marker from the checkout's own `ui/.env`, so an env file pointed at main's no longer switches those rules off.
  - `talaria worktree` takes its docker names from the same table.
  - A shell under a worktree's `talaria dev` no longer turns main's containers into that worktree's. A worktree's `talaria dev` sets `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER`, `TALARIA_REDIS_CONTAINER` and their ports for itself, and its app and everything the app starts inherit them. `talaria box new` and `box seed` read `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER` as main's, so from such a shell they seeded the box from the worktree. The primary compose `up` that `box new` and the primary's `talaria dev` run would recreate main's postgres under the worktree's name, or remove it when the worktree's container holds the name. `box new`, `box seed` (its postgres, storage and, with `--qdrant`, qdrant sources), the primary's `dev` and `reset` now refuse a `TALARIA_*_CONTAINER` whose name is a worktree's or a box's, or whose container docker places in a `talaria-wt-*` or `devbox-*` compose project. The refusal prints the `env -u …` command to run instead. An override naming main's own renamed container still works, and an empty one now means the default, as compose reads it.
  - Such a shell also carries the worktree's `ui/.env` lines: its vite loads the file into its environment, and its api gets the same lines. The primary lets the shell win, so the printed `env -u` command, which unset only the container names and ports, started main's app on the worktree's `DATABASE_URL`, fleet project and api url. Every such refusal's `env -u` list now names each worktree line the shell sets (`TALARIA_WORKTREE`, `DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`, `PORT`, the api port and url, the gateway url, the fleet project, the toolkit, omp-auth and gateway ports). The primary's `talaria dev` now also refuses a shell `TALARIA_WORKTREE` and a `talaria-wt-*` `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT`, as `reset` already did. It refuses a `ui/.env` that marks a devbox while the shell sets no `TALARIA_DEVBOX` too, where it used to bring up main's dev compose. Its readiness probes exec into the containers it started, so an empty `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER` no longer probes a container named `''`.
  - The name-substring `containerNames` and `containerRunning` had no users left and are deleted.

  Running `reset database` live turned up a bug that predates this change: the mode had not worked since the bash script was ported (3368cf6c). The bash script fed its statements on stdin. The port gave psql all three as one `-c`, which is one transaction, and Postgres refuses `DROP DATABASE` inside one. The mode had already terminated every connection by then. Each statement now runs as its own `-c`, and the drop is `with (force)`. Reset's counts each print on their own line again. Docs: WORKTREES.md, CLI.md and BACKUPS.md.

  Verified: `bun run gate` (check, cli typecheck, cli tests). New unit tests resolve every command's target in a worktree and in the primary: stack.test.ts, reset, dev, deploy, service, backup and restore. The dev, deploy and restore refusals added after review are proven by those unit tests and by the live refusals listed below. The live destructive runs came before them and were not repeated, since the reset path they exercised did not change beyond the database and role check. Live, in the fu-reset worktree, with this branch's CLI only (the unfixed reset was never run):
  - The dry-run plan for each mode named only `talaria-pg-fu-reset`, `talaria-wt-fu-reset` and `talaria-wt-fu-reset-fleet`.
  - `reset secrets` cleared that DB's sealed rows and kept its board and user.
  - `reset fleet` removed the three containers labelled for that fleet project: a compose-made agent, a compose orphan and a label-only stray. It also removed the rendered files and kept `chassis.yml`. A decoy named `talaria-fleet-agent-decoy-fu-reset`, with no project label, is what the old name filter would have taken. It kept the same `Id` and `StartedAt`. The fleet was a hand-written compose project in the renderer's shape, not a real Hermes hire.
  - `reset database` dropped and recreated that DB.
  - These were each refused before any docker call: a shell `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER=talaria-postgres-dev`, the CLI run from another checkout, `deploy down` and `service install`.
  - After review, each of these was refused live too, before any docker call: `dev` with main's `DATABASE_URL`, with `TALARIA_FLEET_PROJECT=talaria-fleet` and with `TALARIA_PG_PORT=5544` exported; `dev` with the fleet line taken out of `ui/.env`; `deploy up` with only `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` of its own (the refusal named the other four keys); `deploy down` with a `talaria-wt-*` fleet project; `restore --db-only` with a `TALARIA_ENV_FILE` naming main's `DATABASE_URL`. Dry runs of all three reset modes passed the new database and role check and printed the same plan.

  - The inherited-container refusals (round 3) are proven by unit tests in stack, box, dev and reset, and live with this branch's CLI behind a docker wrapper that logged every call and let only `--version` and `inspect` through. Running worktree dev processes on this host carry the four variables. rc's `box seed`, given a container labelled `talaria-wt-fu-reset`, ran `pg_dump` in it. This branch refused the same run after one `inspect`. With `talaria-pg-fu-reset` and the ports exported, `box seed` and `box new` refused with no docker call beyond `--version`. A primary-shaped copy of this branch's CLI refused `dev` and `reset secrets|database|fleet` with no docker call at all. Two controls passed the check: an override in a project of its own, and the printed `env -u` command, which seeded from `talaria-postgres-dev` again. A throwaway compose project showed the recreate and the conflict removal.
  - The complete `env -u` list was proven the same way, with primary-shaped copies of the CLI before and after the change and a wrapper that answered `compose` and `exec` itself, so no real container was started or probed. A shell carrying all fifteen worktree variables was refused by both copies. The old copy's printed command left `TALARIA_WORKTREE`, `DATABASE_URL`, the fleet project, the api url and `PORT` set, and its boot went on to `compose up`, the probes and the vite start with all of them in the environment. The new copy refused on `TALARIA_WORKTREE` with no docker call, and running its printed line verbatim reached `compose up` with none of the fifteen set. A lone `talaria-wt-*` fleet project was refused with no docker call; the old copy booted with it. With `TALARIA_PG_CONTAINER=` and `TALARIA_REDIS_CONTAINER=` empty, the old copy probed `docker exec ''` and the new one probed `talaria-postgres-dev` and `talaria-redis-dev`.

  Main's postgres, redis, embeddings and searxng containers kept the same `Id` and `StartedAt` across the runs. Its database read the same before and after through a hand-run `docker exec talaria-postgres-dev pg_dump -U talaria -d talaria`, the same argv the worktree seed uses. It held no tables before the runs, so that half of the check compares empty with empty. CI is the full test line.

- **A chat whose agent died mid-turn keeps working, a tool call Hermes refused is saved as failed and shows failed in the open tab, pinned agents say why they have no tiers, effort chips appear on a fresh page, and a turn Talaria lets go of is stopped in the agent instead of left to run for nobody.** Five follow-ups from the Hermes-overlap rollout (C1, B9, C2, C5, C9), one recorded decision (C7), round two's R12–R15, and round three's S9–S11.
  - **The completions arm no longer wedges after a crash (C1).** Hermes files a header-less `/v1/chat/completions` turn under a session it derives from the turn's opening, so a conversation keeps one derived session for life. After a non-graceful restart (OOM, `docker kill`), v0.22 fenced that session's head as `unknown` and refused every later turn of the conversation with `unknown_execution`, keeping each refusal queued. That arm is every chat of an agent without pinned sessions, so the conversation was dead for good. The gateway now watches each completions turn's opening (`heal_lost_completion` in `fleet_lost_turns.rs`). On that refusal, or `queue_full`, it sends the turn again once, with one more system row in its opening (`SESSION THREAD: n`). That lands it on a fresh derived session. Nothing is discarded, so the lost turn and every refusal queued behind it stay parked, never run. A chat keeps its thread on the new `conversations.hermes_epoch` column, so later turns open on the fresh session. A one-shot (harness, app or channel turn) takes a random thread. The log names the abandoned `api-…` session at warn.
  - **A refused tool call lands as `error` (B9).** v0.22.4's completions stream ends every finished tool `completed`, an approval-denied `rm -rf` included. The agent's talaria-events plugin already reported the real verdict to `/api/agents/tool-events`. That door now keeps it in Redis (6 h), keyed by the conversation the plugin's session names and the tool-call id, with the time the call finished. It marks the call on the reply that was running at that moment. A call id is not unique across turns (Hermes mints `deterministic_call_id(name, arguments, index)` when a provider sends none, and some providers number their calls), so a verdict reaches only its own conversation, and a turn takes only the verdicts from after it was sent. A session that names no conversation of the agent's (a work session, a one-shot) keeps nothing, and the wire's word stands. The chat turn folds its verdicts into its tools when it lands, and reads them again after the write, so the plugin's post and the turn's own writes can arrive in either order.
  - **An open tab shows the refused call failed, without a reload (R14).** The tab drew the call from the stream, which says `completed`. The door now rings the conversation's readers (an id-only `conversation` event on `/api/me/events`) when it keeps a verdict, and the chat view re-reads the conversation and takes each call's `error` from the stored row: prose, chips and the live row's own state stay the view's. A row the tab drew itself (no id until the post-turn stamp) takes a verdict only from the server's row in its place, never from the newest one, because Hermes mints the same call id again on a later turn. The live turn's one-second chips poll takes verdicts the same way, and the turn's streaming flush folds kept verdicts in too, so its 400 ms writes no longer put the stream's `completed` back over the door's mark mid-turn. Only ever toward `error`.
  - **Session-arm usage reads Hermes' spelling (C2).** `session_usage` takes `input_tokens`/`output_tokens` (what `run.completed` carries) as well as the chat-completions spelling. The tests now use a captured v0.22.4 session turn.
  - **Persona payloads stop sending `tools: []` / `tool_choice: "none"` (C5)**, Rust and TS. Hermes reads neither off a chat-completions body. The `ToolPolicy` docs now say plainly that nothing on the completions arm enforces `none`: Hermes runs its own tools whatever the turn asks, and what the runner does is read the tool names the stream reports into the guard pass, so a harness that keeps `zero_tool_claim` still judges a claimed action against the calls that ran (R13).
  - **Pinned agents show the tier chip off, with the reason (C9).** A pinned session runs the agent's main model whatever a message picks. `/api/agents` now carries `pinnedSessions`. The DM composer and the Plan/Work header disable the tier chip for such an agent, with "This agent keeps pinned sessions, which always run its main model…" on hover, and hold no tier for the send.
  - **A disabled composer chip looks disabled (R15).** The shared rail chip (`chat-chrome`, behind `ComposerPicker`) now takes the primitives' own disabled reading (`dimDisabled` from `ui/control.ts`, the dim a disabled outline or ghost `Button` has), a not-allowed cursor, and no hover fill. That covers the pinned tier chip, the inbox panel's effort chip while a reply is busy, and the model editor's effort slot, so the C9 call sites no longer dim their chip by hand.
  - **Hermes' `todo_list` stays closed until the session arm is the chat default (C7).** Its list lives only in the session transcript, which a completions-arm turn does not carry, so it would reset every turn. The decision, the unblock condition and the migration plan are in `MANDATORY_DISABLED` (talaria-agent-defs), talaria-agent-todo's header, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` and the toolset row's tooltip.
  - **Effort chips appear on a fresh page (S9).** The DM composer, the inbox assistant panel, the agent editor's model rows, the Models view's role slots and Settings' default-effort picker each destructured `useModelEfforts(...)`, whose fields are getters over a live query, so each read the levels once, at mount: `[]` on a fresh page, and the chip never appeared. They now keep the object and read through it. The agent editor's main row also cleared a saved level on load (it judged the level against the `[]` of a read still in flight), so saving the form straight after opening it dropped the agent's effort. It now waits for the model's answer (`answered`) before it clears anything.
  - **An app turn whose caller left is let go of at once (S10).** `talaria-app-agents` noticed a closed caller only when it next wrote, so a one-shot whose caller gave up while Hermes held the turn was still read on: moved to a fresh session if Hermes refused it, and run for nobody. The drive now waits on the caller's hang-up beside the agent's next frame, during the hold too, and lets go of the turn the moment the caller does.
  - **A completions turn Talaria lets go of is stopped in the agent (S11).** Hermes keeps an admitted turn alive past its request: a turn still queued when its stream was dropped ran later for nobody, or stayed parked behind a lost one, and a running one went on until Hermes next failed a write. While the request is open, the completion id every chunk names (`chatcmpl-…`) is also the turn's run id, so the gateway now posts `/v1/runs/{id}/stop` for a stream let go of early (a queued turn is cancelled, a running one interrupted) and holds the request open until Hermes has ended the turn (`fleet_abandoned.rs`). It reads the dropped stream on for that. A turn whose reader never read a frame is named by the role chunk Hermes already wrote. A move to a fresh session is followed to the fresh turn, and a turn let go of is never moved. A stop sent before Hermes bound the id (it writes that chunk before the turn's admission commits, and on a starved agent store that commit took minutes) is sent again, backing off, for up to the five minutes Talaria gives an agent's headers. Once a stop lands, the stream is read to its end for at most the 10 s control window. That covers a harness past its deadline and an app turn whose caller left, including one who left while the turn's key was being recorded. A turn let go of before the agent's response headers arrived has nothing naming it yet, and stays Hermes' to handle. The inbox brief, which runs detached with nobody waiting, now gets 90 s instead of 10, the bound the same assistant gets for a reply and still inside the card's two-minute retry window.

Every reply was the mock's, not a real model call. The mock names each user turn it was sent and the thread row it saw.

The auto-resume's turn was refused and parked `queued` on `api-e567aebbb9e552b7`. It never reached the model. The resume moved to thread 1 (`api-82563e8a263e0f6b`) and landed "SEEN 2 user turns: alpha one | alpha two HXSLOW". The conversation's `hermes_epoch` became 1, and the next message went straight to thread 1 with no refusal. Sending that unchanged opening straight to the container reproduced the wedge Talaria used to hit: `unknown_execution` every time, each one parked `queued`. Adding the thread row opened a fresh session that answered.

A slow variant showed the race the fold covers: the door marked the row `error`, the turn's own flush wrote `completed` over it, and the landing write put `error` back. A successful `echo` stayed `completed`. A verdict posted to the door for a reply that had already landed marked that row. **After review, with the mock sending one fixed call id on every call** (what Hermes' `deterministic_call_id` does for a provider that sends none), Hermes kept `call_fixedrepeat0` in every turn, and:

      - The kept keys are per conversation (`tool-failed:ada-ops:<conversation>:call_fixedrepeat0`, valued with the call's finish time). Verdicts posted by hand for a session that names no conversation (`api-ffff…`, and a uuid that is no conversation) kept nothing and marked nothing. One posted for A's derived session, timed during turn 2, marked turn 2 and no other row.
    - **C2.** A direct session turn's `run.completed` carried `usage: {input_tokens: 10, output_tokens: 5, total_tokens: 15}`, and `assistant.completed` carried none. That frame is the new test.

The editor without the `answered` guard showed `auto`, and Save version straight after opening wrote a version with no effort; with the guard it showed `high` and the same save changed nothing.
    - **S11, the brief's deadline.** A brief whose model waited 25 s before answering, on a loaded host, ran 61.5 s (`harness_runs.latency_ms`) and landed; the old 10 s cap would have dropped it.
    - **S11, an abandoned brief is stopped.** A brief whose model held it past 90 s was let go of at the deadline, and the gateway stopped its run (`chatcmpl-1736…`, Hermes answered `stopping`; the admission ended `interrupted` and the model's connection closed). A second brief for the same card, queued behind a direct turn with the same opening (so its derived session's head was busy), was cancelled at its deadline (admission `terminal`/`cancelled`) and never reached the model. The control, the same queued turn with a caller that only hung up: its admission stayed queued, and when the head finished it started and called the model for nobody.
    - **S10, a curl that gives up.** A throwaway local app (never committed, uninstalled with its data after) answered `ctx.agents.turn` with no session key. Its turn queued behind a direct turn with the same opening, and the `curl` calling the app gave up after 10 s. Three seconds later the gateway stopped the queued turn (admission `cancelled`), and the turn never reached the model.
    - **After review: a turn let go of before anything read it, and a stop sent before Hermes bound the id.** The api was rebuilt from this head; the same agent and mock were used.
      - *Gates.* `bun run gate` passed again: `check`, svelte-check, the ui vitest (157 files, 2441 tests), and clippy plus tests for the same twelve packages (talaria-gateway 138 passed, 5 ignored). The new guard tests cover a stream let go of before its first frame, a stop resent until Hermes can place it (past the control window too, and given up at the place window), a move still in flight when the reader left, and a let-go turn that is never moved. Two fail with the old behaviour put back.
      - *Hermes' bind gap, probed straight against the agent* (no Talaria in the path, the host at load ~70 and IO full-pressure ~50%). A stop sent the moment the role chunk arrived answered 409 `not_found`, and so did every resend for 10 s. That admission, and two more from probes still waiting on headers, were still not in the agent's store more than a minute and a half after the role chunk; their turns started 3.3 minutes after it.
      - *The review's window.* A direct turn held a derived session's head, and a SHARE lock on `usage_attributions` stalled the app turn's opening after its headers. The app turn's `curl` gave up at 10 s. The opening was dropped with nothing read, and 21 ms later the gateway stopped the turn (`chatcmpl-747ae1a9…`). Its admission ended `terminal`/`cancelled` while the lock was still held, and the model saw only the head's call.
      - *The resend phase.* The same setup, plus a 16 s write lock on the agent's own `state.db` (inside Hermes' 20 s writer patience), so the app turn's admission had not committed when the `curl` gave up. The first stops found nothing to stop. The stop landed 8.2 s after the hang-up, once the lock was gone. The admission ended `cancelled`, and the model never saw it.
      - *The plain case.* With no lock, a caller that left mid-read had its queued turn stopped 0.5 s after the hang-up (`cancelled`). A plain app turn still answers (`SEEN 1 user turns: fin smoke one`).
      - For these runs the worktree Postgres ran with `synchronous_commit = off`: its commits were waiting minutes on WAL sync. That is test plumbing, not product.
    - **Not exercised live:** a refusal on a wedged derived session arriving after the brief's deadline. This host answered refusals in milliseconds, so the queued-behind-a-busy-head case stood in for it. It is the same Hermes state (a queued admission whose request is gone), and `cancel_session_input` checks only the admission's own status, not its session's head.
  - The host was IO-starved through round two (Postgres commits of a minute and more), so this worktree's own Postgres ran with `synchronous_commit = off`. That is test plumbing, not product. Round three ran without that setting, until the after-review runs above needed it again.

- **Fixed: a thread schedule's report that the push lost is pulled into the thread; Admin → Search tests the search URL from inside an agent too; Hermes's minute intervals read as hours and days; and the redispatch sweep stops counting people-only tickets as re-offered.** A schedule made from a conversation reported back only through the talaria-events plugin's fire-and-forget POST, so an api restart, a timeout or a full queue at fire time lost that run's report for good. A new five-minute `cron-output-pull` job (`talaria-cron-output`) reads each listening agent's own `GET /api/sessions?source=cron` and lands any settled run whose report never arrived, through the same landing code as the push (clamp, scrub, reply guard, responsible-user stamp, fan-out). Only a run Hermes booked `cron_complete` is landed, and only its last assistant row when that row asks for no tools, so a run that died after a tool call never posts its mid-loop narration as the report. The listing does not name the job, so a run is matched by its title against every job the agent has (Hermes titles a run with its job's name) and must have been sent that job's prompt; when names collide the prompt decides. A same-named fleet-wide job's runs are not landed in a thread while Hermes lists that job, and a run of a same-named job deleted since lands only if it was sent the thread job's prompt. Both roads stamp the Hermes session id on the row and dedupe on it under one advisory lock per thread and session, and the pull also treats a row of the same job that landed during the run as delivered, so reports pushed before this change are not landed twice. An agent that answers the pull's reads with a refusal (a key that no longer matches) is logged at warn after three passes in a row and then hourly; a database failure fails the pass. Admin → Search showed one green dot from the app's own probe even when every agent got "connection refused" (a SearXNG on the host's loopback); it now shows **from app** and **from agents**, the second running the same canary inside a running agent over `docker exec` against the URL as the agents dial it, with **not probed** when no agent runs. Hermes stores `every 6h` as `every 360m`; the schedule rows now read "Every 6 hours" / "Every day" (display only, the stored string round-trips untouched). The work redispatch sweep offered and counted a ticket whose only assignees are people; it now offers only tickets with an agent assignee. Verified: `bun run gate` (check, svelte-check, 2,439 ui tests, clippy `-D warnings` and `cargo test` for the ten touched packages); `cargo test -p talaria-cron-output --lib -- --include-ignored` (unit tests built from frames a live v0.22.4 agent answered, among them the listing row and messages page of a run that died after a tool call, and a live-DB test of both roads: push then pull, pull then a late push, two pushed turns of one run, a re-delivered push, a re-delivery mending a lost responsible-user stamp, a session-less push, a simultaneous push and pull landing one row, and the pre-change window check); `cargo test -p talaria-work-dispatch --lib -- --include-ignored` (the sweep's query on real rows: a people-only ticket in a pickup column is neither offered nor parked). Live on a worktree stack with an agent on the pinned `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a69…`, a scripted mock model behind the gateway (no real model calls): a thread schedule `every 6h` read back from Hermes as `every 360m` and showed "Every 6 hours"; a run-now's report was pushed with its session stamped; with the agent's door key withheld so the push was refused, the next pass pulled the run in once, attributed to the scheduler and stamped "scheduled run", later passes were no-ops, and a hand-sent late push of that run answered the pulled row's id and wrote nothing; with an unlistened fleet job of the same name and two threads each listening to a job named "Digest", one blocked pass landed exactly the three listened runs in their own threads and left the fleet job's run alone; after the agent was stopped and started again, the final build's passes skipped every earlier run and landed the next two blocked "Digest" runs in their own threads; a pulled turn raised the thread's agent-reply notification; on the final build, with pushes blocked, a thread run scripted to narrate ("Let me check the inbox first.") on a tool call and then have its next model call refused was booked `cron_incomplete_no_output` by Hermes and was not landed, a run of a same-named fleet job deleted after it ran was not landed in the thread, and in the same pass a thread-two run was pulled in; the next pass pulled in thread one's normal run, and with the push restored a run's report was pushed with its session stamped. Admin → Search against the dev SearXNG published on `127.0.0.1:8888`: from app up, from agents down with `[Errno 111] Connection refused` (Hermes's own SearXNG provider in the container failed the same way); with a forwarder on the docker bridge both read up; with the agent stopped, from agents not probed (screenshots taken). With SEARXNG_URL unset so the stored URL is in force, saving `http://127.0.0.1:8888` in the panel made one PUT and no GET, and the dots read from app up, from agents down from the PUT's answer (screenshot); clearing it made one PUT as well. A people-only ticket in a pickup column logged no re-offer, and an agent ticket beside it logged "re-offered 1 ticket(s)". CI is the compile and test proof line for the rest of the workspace.
- **Fixed: a thread schedule's run that had nothing to report posts nothing, by either road, instead of a message reading `[SILENT]`; and a `SEARXNG_URL` that is set but empty no longer hides the URL saved in Admin → Search.** The cron prompt tells an agent to answer exactly `[SILENT]` when there is nothing new, and Hermes then skips its own delivery, but the talaria-events push sees the text before that decision and the cron-output pull reads the stored session, so both landed the sentinel in the thread. Both now read it with Hermes v0.22.4's own rule (`is_autonomous_silence_response`, ported in `talaria-cron-output`'s `silence`: the sentinel alone or dressed in edge punctuation, `SILENT` / `NO_REPLY` / `NO REPLY` and the zh-Hans forms, a bracketed `[SILENT]` opening a short note, or a marker on its own first or last line; one buried mid-sentence is a report and still lands; the push judges the plugin's first 20,000 characters, so a longer report whose only marker is its own last line still lands by the push), write no message and ring nobody, and record the run in a new `cron_silent_runs` table as delivered silent, under the session id the two roads dedupe on. The pull reads that record as delivered, so a quiet run is never re-read or landed, and drops records past its look-back. The push answers `silent: true` with no message id. Separately, `talaria_search::search_url` let a set-but-empty `SEARXNG_URL` win over the stored setting (no search at all) while Admin → Search reported `fromEnv: false` and kept its field editable, so a URL saved there was ignored; blank now counts as unset in every reader (`env_search_url`, which the panel's `fromEnv` reads too, and the TS twin `envSearchUrl`). Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-cron-output --lib -- --include-ignored` (19 passed: the matcher against every rule above, the pass line, and a live-DB test of a quiet run by both roads — push then re-delivery then pull, pull then a late push, a session-less push, nothing in the thread and no notification, the pull's delivered check by session and by the job's window, the prune, and the cascade with the thread) and `cargo test -p talaria-search --lib`; and `cargo test -p talaria-api --test it conversation_schedules_live:: -- --ignored` against the worktree's database (10 passed, among them a new case for the push door's `silent: true` answer, which CI runs again on its own database). Live on a worktree stack, an agent on the pinned `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a69…` and a scripted mock model (no real model calls): a thread schedule answered `[SILENT]`, the push recorded it (`via push`, the session Hermes lists) 1.7 s before Hermes logged "agent returned [SILENT] — skipping delivery", and the thread stayed empty; with the agent's door key withheld so the push was refused, a run answering a note then `[SILENT]` on its last line was recorded by the next pull pass ("recorded 1 quiet run(s) the push lost as delivered silent"), nothing landed, and Hermes suppressed it too; with the key restored, a run whose report only mentions `[SILENT]` landed by the push as a normal "scheduled run" turn (screenshots of all three threads). Admin → Search in a browser, with the api restarted for each state: unset and set-but-empty both used the stored URL (field editable, both dots up against the stored mock SearXNG, the render handing the agents that URL), and a URL saved while empty took effect at once; set, the env URL won (field disabled, "Set by SEARXNG_URL", both probes against the env mock).
