Before, with rc 65dbae86's array applied (67 statements, 526 in all): main booted "schema already current (459)", `GET /api/workbench/github` read `configured: false, patSet: false`, and main's own inserts into `workbench_repos` (the grant), `workbench_jobs` (`start_job`) and `workbench_repo_requests` each failed `null value in column "host_id"`. Its render put `fleet-gateway` back, the re-upgrade applied 0 statements, and on rc 65dbae86's binary a relay call on the `fleet-gateway` key reached the mock upstream (18 tokens) and booked no `usage_events` row. With this change's 11 statements applied while main kept serving, main read `configured: true, mode: pat` and GitHub answered 401 to the moved PAT, so main opened it; all three inserts landed on `host_id = 'github'`. After a restart (Roll back), main's own panel writes reached the `github` row: a token main sealed and a new repo-creation org, a disconnect (both copies `mode: null`) and a reconnect (both copies the same sealed token). rc's `POST /api/workbench/git-hosts/github/test` opened that token (GitHub 401). On this change's binary the same `fleet-gateway` call, with the list unchanged, booked one row (11/7 tokens), and a call on the operator's listed `ops-shared-key` booked none. Main's flow edit still answers 500, as documented. The new relay unit test fails on the old inline check (`assertion failed: !listed_unmetered(&after_rollback, PERSONA_KEY)`). With its baseline set to the #611 block, the guard flags all eight #611 contract steps; its self-test fails under the old pattern list; an appended `drop default` fails bare and with `-- deliberate:`, and passes only with `-- contract: … unread since #N`. The schema snapshot is regenerated from a fresh replay (`bun run migrations:snapshot`, 537 statements). `bun run gate` passed on the merged head: `check`, the ui typecheck and tests (2940), and `talaria-routes-fleet`'s fmt, clippy and tests (65).

- **Fixed: Talaria Desktop on Windows no longer freezes for good the first time you connect an instance. Every Windows release so far has this bug, from the first (v0.1.0) through desktop-v0.11.0, and a frozen copy cannot reach Check for updates, so Windows users must download the new release from the Releases page (github.com/outcrop-labs/talaria/releases) and install it by hand, with the same kind of installer they used before: `Talaria_<version>_x64-setup.exe` installs over an earlier -setup.exe copy, and the `Talaria_<version>_x64_en-US.msi` of a stable release over an earlier .msi copy, both keeping your instances, sign-ins and settings. Someone who installed the .msi and runs the -setup.exe gets a second copy beside the frozen one, whose Start-menu entry still freezes: uninstall the old copy first (Settings → Apps; your instances and settings stay). End a frozen Talaria in Task Manager before installing. The installer is not signed yet, so SmartScreen asks first: More info → Run anyway.** Opening an instance created its WebView2 inside the launcher's own WebView2 IPC callback (`activate_instance` was a sync command), and WebView2 cannot finish creating a webview while one of its handlers is on the stack: the window kept repainting, but the Add dialog stayed at "Checking…" and no button, titlebar control or close answered again. The instance was already saved, so every relaunch reopened it and froze at once; the in-app switcher and a suspended instance coming back did the same. Now every path that makes an instance webview runs as a main-thread task of its own (the launcher, the switcher, a restore when the window comes back, a notification click, a tray row, the launch-time preload), and a second open of an instance still being created changes nothing. Also: the shell writes a log file — `%LOCALAPPDATA%\app.talaria.desktop\logs\talaria-desktop.log` on Windows, `~/Library/Logs/app.talaria.desktop/` on macOS, `~/.local/share/app.talaria.desktop/logs/` on Linux — rotated at about 1 MB, so a problem report can carry evidence; a panic is written there too; and instance webviews no longer install Tauri's file-drop handler, which swallowed every drop (a file dropped on a composer never reached the page) and on Windows blocks HTML5 drag and drop (boards, the Gantt): drops reach the page as in a browser tab — its drop zones, and text, a moved selection or a file dropped into a form field — and a drop the page does not take does nothing: it never replaces the page with the dropped file. Verified on Linux; drag and drop is untested on Windows and macOS. CI now runs clippy and the tests on Windows, and a connect smoke on Linux, macOS and Windows, on every desktop pull request; and `bun run check` fails any shell command or callback that could create a webview inline.
  Verified: the new Windows connect smoke (CI, `windows-latest`, a debug build with the launcher embedded, a fake instance on localhost registered as the last view) failed on rc's code — the launcher probed the beacon at +11.9 s, the instance page was never requested in 30 s, the shell was still running, and the data dir showed the freeze's signature (`instances\<id>\webview` made, `lastOpenedAt` null) — and passes with the fix: page and script 1.4 s after the probe, `lastOpenedAt` set, and the log file written at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\app.talaria.desktop\logs\talaria-desktop.log`. The new `bun run check` rule fails on rc's tree with exactly one finding (`activate_instance → activate → create_instance_webview → .add_child(`) and is clean here; its fixture and three mutations (an async command creating from its worker, a sync command through a helper, a sync command wrapping the preload in `run_on_main_thread`) are caught. Clippy `-D warnings`, the tests and the connect smoke pass on Linux (under xvfb), macOS and Windows in CI, the smoke's page 0.6 s after the probe on Linux and macOS and 1.2 s on Windows, the log file written on each; the Windows job's first runs found one dead-code error and one test whose 600 ms bound is shorter than Windows' ~2 s refusal of a closed port, both fixed. On Linux, on a private headless rig (its own mutter and session bus, two fake instances, WebDriver on the launcher), with the shell built in the Fedora 44 rig image: a refused address answers in 0.3 s; Cancel on a black-holed probe closes the dialog and nothing lands 15 s later; Add opens the new instance (page loaded 1.0 s after Connect, twice); the same instance by another origin reads "already added"; switching from an instance page to a live instance and back, two activations at once, back to the launcher from a page, and a row click all work; at relaunch the last instance is probed and reopened (+1.3 s, +2.0 s), the other is preloaded hidden and suspended, a switch from a page into the suspended one recreates it in 0.6 s, and after it was suspended with the window minimized a second launch brought the window back and restored it 1 ms later (the queued restore); the connect smoke passes on Linux too (page 0.7 s after the probe); and the log file carries every line with its timestamp. Drops, with real Wayland drags from another app's window into an instance page on the same rig: a file onto the page's drop zone reached it (as a URI list) and the page stayed; a file or a link released outside any zone did nothing; with the page's drop guard bypassed (a page that stops the drag's propagation), WebKit tried to load the dropped file and the shell refused it (`refused a navigation to a local file`, the page stayed), while a dropped link — which only the guard covers — loaded, the default the guard exists to stop; and an in-page HTML5 drag (a draggable element onto the zone) landed. Native fields, the same way: text dragged from another app into a plain input landed, a file onto an `<input type=file>` was taken as a File, a selection moved inside a textarea moved, a stray file elsewhere still left the page alone, and the Kanban, Gantt and workchain drag patterns as ui/ writes them landed; on the build before the guard learned about fields, the first three were refused. Not verified on a real Windows desktop, with an installed release build, or against an instance behind Cloudflare; the switcher and suspend paths ran on Linux only; drag and drop ran on Linux only (and a dropped file reached the zone there as a URI list, not as a File, so a composer's file drop on Linux is not proven); macOS at run time through CI's connect smoke only.

- **Added: agents keep themselves on Hermes' stable releases, unattended — so before upgrading, an operator who wants every agent held where it is sets `HERMES_IMAGE` in `fleet/.env` (or Pins a version on the panel afterwards), and sets the workspace time zone so the 02:00–05:00 maintenance window falls at night. Otherwise each instance checks `nousresearch/hermes-agent:stable` every six hours, waits until a release has been on stable for 48 hours, tests it in a throwaway canary, moves its agents onto it one at a time in the window, watching each before the next, and puts every agent back by itself if the release fails. A Hermes release needs no Talaria release — unless it changes something Talaria relies on, and then it is held for an admin.** Until now every agent ran the Hermes pin compiled into the release (`v0.22.4`), so each Hermes release waited for a Talaria pull request, release and upgrade. The check is an anonymous manifest HEAD, which Docker Hub does not count against its pull limit. A release is not even downloaded until stable has named it for 48 hours (`TALARIA_HERMES_MIN_STABLE_HOURS`, counted from the first check that saw it there and started again whenever stable moves), and a waiting release that stable stops naming is never rolled out: it gives way to whatever stable names now. The download goes through the agents' own, after any other download, and never past the disk's room — the docker disk must hold the image and keep a tenth free (a rollback's, a fiftieth), or the release waits and the admins hear it; a disk the api cannot read holds the download until Roll now. The image is read with networking off for its own config schema version, the env names its Hermes strips and its drain tools, and its contract with Talaria is checked, in a container with networking off, read-only, as nobody and with no capabilities: Hermes' own config migration must change nothing Hermes reads of any agent's rendered config — MCP servers, platforms and toolset lists included, a credential typed in literally replaced by a stand-in (Talaria stamps the image's own version, so Hermes never migrates the read-only config) — sealed `CONFIG_*` credentials must stay out of an agent's commands, a scheduled job Hermes claims must still read as running, and the canary must answer the fields Talaria reads to tell whether an agent is working. A release that fails one is **held for review** on the panel, with what changed, until an admin presses **Accept and roll out** — which covers those problems only; a new one holds it again. Then, in the window (the workspace's time zone, else the server's `TZ`, else the zone most admins chose, else UTC — the panel says which) or on **Roll now**, it boots as a canary with a rendered config and no channels, users, credentials or model to call, and soaks for 5 minutes. Agents then restart onto it one at a time. An agent that is working or about to is passed over and asked again a minute later: a reply being written or a conversation in the last 10 minutes, a turn in flight in its Hermes API server, a messaging-platform turn, a scheduled job running (the claim Hermes refreshes every minute while the run lives) or due within 3 minutes, a work session or workbench job. One whose Hermes does not answer is not restarted on its own — Roll now and Pin restart it — and a Hermes from before the channel (v0.21.4, with no live run counts) is judged by the rest of its answer; one busy all window moves in a later window, and one left behind three windows in a row is said to the admins, again every week. An agent that is down — stopped with **Stop**, `docker stop` or `compose stop`, removed by `compose down` — is assigned the new image and starts on it when someone starts it: the channel never starts it. It recreates a down agent only when docker says it crashed (seen twice), or when the channel's own recreate left it down; a Stop pressed during a recreate stands. (A chassis whose agents run `restart: no` leaves a crash exited, which reads as stopped.) No agent is moved onto an older Hermes than it runs, and an agent that fails goes back to what it ran. An agent counts as moved only once its container runs the image, so a roll that did not land is moved again, and one running another image than its own opens a catch-up onto it; one that fails a catch-up is left on what it ran, and the admins told, until the image changes or Roll now. Each moved agent is watched (healthy, its restart count unchanged, no new config error in its log) for 10 minutes after the first and 3 after each later one, and the whole rollout soaks 15 minutes before the release is called good. A failure the host caused (docker slow or refusing, the network between the api and the fleet, a pull that failed, a full or saturated disk) is retried after 15 minutes, then twice as long each time to six hours, and the third in a row tells the admins once. A failure the release caused puts that agent back and is tried once more; the same thing failing again, or a third failure of anything, marks the release bad, rolls back every agent on it, and notifies every admin. A reboot or docker restart during a soak is the host's; a release no agent ran is not called good; a release stable withdraws after some agents moved onto it takes them back first. **Allow again** lifts a ban. **Roll back** moves every agent on the version being left now, mid-turn included. A version already known good here is never banned; a Pin to one stops at its first agent that will not come up healthy. A channel state this release cannot read (one a later release wrote) pauses only the updates — hiring, starting and editing agents never read it — and **Reset** on the panel sets it aside and starts afresh. **Manage → Agent image** (admins) shows the version each agent runs, the channel, the last check, the rollout, held and banned versions with their reasons, and the history. The previous version stays on the server for three days after the new one is good, a candidate nobody rolled out for a week; then images the instance downloaded itself are removed. `TALARIA_HERMES_MIN_STABLE_HOURS` and `TALARIA_HERMES_STABLE_REF` pass through `docker/compose.yml`. A server that cannot reach Docker Hub keeps its agents where they are and shows the failed check. **On a server upgrading from an earlier release, the channel keeps what it finds.** Its first step (1½ min after boot) records the stop of every agent found down, so each stays stopped, and assigns every running agent the image it runs (`:latest`, recorded as found), so nothing but the channel changes an agent's Hermes. On image installs, the deploy's own fleet roll waits for that step (at most 30 min) and restarts each running agent on its own Hermes. Agents on an older Hermes than the compiled pin (main's `:latest` was v0.21.4 on most hosts) move onto the pin in the first window: the pin is inspected and canaried, the agents move one at a time, each watched, and the move stops at the first agent that will not come up, which goes back on what it ran while the admins are told. Agents at or above the pin stay where they are. Stable's release then takes the whole fleet on, once it has been on stable for 48 h (typically night 3). The old `:latest` is kept (it was found, not pulled here, and another stack may use it): remove it with `docker image rm nousresearch/hermes-agent:latest` once no stack uses it. Plan for about 15 GB free on the docker disk on release day, with 10 % kept free; the pin downloads within hours of the upgrade, and stable's release when its 48 h are up, while only canaries and moves wait for the window; fleets above about 25–30 agents spread each move over more nights. Log and fault text from the agents never reaches a stored reason, a notification or the log with a secret in it. Pre-pulling the pin (`docker pull nousresearch/hermes-agent:v0.22.4@sha256:7a69201726bc64db2072a1371557137c23312d29705cda2b8ea2a0214a50a4cf`) saves night 1 its download.

  Verified: live on this branch's worktree stack (app :5304, api :5404), against Docker Hub in the first round and test images built `FROM` v0.22.6 in a local registry since, soaks shortened. **The upgrade from main, end to end, twice**: the stack ran main's own code (805e6799) and chassis with two agents, relbot running main's `:latest` and stopbot hired and then stopped on main, then booted this branch with the containers left running. The first step recorded stopbot's stop and kept relbot on its own `:latest` (inspected: Hermes 0.21.4); a Roll all, the recreate the deploy's fleet roll makes, restarted relbot on that same image. In the window, the pin was inspected and canaried, and relbot's move onto it was made to fail; relbot went back on its v0.21.4, the move halted, the admins were told, and stable's v0.22.7 then took relbot on through its own canary and soak. stopbot was never started; the old stand-in `:latest` was pruned only once a person started stopbot (round five; since round six the channel never prunes an adopted image), which came up on v0.22.7. With main's `:latest` at v0.22.6 instead, nothing moved down: relbot stayed on v0.22.6 until v0.22.7 took it on. Both runs had host faults (the canary's port unreachable, docker stalling) that were retried, never counted against an image. **Every agent's config**: two test images whose schema-53 migration renames `mcp_servers.*.headers`, or `platform_toolsets`, are held by the shipped inspection (the previous check passed both); v0.22.4 and v0.22.6 pass. A live-DB suite of 64 tests drives the state machine against a scripted fleet whose rolls can fail leaving the old container running or the agent down; each round-four and round-five fix's test failed on the previous head first. A real cut-over from v0.22.4 to v0.22.6 read v0.22.6's own `_config_version` 52 and ended with the agent on v0.22.6. **A release Hermes replaced while it waited**: with stable on v0.22.7 waiting its time, stable moved to v0.22.8 and the next step said "v0.22.7 left stable for v0.22.8: it is not rolled out"; v0.22.7 never ran. **A nightly job mid-run**: an agent with a no-model job sleeping 600 s was passed over every minute — "its scheduled job "nightly-sleeper" is running" — while `/health/detailed` read idle in every field, and it rolled 40 s after the job completed; the job ran to the end. **A release that changed a contract** (a test image whose secret scan returns nothing) was held — "Hermes no longer keeps a platform plugin's declared secrets out of the commands an agent runs" — five admins were told once, and Accept rolled it out through the canary. The first live run held a good release too, because the check read the migrated config with a YAML library the image does not ship; it now asks Hermes' own loader, and run by hand on the images it passes v0.22.6 and holds a config carrying `browser.backend`, which v0.22.6's migration drops. **A rollback onto an image an operator had pruned**, with the agent stopped by a person: the image was pulled again ("about 6.4 GB needed on the docker disk, 177.8 GB free"), the agent was assigned it and stayed stopped, and started on it when a person started it. **A state row a later release wrote**: restarting an agent still rendered, the admins got "Agent image updates are paused", and Reset set the row aside unchanged and started afresh. **The api in a container on the fleet network** (production's container dial): the canary answered by container name and the agent rolled; with the api cut off that network, the canary failure read "the network between the api and the fleet, not the image" and banned nothing. A config stamped 51 under a container on a 52 image restarted healthy, with no migration attempted. A canary container removed by another stack's cleanup mid-soak now counts as the host's. Each round-three blocker's test failed on the previous head first, and 27 mutation checks put a fix back and watched its test fail. `bun run gate` passes. Not verified live: a crash-looping agent during a real rollback and two api processes racing the lock (both in the live-DB suite), and the disk-full hold (a unit test; the room check itself ran live).

- **Fixed: `GET /api/working` names its lead item correctly in four cases an adversarial review found reading wrong.**
  - A direct-message room was created with an empty name, so a streaming DM reply led Comms with a blank label. It now shows the other person, or the other members by name, using the rule the room index already uses, now one macro both reads share. A DM holding only you and agents had no name in either read: both now name it after its agents. That includes the room index, which showed a blank title for these rooms.
  - A thread with an empty title falls back to its agent the way a missing title does.
  - A research run whose discussion thread is streaming counted as one item but kept only the run's own stamp, so an older thread could lead Work. The run now takes the later of the two.

  Verified: `bun run gate`. Four new live-DB tests against a seeded worktree database, each a case the previous code got wrong:
  - a streaming DM leads with the other person's name;
  - a DM of you and two agents leads with the agents' names (it read blank before, and the index's own title expression on rc returns blank for the same room);
  - an untitled chat leads with its agent;
  - a run updated an hour ago, with its thread streaming now, leads over a work thread that streamed a minute ago, with count 2.

  The seven live tests in the module pass.

- **New: `GET /api/working` answers which views an agent is working in right now, `{ comms, work, boards }`, each `{ count, label, href }` for its freshest item or null, and `useWorking()` reads it in the app.** The tab bar's waiting glyphs will draw only from this read. Comms counts your chats whose reply is streaming and the rooms you're in with an agent reply streaming. Work counts streaming work sessions, plans and research threads, plus research runs that are queued or running (a run parked on a question is waiting on you, not working). Boards counts tickets on boards you can see with a work session queued or running. Every arm reuses its engine's own predicate rather than a copy: the sidebar's `working` flag and its audience, the room page's 15-minute dead-stream silence, the research status projection, and board visibility. The conversation list, the unread badges and this read now share one spelling of each audience. One failed arm fails the whole read with a 500, and the client reads a failed read, or a failed refetch, as no reading at all, so no glyph outlives its signal. Room replies and ticket sessions send no event when they end, so the read polls every 5s while anything is lit and every 30s when idle.
  Verified: `bun run gate`. Live-DB tests against a seeded worktree database: a streaming chat reply lights Comms with the thread's title and link and stops counting once silent past five minutes, a streaming room reply lights Comms and stops once silent past fifteen, and another person's streaming chat never counts. The client test reads a 500 as null, never as "nothing working", and drops an earlier good reading when a refetch fails. On a running worktree stack with real agents, polling the route every second:
  - A chat turn read Comms 0, then 1, then 0, and stopping a reply mid-stream cleared Comms within a second.
  - A work session and a research run each lit Work while they ran.
  - Putting an agent on a ticket lit Boards for the 22 seconds the session ran.
  - A chat and a ticket session at once lit both arms.
  - A member outside a plan read nothing while the plan streamed, and read it once they were added.
  - Killing the agent container mid-reply cleared Comms within a second, because the reply closes as an error.
  - Renaming a table under one arm made the route answer 500, and the app's query read null.
  - With no session the route answers 401, and rc answers 404 for it.
  - Over five rounds of 200 interleaved requests, `/api/working` p95 was 1.9 to 2.3 ms against `/api/unreads` at 2.0 to 3.1 ms. On a synthetic 40k-message, 20k-run volume it was 2.9 to 3.3 ms against 42.9 to 44.5 ms.

- **Fix: reading a thread's replies now clears the channel's unread badge — the per-thread read cursor.** The bug: the thread panel posted no read at all, and the channel cursor advanced only on the main feed (`useChannelMessages` filters `thread_root_id is null`), so a reply's seq — drawn from the same `channels.msg_seq` counter — could never clear the badge counting it. The fix, mirroring `conversation_reads`: a `channel_thread_reads` table (PK `(thread_root_id, user_id)`, cascading FKs to `channel_messages`/`users`, monotonic `greatest` upsert `mark_channel_thread_read`), a thread arm on `POST /api/channels/{id}/read` — `{ threadRootId, seq? }`, seq computed server-side as the thread's newest complete reply when absent, root normalized `thread_root_id.unwrap_or(root.id)` and 404'd when not the channel's — and one clause, `thread_read_covers_sql!`, that every unread predicate (`list_channels`, `channel_unread_total`, `shared_rooms_sql!` — the rail pill, the rail badge and the profile drawer) and both caught-up gates share, so a reply a thread cursor covers is read everywhere at once. The clause is a bare `exists` that every caller negates as a top-level `not exists`, which Postgres plans as an anti-join over the viewer's own rows on `channel_thread_reads_user_idx (user_id, thread_root_id) include (last_read_seq)`. Written as `not (… and exists …)` it was a per-row SubPlan whose cost estimate pushed the rail's queries into full JIT. The whole-channel gate (`channel_read_caught_up`) counts a thread-read reply as read: it used to need the channel cursor past the newest message, which the main feed (no replies) never reaches when that message is a reply, so the badge read 0 beside a lit @mention or DM row. A thread read clears that thread's own bell rows by `group_key` (`reply:<root>`), never by href, so an @mention row on the same channel keeps waiting while anything on the channel is unread; when the thread read leaves the whole channel caught up, the channel's href sweep runs instead. The panel (`ThreadPanel.svelte`) posts the read on mount and as replies land, only while the person is looking (`lib/looking.ts`), keyed by root through `readCursorToPost` like `ChannelView`'s channel key: the panel is not remounted between threads, and a bare high-water mark skipped a second thread whose newest reply was older than the first's. Each read refreshes both counts it moves, the sidebar pill (`['channels']`) and the rail's Comms badge (`['unreads']`), which otherwise waited for its 30 s floor whenever the read cleared no bell row. Replies landing in a burst are one read (`lib/thread-read.ts`: trailing 750 ms, 3 s ceiling; a thread just opened reads at once). A full page, the thread's oldest 300 rows, posts no seq, so the server reads to the newest complete reply and a long thread still clears. A follower whose thread cursor already covers a reply is not rung for it: an agent's reply streams with its seq while the open panel reads it, and its fan-out runs only at completion.
  Verified: `bun run gate` (check, svelte-check 0 errors, ui vitest, cargo fmt + clippy `-D warnings` + tests on talaria-api, talaria-channel-replies, talaria-channels, talaria-notify and talaria-routes-comms). The CI migrations job replayed on scratch postgres:16-alpine: fresh replay against the regenerated snapshot, the upgrade from main's ledger, the git-hosts mirror, and a second replay applying 0. Perf on stock PG16 with 50 rooms × 10k messages and 250k thread reads, timing the binaries' own SQL; the PR's first spelling against the anti-join with the index, plain execution, 100 unread per room: `channel_unread_total` 379 → 211 ms (rc 174), full JIT gone; `list_channels` 637 → 60 ms (rc 56). The five `#[ignore]`d live tests in `api/tests/it/channel_thread_reads.rs` pass against the worktree's Postgres and Redis. `a_reply_read_in_its_thread_rings_no_one_who_watched_it`: a follower whose cursor covers the reply files no `thread-reply` row, one whose cursor is behind does. `unread_predicates_honor_the_thread_cursor`: the pill, the rail badge and the drawer agree at every step, and one thread's cursor never covers another's. `caught_up_gates_read_a_thread_read_as_the_badge_does`: the channel catches up when its last reply is read in the panel, and a streaming reply holds neither gate. `thread_read_clears_only_its_bell_rows`: another thread's row, the `mention` row and the activity row on the same href stay. `the_read_route_clears_what_the_badge_says_was_read`, through the real router: feed first, then threads, the @mention survives a thread read while another thread is unread, and clears when the last thread is read. Exercised on a worktree stack with two minted users, Ada in a headless browser and Bo over the API. Bo's two replies count 2 on Ada's sidebar pill and rail badge, and opening the channel's feed leaves them at 2. Opening the thread drops both to 0 on her screen without a reload. With Ada focused but idle, so the notification runtime's visit rule cannot read rows on sight, the checklist thread's read answered `cleared: 1` (its own row) while an @mention in another thread kept its bell row. Switching the open panel to that older thread posted its read, and with the channel then caught up the @mention cleared. A fresh @mention on the main feed cleared when the feed posted its read. A thread of 320 replies counted 320 and cleared on opening: the full page posted no seq, and a 321st reply landing while the panel was open was read by one more post.

- **Fixed: a chat with an agent that is slow to its first word, and a cron change on a slow agent, now answer inside Cloudflare's 100 s instead of getting its 524.** Every real instance sits behind a Cloudflare tunnel, which answers 524 when the origin has sent no headers for 100 s. `/api/chat` held its headers until the agent opened the turn, and an agent that has taken the turn but is slow to its first frame (a long context, a compaction) gets five minutes for that. So the person got a 524 for a reply that went on and landed. Now the route waits at most 30 s for the agent's own answer. Past that it answers 200 `text/event-stream` at once and sends a `: waiting for the agent` comment every 15 s until the agent speaks, and then the reply streams as before. That also names a new thread sooner, so a Stop on its first turn has an id to use. A turn that opens within 30 s is answered exactly as before. If the agent answers with an error status after the 200 has gone out, the error goes into the stream as a failure frame, and the reply lands as an error that says why. The web chat and the phone read that frame, and the agent's own failure frames, and show the reason at once; a phone on an older build shows an empty reply for such a late error until it updates. Only the agent's or the gateway's own error can arrive this way: the route's own answers (400, the 402 budget refusal, 403, 409 and the 202 queue acknowledgement) are decided before the turn and are still real HTTP statuses. A cron create, schedule edit or run is several calls on the agent. Each call had its own 40 s bound, but the whole had none, and a guarded schedule edit can be six calls. Now the request waits 75 s for the whole change, and past that it answers 503 that the change may still land, while the change runs on to its end and its outcome is logged. A run-now that is not confirmed says the run may still be queued and warns that running it again could run it twice, since the job list cannot show a queued run. An unconfirmed create is audited as `cron.create` with `confirmed: false`. A thread's schedule writes its row in that same task, so a create that lands late still reports into the thread. Creating one job on many agents now answers by one shared 75 s deadline, writes at most 8 agents at a time and each named agent once, and the cron work done when a thread is deleted, archived or restored waits at most 75 s. One trade-off stays, set deliberately in #647: when a person is reading a chat and the agent comes back 80 to 120 s after a restart, they get the "didn't come back within 80 seconds" reply where the two-minute hold used to wait for it. That reply is kept in the thread and tells them to send the message again. An app's agent turn (`/api/llm` on an app's key) keeps its two-minute hold. Only the app host holds an app key, and it reaches the api over the instance's internal URL, never through the edge.
  Verified: live on a worktree stack, through the app's proxy (:5307), with a test admin and a stand-in for the hired agent's API server on its gateway port: it withholds a chat turn's headers for 120 s and holds each `/api/jobs` write 39 s before applying it. No real model calls were made. First on the rc binary (678dd627): a chat's first byte came at 159.2 s (the agent's headers at 120 s, then a 37.7 s Postgres stall on the turn's attribution insert), and a guarded schedule edit answered 200 at 118.2 s. Both are past the edge. On this branch: the chat answered 200 `text/event-stream` with its first `: waiting for the agent` at 30.03 s, then one every 15 s, and the reply at 120.07 s, which landed `complete`. A turn the agent failed with a 500 after 40 s answered the keepalive at 30.03 s and the failure frame at 40.07 s, and its row landed as an error with `(agent error: the model provider refused the turn …)`. A turn that opened in 2 s answered as before, 200 with no keepalive. The schedule edit answered 503 with the may-still-land sentence at 75.01 s and was applied at 117 s (armed, `every 240m`), with the late finish logged. A thread schedule answered 503 at 75.03 s, and its job was started and its `conversation_schedules` row written 3 s later. New tests, each failing against rc's behaviour put back: an answer opened before a slow agent speaks, over a real loopback HTTP hop; a late error said in the stream and parsed by the drain as the reply's error; a cron change answered at its deadline and running on to its end. Further tests cover a turn that opens in time keeping its status, a late error's sentence, and const asserts against `EDGE_CUTOFF` for the 30 s, the 15 s and the 75 s. `bun run gate` passes. Not verified through a real Cloudflare tunnel (the cutoff is the documented 100 s), and not in a browser or on the phone beyond their parsers, which already skip SSE comments.

- **Fix: a chat, work, plan or research reply now announces its start on the firehose, not only its end, so the tab bar's agent glyph lights when the reply starts.** The app refetches `/api/working` on the firehose's `conversation` event, and a reply sent that event only when it finished, so a reply shorter than the bar's 30-second idle poll could stream and end with no glyph. The chat route and the queued-turn path now insert the streaming reply and ring the same readers its end rings: the sender of a chat, the owner and members of a shared thread. A reply whose row is never inserted rings no one, and a reply that fails (the agent refuses mid-stream or answers a queued turn with an error status, or its stream dies) now rings its end like a finished one, so the glyph its start lit goes dark at once.
  Verified: `bun run gate`. Live-DB tests ring the sender of a chat, the owner and member of a plan and not an outsider, with an id-only payload; ring the readers again when a reply is resumed; and ring no one when the write fails, even for a thread with readers. A reply that ends in an agent error, a dead stream, or a queued turn its agent refuses with a 500 is heard ending on Redis. Moving the fan before the write, or removing any of the start or end rings, fails a test. On a worktree stack with real agent turns, an in-page firehose log showed `conversation` at each reply's start and end, and the Comms glyph lit within 40 ms of send.

- **Starred thread and agent rows in the Comms rail now reserve the hover-actions slot, so a long title truncates with an ellipsis before the Star / Archive (or More / New thread) buttons instead of running underneath them.** The buttons overlay the row's right edge on hover and on keyboard focus (keyboard focus keeps them visible, per accessibility), which is exactly where flat rows' titles used to end — a starred conversation like "Zach and Glyph Making Session" collided with the star on its row. Nested rows already reserved that side with their trailing meta box and pay nothing; they, the other row kinds, and the hover-actions snippet are unchanged.
  Verified: `cd ui && bun run typecheck` (svelte-check, 0 errors), and a real-browser geometry check (headless Chromium over CDP, driven at 900×560) against the row markup and the repo's own compiled Tailwind CSS: the unfixed row shows the reported collision (the star paints 46 px into the title when keyboard focus reveals the actions), the fixed thread and agent rows truncate the title exactly at the button edge (0 px gap, padding-right measured 54 px = right-1 + two 24 px buttons + the 2 px gap) and render clean ellipsis truncation in screenshots; 8/8 checks pass. The full running stack was not exercised in the working box (no Docker), so rc's ui CI and a manual look at the Starred section are the remaining confirmation.

- **Fix: a teammate who reads a plan or work session through a team, and a research run's collaborators, now hear its `conversation` event.** The event that refetches the tab bar's working read and the unread pills went only to a thread's owner and its named members. People the thread is shared with through a team, and a research thread's run owner, members and teams, could read it but never got the event, so their glyph and pill waited for the 30-second idle poll. The event's audience is now everyone the read gates admit, the people the list, the unread badge and `/api/working` count. A chat with a stray membership row now rings only its owner, because the read gates never admitted that member. The reply's start event (#673) reaches the same people once it lands.
  Verified: `bun run gate`. Live-DB tests run the real fan against a captured publish edge. A plan shared only through a team reaches its owner and the teammate. A research thread reaches its owner and the run's collaborator. An outsider hears neither, and a chat with a stray membership row reaches its owner alone. For every person on every membership path, the read gate and the fan agree. The first three tests fail against rc's audience query. The read gates keep rc's predicate. The audience is a union over the same membership paths, and a live test holds the two to one answer. On 10k users and 50k conversations the audience reads in under 0.5 ms (a first cut that scanned every user took 250 to 390 ms). Lists and gates plan exactly as on rc: two cuts that rendered the read predicate from the audience's paths made a list over a large shared team 170 to 1,000 times slower. On a worktree stack with this change, #673 and #669 merged, a teammate who reaches an admin's plan only through a team watched three real turns from Comms. Each time the Work glyph and the "1 working" readout lit 26 to 50 ms after the reply started, and went dark about 150 ms after it ended.

- **Fixed: in Talaria Desktop, links that open a new window now go somewhere, and an instance page can be reloaded.** Before this, a `target="_blank"` link or a `window.open` inside an instance did nothing on every OS: wry drops a new-window request when the shell installs no handler, and none was installed. That covered a Google Drive file, a GitHub settings page, a web source in chat, the coding-harness sign-in link and the MCP Connect button. Now an http(s) link opens in the default browser, whether it points at another site or at a page of the instance (a public artifact). The one exception is the MCP connect (`/api/mcp/oauth/start`): it opens as an in-app window that keeps the instance's session and `window.opener`, which the connect needs to sign in and report back, and on Linux that window closes when the connect finishes. A `mailto:`, `tel:` or `sms:` link goes to the OS only when the person clicks it in the instance's own page; on Linux a clicked `mailto:` did nothing before. The shell's own click script, in the page's main frame, catches that click. Neither a navigation, nor a script, nor an artifact's sandboxed frame can reach the OS. Every other scheme is refused and logged, as are `file:`, `javascript:` and `data:` windows. An app link's https form, such as a Zoom or Teams join link, goes to the browser, which asks before it opens the app. A page gets at most one hand-off a second, so a script cannot flood the browser with tabs. The hand-off goes through `tauri-plugin-opener`'s `open_url` on a background thread; the plugin is not registered, so no page gets an opener command. Reload had no way in at all. Ctrl+R and F5 on Windows and Linux, and Cmd+R on macOS, now reload any instance page; add Shift (or press Ctrl+F5) to skip the cache. The keys are the shell's own script, so they also work on a page whose Talaria UI never loaded, such as a gateway's 502 page. The in-app instance switcher has **Reload page** with its shortcut, and on macOS the menu bar has **View → Reload Page** and **Reload Ignoring Cache**.
  Verified: on a private headless rig (its own mutter, session bus and two fake instances), with real clicks and key presses through mutter's RemoteDesktop. Every launcher the opener tries was replaced by a shim that records its arguments and opens nothing. On rc's build, every link class did nothing: no shim call, no request, the page unchanged, and the Connect popup's `window.open` returned null. No key reloaded anything, and `desktop_reload` did not exist. On this build, three cross-origin links (`target="_blank"`, `window.open` and `window.open(…, 'noopener,noreferrer')`) each reached `xdg-open` with their URL, and the instance page stayed. A clicked in-place `mailto:`, a clicked `target="_blank"` `mailto:` and a clicked `tel:` each reached `xdg-open`. An in-place `zoommtg:`, and `javascript:`, `data:`, `ms-msdt:` and `file:` windows, opened nothing and were logged as refused. A same-origin `target="_blank"` page went to the browser. The MCP-style connect ran its whole round trip with the instance's session cookie: own origin, another origin's authorize hop, then the callback's `postMessage` to the opener, which received it; its window then closed, where before the window fix the empty window stayed until Talaria quit. Ctrl+R, F5 and the switcher's command each reloaded the page, Ctrl+Shift+R, Shift+F5 and Ctrl+F5 reloaded it with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, and Super+R and Ctrl+Alt+R did nothing. On a 502 page from the instance's origin, F5, Ctrl+R and Ctrl+Shift+R reloaded it; on another origin's 502 page, which has no grant, F5 reloaded it through the page's own fallback. `scripts/desktop-reload-keys.mjs` and `scripts/desktop-os-links.mjs` (both in `bun run check`) run the shell's two scripts against stub windows and catch mutations of each: the click script takes only a trusted, primary-button click on a `mailto:`, `tel:` or `sms:` link the page did not handle. Rust tests show that no scheme reaches the OS from either handler (mailto, IDE, Office, Java Web Start, installer, meeting-client and share schemes), that only the connect path stays in the app, and that a burst of hand-offs from one webview is cut to one a second. `bun run check` passes, including the webview-threading rule, and desktop fmt, clippy `-D warnings` and the tests pass in the rig image. Not verified on Windows or macOS at run time: the WebView2 and WKWebView popups, the hand-off through ShellExecute and `open`, the macOS View menu, and macOS's cache-skipping reload. On macOS a self-closing popup's window likely stays open until closed by hand. Also not verified: an installed release build, an AppImage's environment reaching the browser it launches, and a real MCP provider's sign-in.

- **In Talaria Desktop with the themed titlebar, the tab bar is the window's titlebar: it holds the minimize, maximize and close buttons, and dragging its empty space moves the window.** The separate 36px band above it is gone, so every view starts 36px higher. The controls sit at the bar's left on macOS, before the mark, and at its right after the account chip everywhere else. A double-click on empty bar space maximizes the window; a press on a tab, a tile, any other control or an open search panel does only what it does in a browser. Sign-in and the wait for the session have no tab bar and keep the band. A browser, and the OS titlebar setting, show the bar unchanged.
  Verified: `bun run gate` (svelte-check 0 errors, the ui suite), and `bun run test -- titlebar` (empty bar space drags and maximizes; a press inside a link or a button, on the search panel that drops below the bar, a right-click, the OS titlebar setting and a browser do not). In the running app in a browser, the bar on `/work` is pixel-identical to rc's. With the desktop shell stubbed in the browser (no real window), real clicks on empty bar space drag and double-clicks maximize, clicks on tiles, the bell, the window buttons and the open search panel never drag, the controls sit at the right or, under a macOS user agent, at the left before the mark, everything stays on screen at 600px, the OS titlebar setting shows no controls, `/login` keeps its band, and the view starts at 56px instead of 92px. The desktop app itself needs a display and is checked on the operator's host.

- **A document's version history shows every change, an agent's included, and nothing an agent saves can be overwritten by a person's open editor without them knowing.** The **Version history** panel (the ⋯ menu on a KB doc, a space or a file) lists every revision with who saved it (an agent by its name) and when. Opening one shows a **Changes** diff against the version before it, the **Version** itself, and **Restore**. Restore is shown only to people who can edit, and a restore that fails says why in the dialog, which stays open. Files no longer restore on a single click. A document or page open in Read follows the server, so an agent's edit appears without a reload and without any banner. When an agent (or another person) saves a document while you have it open in Edit, your next save is refused instead of replacing their work: one line appears at that moment, "Not saved: this document changed while you were editing", with **Review in version history** and **Keep mine**. A change that only moved the document's metadata (an icon, a move, a promote) never shows the line, and someone else's rename is never undone by your save. What you type after a refusal is kept: leaving the document (another doc, a link, Back, closing the tab, or switching the Work view's file pane to comments) asks first, and the edits stay on this device and are offered back, with **Keep mine** and **Discard**, the next time you open the document. Reading a document and accepting a Muse draft written before an agent changed it is refused the same way, and the draft comes back. Accepting a Muse draft folds into a one-line receipt of what changed (±lines), and the Draft button pulses while Muse writes. On the API, `PUT /api/kb/docs/{id}` and `PUT /api/artifacts/{id}` take `baseUpdatedAt`: the title and body land in one conditional update, or the route answers 409 with the current document. Their GETs answer `canEdit`.
  Verified: `bun run gate`. Ui tests: `save-base.svelte.test.ts` (a refused stale save, Keep mine, a metadata-only retry, ordered saves, a reseed during an in-flight save that must not let the next save through, renames on both sides) and `held-edit.svelte.test.ts` (kept while refused, taken from the live editor as it unmounts, offered on reopen, dropped once decided or already in the document, storage that refuses access). `revisions.svelte.test.ts` covers the read follower. Live route tests (`api/tests/it/doc_save_base_live.rs`, real router and database) check, for files and KB docs, that a stale base gets 409 with the row while the agent's text stays, that a rename over a moved row is refused, that a save with nothing to overwrite lands, that title and body land together, that no base still replaces, that a malformed base gets 400, that a non-editor gets 403 rather than 409, and that `canEdit` agrees with the PUT. In the running app (headless Chromium, an agent key on the toolkit's save routes):
  - Leaving Edit while idle after an agent edit sent no save and showed no line, for a KB doc and a file.
  - A refused buffer survived every exit. A tree click, a breadcrumb and Back each asked first (Cancel stayed with the buffer). Closing the tab asked, and leaving anyway kept the last words through pagehide. A Files sidebar place asked. The Files header crumb, which never reaches the router, kept the buffer as the editor unmounted. The Work view's comments-and-back kept the person's words on screen. Each kept edit was offered on reopen, Keep mine saved it, and Discard dropped it.
  - A quick Read then Edit lost nothing. An agent's rename survived the person's save (a 409, then a silent retry that landed).
  - A failed restore said so in the open dialog. A viewer got no Restore button.
  - A read-mode Muse draft written before an agent edit was refused and came back, and a fresh draft accepted. Muse output was stubbed, since this stack has no model.
  - A page's Discard stopped its pending save.

- **A ticket moves between boards — for people from the ticket and the card menu, and for agents through `move_ticket`.** `POST /api/tasks/{id}/move { boardId, status?, preview? }` re-keys the ticket on the destination's counter and keeps its old ref resolving (`task_ref_aliases`, so `PLAT-118` in a doc or an agent's memory still opens it). The column maps by the caller's choice, else the same name, else the same category, else the destination's intake — and a move never closes an open ticket. Labels the destination lacks are dropped, never created there; a person or agent who is not on the destination is unassigned; a sub-task leaves its parent behind; a reviewer's sign-off does not travel; watchers who cannot see the destination go dormant. Each is named in the answer's `moved`, on the ticket's activity line, and in the audit log (`task.board_move`). A person needs edit rights on both boards. An agent needs board policy on both and keeps its HITL stops: no closed ticket, no ticket in review or blocked, never into a closed column or a pickup column it was not already in. A live work session, a workchain step, or a ticket with sub-tasks refuses with 409. Both boards' views update live; the ticket and its comments are re-indexed under the new board; the destination's watchers, assignees and creator are told, nobody else. Old `/boards/<old>/<ticket>` links follow the ticket to its new board. The "Move to board…" dialog previews what changes before the move.
  Verified: `bun run gate`; `cargo test -p talaria-tasks moving` (the status, label and summary mappings: name → category → intake, never a closed column for an open ticket, an agent never into a closed or pickup column and never out of review or blocked), the sandbox and chips tests, `bun run test -- ticket-move`, and four live-DB tests (`task_move_live::` — the permission matrix for people and agents, the done refusals, the re-key with the old ref resolving, the work-session hold). In the running app on a worktree stack: a person moved PLAT-1 from Platform to Support Desk (renamed columns, different labels) through Move to board…; the dialog said PLAT-1 → SUP-2, In Progress by name, `urgent` dropped, Bo unassigned and his watch going quiet, and offered no Shipped column; the ticket landed as SUP-2 with `Billing` kept, the source board's open tab lost the card and the destination's gained it without a reload, the old /boards/<Platform>/<ticket> link followed it to Support Desk, and the activity line named both refs and what was dropped. An agent with its own key, through the real toolkit over stdio, saw move_ticket in tools/list, previewed and moved PLAT-2 → SUP-1, and was refused for a board it is not on and for `shipped` and `cancelled`; GET /api/tasks/PLAT-2 opens SUP-1 for the person and the agent. The 400s (a done column for an open ticket, a key the board lacks) and 409s (a sub-task parent, a live work session) answered as designed, a sub-task moved without its parent, the audit log carried `task.board_move`, and only the destination's creator was notified (not the mover, not the watcher who cannot see it).

- **A screen reader names the open tab by its view alone: "Inbox", not "Inbox 1", and "Tab Probe", not "⬡ Tab Probe".** The open tab in the tab bar had no `aria-label`, so its badge count (or `!` for an unread count that could not be read) and an app's glyph were read as part of its name. The other tiles, and the old dock's active tile, were already named by their label.
  Verified: `bun run gate`. In the running app as admin, the open tab's `aria-label` reads "Inbox" on /home with an unread badge of 1, and "Tab Probe" on an enabled app's view, where the accessibility tree lists `link "Tab Probe"`.

- **Fixed: the guard that keeps a server release off GitHub's "Latest" now also requires the desktop feed flip to run only on the mint path, and the macOS installer smoke can no longer hang the release on an app that ignores SIGTERM.** #661's review found two gaps. First, `scripts/release-latest.mjs` checked that desktop-package.yml's `gh release edit --latest` came after the `latest.json` upload, but not that it ran only for a minted `desktop-v` release. `attach` also runs for release.yml's `vX.Y.Z` tags, so dropping `if [ "$MINT" = true ]` would have kept `bun run check` green and made the stable server release Latest. The flip must now sit in the `then` branch of a shell `if` that tests `"$MINT" = true` (an `&&` is fine, an `||` is not), or under a step `if:` on `needs.resolve.outputs.mint`, and its step must bind `MINT` to that output. Second, the macOS step stopped the 20 s run with `kill` and then waited for it with no limit, so an app that ignored SIGTERM would have held the job until its 60-minute timeout. It now polls with `kill -0` for up to 10 s, then sends SIGKILL. Every installer smoke step also gets a step timeout (5 to 15 minutes), which bounds the older `Start-Process -Wait` waits on Windows as well. The Linux step's comment no longer claims the deb's Depends are proved to resolve on a stock Ubuntu: the build's own -dev packages already satisfy them.

  Verified: `release-latest.mjs`'s self-test has 8 new fixtures, and it fails on each of these: a flip with its `MINT` guard removed, a flip in the guard's `else` branch, a flip guarded by another test, one guarded by an `||` test, a step that sets `MINT: 'true'`, and an unguarded flip after an unrelated `if … fi`. It passes an `&&` guard and a step-level mint `if:`. On the real desktop-package.yml, `check-invariants.mjs` passes. It fails and names line 916 when the real `if [ "$MINT" = true ]` is removed, and line 917 when the step sets `MINT: 'true'`. The kill sequence, run against a process that traps SIGTERM, ends it in 12 s, and a process that honours SIGTERM goes at once. desktop-package.yml parses (Bun's YAML), every bash step passes `bash -n`, and the five step timeouts land on the intended steps.

- **A local build of the api's integration tests compiles again: the rustc wrapper runs on bash, so `CARGO_BIN_EXE_talaria-api` reaches rustc.**
  `scripts/rustc-wrapper.sh`, the `RUSTC_WRAPPER` the root `mise.toml` sets, was a
  `#!/bin/sh` script. On Debian and Ubuntu that is dash, which drops every
  environment variable whose name is not a shell identifier before it execs.
  Cargo names `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<bin>` after the bin, hyphen included, so
  `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_talaria-api")` in `api/tests/it/code_probe_child.rs` failed
  to compile in every mise-activated checkout, and `bun run gate` went red on
  untouched `rc` for any diff that selects `talaria-api`. CI sets no wrapper, so
  its api job stayed green. The wrapper now runs on bash, which passes such names
  through. `scripts/rustc-wrapper.test.mjs` runs the wrapper by its own shebang
  and checks that a hyphenated `CARGO_BIN_EXE_*` reaches rustc. Verified: that
  check failed before the change and passes after it, `cargo test -p talaria-api
  --test it --no-run` exited 101 on `rc` at `1759fe9e` and exits 0 with the fix,
  and `bun run gate` passes with a whitespace edit in `talaria-conversations`.

- **A Backblaze B2 (or AWS S3) bucket now works as the storage target or the replica — every request was refused.** The S3 signature's `x-amz-date` carried milliseconds (`20261103T173649.020Z`). The built-in bucket let that through, but strict S3 services answer 400 `InvalidRequest`: "Timestamp … is invalid, must be in ISO 8601 format yyyyMMddThhmmssZ". So a replica sync, or a test of the connection, failed on its first PUT. The timestamp is now whole seconds (`20261103T173649Z`), the same instant the signature's scope names. Creating the bucket, reading an object back and deleting one signed with the same timestamp, and are fixed with it.
  Verified: `cargo test -p talaria-storage --lib` — the date vectors (the epoch, a leap day, and the reported instant, with its milliseconds dropped rather than rounded) and AWS's own SigV4 GET example signature. Not verified: a live request against Backblaze B2, since no account was available here.

- **Fixed: a stable server release no longer takes GitHub's "Latest" flag from the desktop updater feed, and the release pipeline now proves each shipped desktop build can open an instance.** The desktop updater reads `/releases/latest/download/latest.json`, so GitHub's Latest release is the feed, and today that is `desktop-v0.11.0`. `release.yml` opened a stable `vX.Y.Z` release with no Latest flag, and GitHub makes a new release Latest by default. The first stable tag would have moved the feed to a release with no `latest.json` until its installers were attached (and with none at all if a desktop job failed), and every installed app's update check would have answered 404. `release.yml` now creates and edits every `v*` release with `--latest=false`. `desktop-package.yml` creates its `desktop-vX.Y.0` mint with `--latest=false` and marks it Latest explicitly (`gh release edit --latest`), after its `latest.json` is uploaded. Before, GitHub's default made the mint Latest when it was created, so the feed also 404'd while its assets uploaded. `bun run check` holds both flags (`release-latest-is-the-desktop-feed`, `scripts/release-latest.mjs`): it fails on a dropped `--latest=false`, a mint left to GitHub's default, a Latest flip before the `latest.json` upload, or any other workflow marking a release Latest. RELEASING.md, the cut-release skill and docs/DESKTOP.md say that the server release is never Latest. `desktop-package.yml`'s installer smoke only asked whether the app was still running after 20 s, which a frozen app passes. It now runs the connect smoke (`desktop/packaging/connect-smoke.mjs`) on what ships: the exe the Windows installer put on the runner, the binary inside the macOS `.app`, and the binary the Linux deb installed. A release build that cannot open an instance now fails before anything is attached. CI gets three changes. The e2e job now runs on any crate under `api/crates/`, since the api binary it boots depends on all 243 of them; shared crates such as `talaria-db` and `talaria-state` used to skip it. The migrations job runs the compensating git-hosts statements (#651) on the fresh and the upgraded database, not only applies them. `scripts/gate.mjs` runs the ui suite for the same files ci.yml's ui surface lists, and its self-test fails when the two lists differ. The release docs no longer say the notes link is pinned to the tag (it is `blob/main/CHANGELOG.md`). They now say what a stable rolls under (its own version) and what to do when the roll refuses on an empty `changelog/` right after an RC: skip it.

  Verified: gh 2.102.0 was pointed at a local fake GitHub API (a throwaway TLS cert, nothing sent to GitHub). release.yml's create and edit commands sent `make_latest: "false"`, for the stable and the RC alike. The desktop mint sent `"false"` and the feed flip `"true"`. A create with no flag sent no `make_latest`, which GitHub reads as Latest. With each flag dropped from the real workflow files in turn, `check-invariants.mjs` failed and named the line: the edit, the create, the mint, the flip, and the flip moved above the `latest.json` upload. Its self-test covers 12 fixtures. desktop-package.yml cannot run from a pull request, so it was read, parsed, and its bash steps passed `bash -n`. connect-smoke.mjs was run as the new steps call it, against a stand-in shell at a path with spaces. It refused an existing registry without `--force`, passed with `--force`, named the hang when the page was never requested, failed a crash right after the open, and stopped on an empty `INSTALLED_EXE`. The mirror check ran on two throwaway postgres:16 containers: a fresh replay (537 statements) and main's array (459) with a connected GitHub seeded, then this branch's. It passed on both and left the data unchanged; the replay afterwards applied 0. It failed, naming what it saw, for each of nine breakages: a dropped default on `workbench_jobs` or `workbench_repo_flow`, either trigger dropped, the delete branch gone, the setting trigger on UPDATE only, the copy-back missing, the setting drifted from the row, and a baseline that differs from the seed. The two new `removeArtifact` tests use stand-in `docker` and `git`. They pass under bun and node, and each fails when its re-check `if` is removed from a copy of the sweep. ci.yml's `changes` matcher, extracted and run on single files: `talaria-db`, `talaria-state`, `talaria-kb`, `api/.cargo/config.toml` and `api/rust-toolchain.toml` now run e2e, and `api/tests/` and `api/package.Dockerfile` still do not. The gate's self-test fails with one ui entry removed.

- **New: a tab shows a waiting mark in place of its icon while an agent is working in that view, and an "N working" readout at the head of the bar's right cluster counts the other views with an agent at work and links to the first of them.** Only Comms, Work and Boards can light, each from its arm of `/api/working`; Inbox, Knowledge, Files and app tabs never do, and a failed read shows no mark and no readout. `/plan` and `/research` count as the open Work view. The marks are core's waiting set, dealt per session like every other waiting mark: a new `tab` slot admits only a single braille cell that keeps above its bottom dot row, or one of the four dot grids that change the fewest dots a frame, so a mark stays inside its tile; it draws at 6 frames a second, woken on the frame its tick falls in, because the bar is on every page. While the lead view's own tab mark is on screen the readout's copy holds still. The readout grows "working" from a medium bar and the lead's title from a wide one. Icon and mark crossfade in place; reduced motion fades only.
  Verified: `bun run gate`. `bun run test -- waiting` asserts every state dealt to a tab site over 500 seeds is one cell wide and never lights dot 7 or 8 (it fails with orbit, scan and snake let back in), both families are dealt, only the named grids reach a tab, and tab sites draw at the slower cadence; `tab-working.test.ts` covers the arm map, the readout's count and lead, the legacy Work addresses and a failed read. On a worktree stack with real agent turns (and the turn-start event from the companion api change): Comms lit 40 ms after a chat was sent and cleared on its end; two views read "2 working" with the lead's title at 1440 px and mark plus count at 420 px with every control on screen; the open view showed its mark and left the count; the readout's click landed on the lead; a member saw the same with no gear; reduced motion played opacity-only keyframes; two idle minutes drew nothing. In headless Chrome with `/api/working` answered in the page (a ranking harness, not the real-agent check), four lit marks added 1.23 points of main-thread time over an idle bar on Knowledge, 1.52 on Work and 1.51 on Comms, five rounds each, against 1.82, 2.18 and 2.16 at 8 frames a second.

- **The top bar is a tab bar now: the view you are in is drawn as a tab cut from the page, with its icon and name, and every other view is a small icon tile.** The open tab takes the page's colour and breaks the bar's bottom hairline, curving out at its feet into the page. The tiles, their badges and tooltips, who sees which tile, the gear for Manage, the account chip lighting on Settings and Admin, and the right cluster's controls and order are unchanged. The mark is larger, and the TALARIA wordmark shows beside it when the bar is wide. On a narrow window the strip of tabs scrolls sideways, a short fade at its right edge says there is more, the open tab is scrolled into view, and the right cluster stays on screen.
  Verified: `bun run gate` (svelte-check 0 errors, the ui suite), and `bun run test -- tab-strip` (the fade is set while tabs remain to the right and cleared at the end of the scroll; the open tab is scrolled into view). In the running app, against rc on a second stack with the same data: every tile and the gear land on the same route as before and light the clicked item; as admin at 1440px and 420px, as a member with no manage grants (no gear), and as a member denied /boards (no Boards tile); Settings lights the account chip and Manage the gear with no tab open; an enabled app's tile follows the core tiles and opens as a tab; every control in the bar takes keyboard focus with a visible ring and the open tab carries `aria-current="page"`; the open tab matches the page colour in the dark and light themes; at 420px the open tab reaches the bar's edge and stays in view on every view. Click to next paint over 20 tile clicks: 71.9 ms median against rc's 77.3 ms.

- **Clicking a tile in the tab bar lifts the new tab and its view up out of the bar.** The tab rises 8px from 92% scale, the view rises 12px out of a 3px blur 40ms behind it, and the old view keeps rising 8px as it fades, all on one 280ms quint ease-out (160ms for the exit). It plays only on a tile click: a deep link, the back button or a link inside a view switches with no motion, and a click mid-switch starts the next one cleanly. Under reduced motion it is a 150ms opacity crossfade. Pressing a tile now dips it to 97% for 150ms (no dip under reduced motion). The fading copy of the old view keeps its scroll position and never loads a video or an app's iframe a second time.
  Verified: `bun run gate`, and `bun run test -- tab-motion` (reduced motion is opacity-only keyframes at 150ms; a click lifts only once its tile opens, also through a redirect inside its route; a back or deep-link change, a modified click, and a click overtaken by a route change elsewhere do not lift). In the running app, against rc on the same stack and data: Work to Boards lifts at head and switches with no motion on rc; five clicks 60ms apart end on the last one with no leftover copy; back, forward and a deep link play nothing; reduced motion is opacity only; at 420px the copy stays inside the viewport; a member with no grants gets the lift and no gear; a scrolled Boards column keeps its offset in the fading copy and the arriving view's scroll matches rc; a video in the old view is fetched once. Click to first paint over 20 switches: 9.4 ms median against rc's 9.5 ms, and 3.45 long frames per switch against rc's 3.40.

- **Cloud usage that a provider publishes a price for is now priced automatically, history included. An admin can fix the rest from Observability → Cost.** Two problems had left "Unpriced cloud usage" firing on every instance with no way to clear it:
  - **OpenRouter agent turns were never priced.** The priced view refused OpenRouter's own `/models` price for any call that did not name its serving endpoint. On main, every agent turn's ledger row is one of those calls.
  - **No price could be set.** The alert sent admins to `/models`, where pricing is read-only.

  Now, in order of precedence:
  - The provider's own charge comes first.
  - An admin can mark a model **included in a plan** (priced at $0, labelled `included`, never a silent zero). This beats a published price, which matters for a Z.ai Coding Plan, whose GLM ids all match OpenRouter's pay-as-you-go entries.
  - Next is the published price: the serving endpoint's when the call names one, otherwise the model's, OpenRouter included.
  - Last is an admin's **manual rate**, per 1M input, output, cache-write and cache-read tokens. It applies only until a source publishes a price.

  Other changes:
  - Cache tokens bill at the catalog's own published cache rates when it has them.
  - No row ever prices below $0, and no price that is not a finite number counts. OpenRouter publishes `"-1"` for its router models (`openrouter/auto`, `openrouter/fusion`, `nvidia/switchyard` and others), meaning the price is variable. The price check refuses that number and records those models as **variable price**, and calls that carry OpenRouter's own charge are still priced. The priced view reads no negative, NaN or infinite rate from any source and floors token counts at zero. A migration deletes any negative rows an earlier price pass stored.
  - The price check now also matches OpenAI's `-YYYY-MM-DD` snapshot ids, older `-MMDD` ids such as `gpt-4-0613`, and Fireworks-style path ids. An id whose base model the live catalog no longer lists, such as xAI's `grok-4-0709`, stays unpriced.
  - The price check records why each model has no price: no published price (and the ids it tried), the source didn't answer (quoting its error and every cause under it), or not looked up yet.
  - The new admin-only **Unpriced models** panel lists each model with its endpoint, tokens and reason, and offers **Set price**, **Included in a plan** and **Retry lookup**.
  - Pricing is read-time, so each fix re-prices that model's past calls, and the alert clears for history. The alert now goes to admins only and links to the panel.
  - The endpoint editor shows the admin's settings beside the published prices.

  New API: `GET /api/cost/unpriced`, `PUT`/`DELETE /api/cost/prices`, `POST /api/cost/unpriced/lookup`, all admin-only.

  **Upgrade note: USD budgets start binding.** On main, OpenRouter agent turns counted as $0, so an org or per-agent dollar ceiling never bound on them. After the upgrade, every row inside the budget window re-prices at once (24 hours by default, up to 365 days), and new calls carry OpenRouter's own charge. An agent whose real spend is already over its ceiling is refused with `429 budget_exceeded` on its first call after the deploy. Review the USD ceilings under **Admin → Security → LLM budgets** before upgrading, or right after.

  Verified:
  - `bun run gate`.
  - `cargo test -p talaria-price-oracle -p talaria-gateway -p talaria-alerts -p talaria-routes-comms --lib`, which covers id matching against ids taken from the live OpenRouter catalog, the price decision, and the reasons.
  - The `#[ignore]` live tests against a migrated Postgres:
    - history re-prices when a manual price lands, then a published price takes over;
    - included is $0 and labelled, and beats a published price but not the provider's charge;
    - OpenRouter rows without a serving variant are priced, both main's per-turn shape and rc's cut-off stream;
    - the SQL agrees with `price_basis` on nine cases;
    - a failed source's error is quoted as the reason;
    - the alert clears when a price lands.
  - The ui tests for the panel's helpers.
  - On a worktree stack, real gateway calls on a Z.ai Coding Plan endpoint, plus OpenRouter and OpenAI rows in the ledger's own shapes. With the catalog first blocked by a proxy, then reachable, each one was seen unpriced with its reason and fixed all three ways in the running app: retry, included and manual, plus the endpoint editor's plan checklist. Unpriced tokens went from 154,572 to 0, the alert cleared, members got 403s, and every write was audited.

  Also verified for the variable prices: the live catalog's `-1` entries are never priced; five `openrouter/auto` rows on a stored `-1` price come out unpriced at $0 in the budget read; a property test over every combination of sources, including negative, NaN and infinite rates and negative token counts, finds no cost below zero; and on a worktree stack an org USD budget of $0.01 refused a real gateway call once the router rows stopped counting negative.

  Not verified: a live OpenRouter or OpenAI key (none was available), and a client instance's own data.

- **A price that was only guessed now says so, and an admin can override it. Catalog matches that would misprice are withheld.** These are follow-ups to the #682 review.
  - **Fuzzy matches:**
    - Every catalog price records the entry it came from, and whether the model's own id found it (exact) or a stripped tag, date or path segment did (fuzzy).
    - A manual rate now beats a fuzzy match, but not an exact one.
    - The new **Priced by a fuzzy match** list and the cost page's legend show "priced as … (fuzzy match)".
  - **Withheld matches:**
    - A dated snapshot the catalog lacks no longer borrows its alias's price when the catalog prices that alias's listed snapshots differently (`gpt-4o-2024-05-13` costs twice `gpt-4o`).
    - On OpenRouter, an `:online` or `:nitro` id with no catalog entry of its own stays unpriced, with the reason, instead of taking the base model's rate.
    - Another host's model matched only by its last path segment (`accounts/fireworks/models/gpt-oss-120b`) is no longer priced at OpenRouter's rate. It is offered as a suggestion the admin can accept.
  - **Path ids:** a dated path id now tries its own dated last segment before the undated one, so `…/deepseek-r1-0528` reaches `deepseek/deepseek-r1-0528`.
  - **"Included" labels:** the By agent list and a ticket's spend say "included" instead of a bare $0.
  - **Smaller fixes:**
    - The spend tile says how much of the month is estimated from published prices.
    - A manual $0 / $0 is refused in favour of "included".
    - Rows with no model id no longer offer fixes the api refuses.
    - Ticking a model "included" on the endpoint editor confirms before it replaces a manual rate.
    - Price changes are audited with the value they replaced, and retries are audited too.
    - The one-row read after a retry no longer scans the whole window.

  Verified:
  - `bun run gate`.
  - `cargo test -p talaria-price-oracle -p talaria-gateway -p talaria-routes-comms --lib`, covering:
    - the dated path chain;
    - exact versus alias kinds;
    - the snapshot-disagreement rule on the live catalog's `gpt-4o` pair;
    - OpenRouter `:online` / `:nitro` against a listed `:free`;
    - the last-segment suggestion;
    - `price_basis` with fuzzy rows;
    - the 0/0 refusal.
  - `#[ignore]` live tests against a migrated Postgres:
    - manual beats an alias match but not an exact one, and the fuzzy list names the entry;
    - a suggestion is offered, never applied, and is cleared by a later lookup;
    - the 1,296-case property test now covers fuzzy rows and finds no negative cost.
  - ui tests for the new labels and bodies; `svelte-check`.
  - On the worktree stack: real catalog lookups for the withheld and suggested shapes, the panel's suggestion and fuzzy rows, and the By agent label.

- **A new worktree starts with its Rust build cache seeded, not empty, and a finished worktree's cache is the first thing `talaria cleanup` reclaims.** `bun talaria worktree` reflink-copies the registry crates' build units into the new `api/target` from the idle checkout whose `Cargo.lock` matches best (`--desktop` seeds the desktop target too, `--no-seed` starts empty, `--seed-from` names the source; `bun talaria seed-target` does it for the checkout you stand in). Nothing of a workspace crate is copied, so every workspace crate builds from the new tree's own sources. Copying a whole target passed another worktree's crates off as this one's, because a path crate's unit hash is relative to the workspace and its freshness is an mtime test. A target a cargo is building in is never read: its locks are checked in `/proc/locks` and the copy runs under shared flocks. A filesystem without reflink gets a cold build, never a byte copy or a hard link. `bun talaria cleanup` now lists the build dirs of every linked checkout, including agent worktrees whose branch was renamed (known by `TALARIA_WORKTREE` in `ui/.env`), which it could not see before. `--apply` drops a cache whose pull request merged or closed at the checkout's HEAD. With the disk over the 85% line, it also drops idle caches of clean, pushed trees, unseeded and least recently used first. It drops at most three per run, and stops once `statfs` says the disk is under the line or a drop frees less than 512 MiB. It never takes one with a cargo lock held, one built in within the hour, one with a running stack, or one a `.talaria-keep` holds. A dirty, unpushed or kept tree is flagged for a human. A cache is renamed aside, checked again, then deleted, and a merged worktree's checkout gets the same lock check before it goes. On btrfs, or anywhere `/proc/locks` cannot be read, nothing is deleted. The stop gate removes no cache and makes no extra `gh` call.
  Verified: on the dev host (XFS, reflink=1), `cargo test -p talaria-boards --no-run` in a fresh rc worktree compiled 245 units in 15 min cold (sccache warm), and in a seeded one compiled 21 units, all workspace crates and no registry crate, in 43 s. Seeding took 0.3 s and moved `df` by nothing measurable, while `du` read 987 MiB. Correctness: in the seeded worktree a constant was changed (`role_rank("owner")` 3 → 7) with a test asserting 7, and its source mtime was set back to before the source tree's build, which is the condition the trap needs. The test ran and passed. The same change in a tree given a whole `cp -a --reflink` copy did not compile it (see the PR). A shared `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` between two copies of a scratch workspace ran the other copy's binary (`ANSWER=1` from sources saying 2), and a second cargo on it blocked for the first one's whole build. `bun run check`, cli `bun test` (482 pass, the reflink path run for real on XFS and the fallback on tmpfs), `tsc --noEmit`, and `scripts/cleanup-sweep.test.mjs` (76 checks; the rename-and-recheck and the merged-worktree refusal run against a real `flock -x` holder).

- **The docs and messages point to LLM budgets where they are: Admin → Security → LLM budgets.** The budget ceilings have always been set on the Admin **Security** tab, in the Settings panel's "LLM budgets" section. There is no Settings tab. The places that said "Admin → Settings" now name that path. In the docs: `docs/user/admin-models.md`, `docs/user/admin-mcp-observability-apps.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/sdk/harnesses.md`, the shipped `talaria-apps` skill's harness reference, and the unreleased #682 and app-gateway changelog entries.
